sections.title: Plane Shapes: Types, Properties, Similarities and Differences

blocks.text: Plane shapes are shapes that lie flat on a surface, so they are called **two-dimensional (2-D) shapes**. The family includes the triangle, square, rectangle, parallelogram, trapezium, circle, and other polygons. A **polygon** is any closed shape that has three or more straight sides. Polygons are named by their number of sides, and their properties show how they are similar to and different from one another.

Look at the three triangles in **fig-01**: isosceles, scalene, and equilateral.

- **Isosceles triangle:** two adjacent sides are equal, marked with a single tick on the two slanted sides. Its base angles are equal, and it has one line of symmetry.
- **Scalene triangle:** no two sides are equal, so no two angles are equal. It has no line of symmetry.
- **Equilateral triangle:** all three sides are equal, marked with a single tick on each side. All three angles are equal, every angle measuring 60°, and it has three lines of symmetry.

The key point for telling them apart is the number of equal sides: equilateral has 3, isosceles has 2, scalene has 0.

blocks.caption: Isosceles: a single tick on each of the two slanted sides, an arc at each base angle. Scalene: one, two and three ticks on the three sides, an arc at each vertex. Equilateral: a single tick on each of the three sides, an arc at each vertex.

blocks.text:
Now compare the **square** and the **rectangle** in **fig-02**. Both have a right-angle mark at each corner, so all four angles are 90°, and both have two pairs of parallel sides.

- **Square:** all four sides are equal, it has four lines of symmetry, and its diagonals bisect each other at a right angle.
- **Rectangle:** opposite sides are equal, it has two lines of symmetry, and its diagonals bisect each other but not at a right angle.

So the extra property of the square comes from having all sides equal.

blocks.caption: Square: a right-angle mark at each corner, a single tick on each of the four sides. Rectangle: a right-angle mark at each corner, a single tick on each of the two longer sides and a double tick on each of the two shorter sides.

blocks.text:
Finally compare the **parallelogram** and the **trapezium** in **fig-03**.

- **Parallelogram:** two pairs of opposite sides are equal and parallel, opposite angles are equal, it has no line of symmetry, and its diagonals divide it into equal triangles.
- **Trapezium:** only one pair of sides is parallel, opposite angles are not equal, it has no line of symmetry, and its diagonal divides it into two unequal triangles.

The main difference is the number of pairs of parallel sides: a parallelogram has two pairs, while a trapezium has only one pair.

blocks.caption: Parallelogram: a single arrow on each of the two horizontal sides, a double arrow on each of the two slanted sides. Trapezium: a single arrow on each of the two parallel sides, and one diagonal drawn in.

blocks.text:
Polygons are named by their number of sides. The table below lists the common polygons, their number of sides, and the number of triangles each can be divided into using the rule number of triangles = n - 2.

| Name of polygon | Number of sides | Number of triangles (n - 2) |
|---|---|---|
| Triangle | 3 | 1 |
| Quadrilateral | 4 | 2 |
| Pentagon | 5 | 3 |
| Hexagon | 6 | 4 |
| Heptagon | 7 | 5 |
| Octagon | 8 | 6 |
| Nonagon | 9 | 7 |
| Decagon | 10 | 8 |
| Hendecagon (or undecagon) | 11 | 9 |
| Dodecagon | 12 | 10 |

The pattern is simple: subtract 2 from the number of sides. A hexagon has 6 sides, so 6 - 2 = 4 triangles; a pentagon has 5 sides, so 5 - 2 = 3 triangles.

**Worked example — triangles in a polygon**

How many triangles can a **heptagon** be divided into?

**Solution.** A heptagon has 7 sides. Using the rule, number of triangles = 7 - 2 = 5. So a heptagon divides into **5 triangles**.

practice.prompt: A polygon can be divided into 9 triangles by drawing diagonals from one vertex to all the non-adjacent vertices. Name the polygon.
practice.worked_solution: Triangles = n - 2, so n = 9 + 2 = 11. The 11-sided polygon is a hendecagon or undecagon.

practice.prompt: Name the type of triangle that has no line of symmetry. Then state how many of its angles are equal.
practice.answer: A scalene triangle; none of its angles are equal.
practice.worked_solution: A scalene triangle has no equal sides, so it has no equal angles and no line of symmetry.

practice.prompt: A square and a rectangle both have right angles and two pairs of parallel sides. State two properties that belong to the square but not to the rectangle.
practice.answer: All four sides are equal, and it has four lines of symmetry. Its diagonals also bisect each other at a right angle.
practice.worked_solution: From the comparison: the square has all sides equal and four lines of symmetry, while the rectangle has only opposite sides equal and two lines of symmetry. The square's diagonals bisect at a right angle; the rectangle's do not.

practice.prompt: How does a single diagonal affect a parallelogram compared with a trapezium?
practice.answer: In a parallelogram, a diagonal divides it into two equal triangles. In a trapezium, a diagonal divides it into two unequal triangles.
practice.worked_solution: Directly from the property table: parallelogram — diagonals divide it into equal triangles; trapezium — a diagonal divides it into two unequal triangles.

practice.prompt: An octagon and a decagon are divided into triangles using the same rule. How many more triangles does the decagon form than the octagon?
practice.worked_solution: Decagon: 10 - 2 = 8 triangles. Octagon: 8 - 2 = 6 triangles. Difference: 8 - 6 = 2.

blocks.text:
A circle is a plane shape with no corners: every point on its boundary is the same distance from its centre. The curved line that forms the round boundary of the circle is its **circumference**. fig-04 shows two labelled circles so you can see each part sitting on a real circle.

- The **centre** is the point in the middle of the circle.
- The **radius** (plural *radii*) is any straight line joining the centre to the circumference. In the second circle of fig-04 a radius is drawn from the centre out to the circumference, and the right-hand bounding line of the sector below is also a radius.
- A **chord** is any straight line joining two points on the circumference. The second circle in fig-04 has a chord drawn near the top.
- The **diameter** is any chord that passes through the centre of the circle. In the first circle of fig-04 the diameter is drawn straight across through the centre. Because it goes through the centre, it is the longest chord a circle can have, and it is twice as long as the radius.
- An **arc** is a curved part of the circumference. In the first circle of fig-04 a part of the circumference is marked and named the arc.

The figure also shows three more parts:
- A **segment** is the region of the circle cut off by a chord — the shaded part above the chord in the second circle.
- A **sector** is the region bounded by two radii and the arc between them — the shaded part below in the second circle, whose two straight sides are both radii.
- A **tangent** is a straight line that touches the circle at exactly one point, as shown touching the right side of the second circle.

sections.title: Finding the Perimeter of Plane Shapes

blocks.text:
**Perimeter** is the distance all the way round a shape. For straight-sided shapes, add every outer side once — but take each length exactly as it is marked on the diagram. A common slip in trapezium perimeter problems is to use the correct method and still misread one side, for example copying an 8 cm base as 5 cm; the sum is then 3 cm short even though every side was added. Checking each number against the diagram prevents that.

For a circle, the perimeter has a special name, the **circumference**: $C = 2πr = πd$, using π ≈ 22/7 or 3.14. Equal or opposite sides make the work shorter: square $P = 4L$, rectangle $P = 2(L + b)$, parallelogram $P = 2(a + b)$, and a regular polygon with n sides each s has $P = ns$.

**Example 1 — a square.** In fig-05 each side is $L = 15$ cm. All four sides are equal, so

$P = 4L = 4(15) = 60$ cm.

**Example 2 — a rectangle.** In fig-06, $L = 10$ cm and $b = 7$ cm.

$P = 2L + 2b = 2(10 + 7) = 34$ cm.

**Example 3 — finding a missing breadth.** In fig-07, the rectangle has perimeter 60 cm and length 17 cm. Since $P = 2L + 2b$,

$60 = 2(17) + 2b = 34 + 2b$

so $60 - 34 = 2b$, giving $2b = 26$ and $b = 13$ cm.

blocks.caption: A rectangle with both long sides marked $L = 17$cm and both short sides marked $b$.
A rectangle with both long sides marked $L$, the top one also 10cm, and both short sides marked $b$, the right-hand one also 7cm.
A square, named *Square* at its left, with all four sides marked twice — $L$ and 15cm.

blocks.text:
**Example 4 — a trapezium.** In fig-08 the four sides are 11 cm, 9 cm, 5 cm and 4 cm. Its perimeter is the sum of all four sides, with no equal-side shortcut:

$P = 11 + 9 + 5 + 4 = 29$ cm.

Since every side is different, each length has to be read accurately from the figure and copied correctly.

**Example 5 — a parallelogram.** In fig-09, opposite sides are equal, with $a = 9$ cm and $b = 5$ cm.

$P = 2a + 2b = 2(a + b) = 2(9 + 5) = 28$ cm.

**Example 6 — a regular hexagon.** A regular hexagon has six equal sides (fig-10), each 5.2 cm.

$P = 6 × 5.2 = 31.2$ cm.

blocks.caption: A regular hexagon, named above the drawing, with each of its six sides marked 5.2cm.

A parallelogram with a single arrow on each of its four sides: the two horizontal ones both lettered $a$, the lower also measured 9cm, and the two slanted ones both lettered $b$, the right-hand one also measured 5cm.
A trapezium with each side lettered and measured: the top $c$, 5cm; the left $b$, 9cm; the right $d$, 4cm; the base $a$, 11cm.

blocks.text:
**Example 7 — a circle.** In fig-11 the radius is 7 cm. Using π = 22/7,

$C = 2πr = 2 × 22/7 × 7 = 44$ cm.

Using the diameter instead: $d = 2 × 7 = 14$ cm, so $C = πd = 22/7 × 14 = 44$ cm.

**Example 8 — rope wound round a cylinder.** One complete turn round the cylinder is one circumference. With radius 25 cm and π = 3.14,

$C = 2πr = 2 × 3.14 × 25 = 157$ cm.

Fifty turns of rope therefore measure $157 × 50 = 7850$ cm.

**Example 9 — finding the radius from the circumference.** If the circumference is 440 cm and π = 22/7,

$440 = 2πr = 2 × 22/7 × r = 44r/7$.

Cross-multiplying gives $440 × 7 = 44r$, so $3080 = 44r$ and $r = 70$ cm.

blocks.caption: A circle with a radius drawn from the centre to the right of the circumference, marked 7cm.

blocks.text:
**Example 10 — a quarter circle.** The shape in fig-14 is made of two straight sides of 4.9 cm and a curved part that is one quarter of a full circumference.

The curved part is

$arc = 1/4 × 2πr = 1/4 × 2 × 22/7 × 4.9 = 7.7$ cm.

Do not forget the two straight sides: $P = 4.9 + 4.9 + 7.7 = 17.5$ cm.

blocks.caption: A quarter circle: an upright side and a base meeting at a right angle, each marked 4.9cm, with an arc closing them from the top of the upright to the end of the base.
An upright cylinder with a rope wound round it, drawn as a series of turns spiralling down the body from the top face to the base.
A circle with a radius drawn from the centre to the right of the circumference, marked $r$.

practice.prompt: A regular pentagon has perimeter 45 cm. How long is each side?
practice.worked_solution: A regular pentagon has 5 equal sides, so each side is 45 ÷ 5 = 9 cm.

practice.prompt: A rectangle has perimeter 40 cm and length 13 cm. Find its breadth.
A parallelogram has perimeter 48 cm. One pair of opposite sides are each 15 cm. How long is each side of the other pair?
practice.worked_solution: The two 15 cm sides total 30 cm. The remaining perimeter is 48 − 30 = 18 cm, split equally between the two other equal sides, so each is 9 cm.

practice.prompt: The circumference of a circle is 264 cm. Using π = 22/7, find its radius.
practice.worked_solution: $C = 2πr$, so $264 = 2 × 22/7 × r = 44r/7$. Multiplying both sides by 7 gives $1848 = 44r$, so $r = 42$ cm.

practice.prompt: A square and a regular hexagon each have a perimeter of 60 cm. Which has the longer side, and by how much?
practice.answer: The square — its side is 5 cm longer.
practice.worked_solution: Square side = 60 ÷ 4 = 15 cm; hexagon side = 60 ÷ 6 = 10 cm. The square's side is 15 − 10 = 5 cm longer.

practice.prompt: A quarter-circle has two straight sides of 7 cm. Using π = 22/7, find its perimeter.
practice.worked_solution: Arc = 1/4 × 2 × 22/7 × 7 = 1/4 × 44 = 11 cm. Add the two straight sides: 7 + 7 + 11 = 25 cm.

practice.prompt: A trapezium has perimeter 49 cm. Three sides measure 10 cm, 6 cm and 25 cm. Find the fourth side.
practice.worked_solution: The three known sides total 10 + 6 + 25 = 41 cm. The fourth side is 49 − 41 = 8 cm.

practice.prompt: A rectangle’s length is three times its breadth, and its perimeter is 64 cm. Find its length and breadth.
practice.worked_solution: If breadth is b, length is 3b. Then $P = 2(3b + b) = 8b$, so $8b = 64$ and $b = 8$. Therefore length = $3 × 8 = 24$ cm.

sections.title: Plane Shapes: Their Types, Properties, Similarities and Differences

blocks.text: Plane shapes are shapes that lie flat on a surface, so they are also called two-dimensional shapes (2-D shapes). The plane shapes you will meet include the triangle, the square, the rectangle, the parallelogram, the trapezium, the circle and other polygons. A polygon is any closed shape that has three or more straight sides. Let us look at each family of plane shapes, its properties, and how the shapes are similar to or different from one another.

Look at the three triangles in fig-01: the isosceles, the scalene and the equilateral. Their names tell you how their sides compare. - An isosceles triangle has two adjacent sides equal (the two slanted sides carry a single tick each). Its base angles are equal, and it has one line of symmetry. - A scalene triangle has no side equal to another — each side carries a different number of ticks (one, two, three). No angle is equal to another, and it has no line of symmetry. - An equilateral triangle has all three sides equal (a single tick on each side). All three angles are equal, each measuring $60^\circ$, and it has three lines of symmetry. So the key differences come down to how many sides are equal: an equilateral has three equal sides, an isosceles has two, and a scalene has none.

blocks.caption: Isosceles: a single tick on each of the two slanted sides, an arc at each base angle. Scalene: one, two and three ticks on the three sides, an arc at each vertex. Equilateral: a single tick on each of the three sides, an arc at each vertex.

blocks.text: Now compare the square and the rectangle in fig-02. Each has a right-angle mark at every corner, so both have all angles equal, each measuring $90^\circ$, and both have two pairs of parallel sides. The difference lies in the sides. - A square has all four sides equal (a single tick on every side). It has four lines of symmetry, and its diagonals bisect each other at a right angle. - A rectangle has only two opposite sides equal — the two longer sides carry a single tick each and the two shorter sides a double tick each. It has two lines of symmetry, and its diagonals bisect each other but not at a right angle.

blocks.caption: Square: a right-angle mark at each corner, a single tick on each of the four sides. Rectangle: a right-angle mark at each corner, a single tick on each of the two longer sides and a double tick on each of the two shorter sides.

blocks.text: Finally, compare the parallelogram and the trapezium in fig-03. - A parallelogram has two pairs of opposite sides equal and parallel (its two horizontal sides carry a single arrow and its two slanted sides a double arrow). Its opposite angles are equal, it has no line of symmetry, and its diagonals divide it into two equal triangles. - A trapezium has only one pair of parallel sides (the two parallel sides carry a single arrow each, and one diagonal is drawn in). Its opposite angles are not equal, it has no line of symmetry, and its diagonal divides it into two unequal triangles. The great difference between them is the number of parallel sides: a parallelogram has two pairs, a trapezium has only one pair.

blocks.caption: Parallelogram: a single arrow on each of the two horizontal sides, a double arrow on each of the two slanted sides. Trapezium: a single arrow on each of the two parallel sides, and one diagonal drawn in.

blocks.text:
Polygons come in many forms, and each is named by its number of straight sides. The table below lists the common polygons, their number of sides, and how many triangles each can be divided into by drawing diagonals from one vertex to all the non-adjacent vertices.

| Name of polygon | Number of sides | Number of triangles ($n-2$) |
|---|---|---|
| Triangle | 3 | 1 |
| Quadrilateral | 4 | 2 |
| Pentagon | 5 | 3 |
| Hexagon | 6 | 4 |
| Heptagon | 7 | 5 |
| Octagon | 8 | 6 |
| Nonagon | 9 | 7 |
| Decagon | 10 | 8 |
| Hendecagon (or undecagon) | 11 | 9 |
| Dodecagon | 12 | 10 |

The rule that produces the third column is simple: take the number of sides $n$ and subtract $2$. A hexagon has 6 sides, so it divides into $6-2=4$ triangles; a pentagon has 5 sides, so it divides into $5-2=3$ triangles.

Worked example — triangles in a polygon How many triangles can a heptagon be divided into if you draw diagonals from one vertex to all the non-adjacent vertices? Solution. A heptagon has 7 sides. Use the rule: number of triangles $= n-2 = 7-2 = 5$. So a heptagon divides into 5 triangles, which matches the table.

A circle is a plane shape with no corners: every point on its boundary is the same distance from its centre. The curved line that forms the round boundary of the circle is its **circumference**. fig-04 shows two labelled circles so you can see each part sitting on a real circle.

- The **centre** is the point in the middle of the circle.
- The **radius** (plural *radii*) is any straight line joining the centre to the circumference. In the second circle of fig-04 a radius is drawn from the centre out to the circumference, and the right-hand bounding line of the sector below is also a radius.
- A **chord** is any straight line joining two points on the circumference. The second circle in fig-04 has a chord drawn near the top.
- The **diameter** is any chord that passes through the centre of the circle. In the first circle of fig-04 the diameter is drawn straight across through the centre. Because it goes through the centre, it is the longest chord a circle can have, and it is twice as long as the radius.

sections.title: Finding the Perimeter of Plane Shapes

blocks.text:
The perimeter of a shape is the distance all the way round it. To find it you simply add the lengths of every side. For a straight-sided shape, this means adding each side once. For a circle, the perimeter has a special name — the circumference — and you find it using the radius (or diameter) and the number π (pi), which is about $\frac{22}{7}$ or 3.14.

Because some shapes have equal sides, you can often write a short formula instead of adding each side separately. Work through the examples below to see how each shape's perimeter is found.

Example 1 — a square. A square has four equal sides. In fig-05 each side is marked $L$ and measures 15cm. Its perimeter is four lengths added together: $$L + L + L + L = 4L$$ $$= 15 + 15 + 15 + 15 = 4(15) = 60\text{cm}.$$ Example 2 — a rectangle. A rectangle has two long sides $L$ and two short sides $b$. In fig-06, $L = 10\text{cm}$ and $b = 7\text{cm}$. Adding all four sides: $$P = L + b + L + b = 2L + 2b = 2(L + b)$$ $$= 2(10 + 7) = 2(17) = 34\text{cm}.$$ Example 3 — a missing side. Sometimes you are given the perimeter and one side and must find the other. Suppose a rectangle has perimeter 60cm and length 17cm (fig-07). Write the perimeter formula and solve for $b$: $$P = 2L + 2b$$ $$60 = 2(17) + 2b$$ $$60 = 34 + 2b$$ Collect like terms: $$60 - 34 = 2b$$ $$2b = 26$$ Divide both sides by 2: $$b = 13\text{cm}.$$

blocks.caption: A rectangle with both long sides marked $L = 17$cm and both short sides marked $b$.
A rectangle with both long sides marked $L$, the top one also 10cm, and both short sides marked $b$, the right-hand one also 7cm.
A square, named *Square* at its left, with all four sides marked twice — $L$ and 15cm.

blocks.text: Example 4 — a trapezium. A trapezium has four sides, usually of different lengths. In fig-08 they are $a = 11\text{cm}$, $b = 9\text{cm}$, $c = 5\text{cm}$ and $d = 4\text{cm}$. The perimeter is all four added: $$P = a + b + c + d$$ $$= 11 + 9 + 5 + 4 = 29\text{cm}.$$ Example 5 — a parallelogram. A parallelogram has opposite sides equal: two of length $a$ and two of length $b$ (fig-09, where $a = 9\text{cm}$ and $b = 5\text{cm}$). So $$P = a + a + b + b = 2a + 2b = 2(a + b)$$ $$= 2(9 + 5) = 2(14) = 28\text{cm}.$$ Example 6 — a regular hexagon. A regular hexagon has six equal sides. In fig-10 each side is 5.2cm, so $$P = 6 \times 5.2 = 31.2\text{cm}.$$

blocks.caption: A regular hexagon, named above the drawing, with each of its six sides marked 5.2cm.

A parallelogram with a single arrow on each of its four sides: the two horizontal ones both lettered $a$, the lower also measured 9cm, and the two slanted ones both lettered $b$, the right-hand one also measured 5cm.
A trapezium with each side lettered and measured: the top $c$, 5cm; the left $b$, 9cm; the right $d$, 4cm; the base $a$, 11cm.

blocks.text: Example 7 — a circle. The perimeter of a circle is its circumference, found with either formula: $$C = 2\pi r \quad\text{or}\quad C = \pi d.$$ In fig-11 the radius is 7cm, using $\pi = \frac{22}{7}$: $$C = 2 \times \frac{22}{7} \times 7 = 2 \times 22 = 44\text{cm}.$$ Using $\pi d$ instead: since $d = 2r = 2 \times 7 = 14\text{cm}$, $$C = \frac{22}{7} \times 14 = 22 \times 2 = 44\text{cm}.$$ Example 8 — a rope wound round a cylinder. One turn round the cylinder is one circumference. With radius 25cm and $\pi = 3.14$, $$C = 2\pi r = 2 \times 3.14 \times 25 = 157\text{cm}.$$ Wound 50 times, the rope's total length is $$157 \times 50 = 7850\text{cm}.$$ Example 9 — the radius from the circumference. If the circumference is 440cm, find $r$ ($\pi = \frac{22}{7}$): $$440 = 2\pi r = 2 \times \frac{22}{7} \times r = \frac{44r}{7}.$$ Cross-multiply: $$440 \times 7 = 44r \quad\Rightarrow\quad 3080 = 44r.$$ Divide both sides by 44: $$r = \frac{3080}{44} = 70\text{cm}.$$

blocks.caption: A circle with a radius drawn from the centre to the right of the circumference, marked 7cm.

blocks.text: Example 10 — a quarter circle. The shape in fig-14 is made of two straight sides of 4.9cm each and a curved part that is one quarter of a full circle. Its perimeter is the two straight sides plus that curved part. First find the curved part. It is $\frac{1}{4}$ of a full circumference: $$\frac{1}{4} \times 2\pi r = \frac{1}{4} \times 2 \times \frac{22}{7} \times 4.9$$ $$= \frac{1}{4} \times \frac{44}{7} \times 4.9 = \frac{11}{7} \times \frac{49}{10}$$ $$= \frac{11 \times 7}{10} = \frac{77}{10} = 7.7\text{cm}.$$ Now add the straight sides and the curved part: $$P = 4.9 + 4.9 + 7.7 = 17.5\text{cm}.$$

blocks.caption: A quarter circle: an upright side and a base meeting at a right angle, each marked 4.9cm, with an arc closing them from the top of the upright to the end of the base.
An upright cylinder with a rope wound round it, drawn as a series of turns spiralling down the body from the top face to the base.
A circle with a radius drawn from the centre to the right of the circumference, marked $r$.

practice.prompt: Find the perimeter of a square with sides of 8cm.
practice.worked_solution: A square has four equal sides, so $P = 4 \times 8 = 32\text{cm}$.

practice.prompt: Find the perimeter of a rectangle of length 7cm and breadth 4cm.

sections.title: Plane Shapes: Their Types, Properties, Similarities and Differences

blocks.text: Plane shapes are shapes that lie flat on a surface, so they are also called **two-dimensional shapes (2-D shapes)**. The plane shapes you will meet include the triangle, the square, the rectangle, the parallelogram, the trapezium, the circle and other polygons. A **polygon** is any closed shape that has three or more straight sides. Keep one idea in mind from the start: a polygon is named by its number of sides, but the number of triangles it can be divided into is **not** the same as its number of sides.

Look at the three triangles in fig-01: the **isosceles**, the **scalene**, and the **equilateral**. Their names tell you how their sides compare.

- An **isosceles** triangle has two adjacent sides equal. Its base angles are equal, and it has one line of symmetry.
- A **scalene** triangle has no side equal to another. No angle is equal to another, and it has no line of symmetry.
- An **equilateral** triangle has all three sides equal. All three angles are equal, each measuring 60°, and it has three lines of symmetry.

The key difference is how many sides are equal: an equilateral triangle has three equal sides, an isosceles triangle has two, and a scalene triangle has none.

blocks.caption: Isosceles: a single tick on each of the two slanted sides, an arc at each base angle. Scalene: one, two and three ticks on the three sides, an arc at each vertex. Equilateral: a single tick on each of the three sides, an arc at each vertex.

blocks.text:
Now compare the square and the rectangle in fig-02. Each has a right-angle mark at every corner, so both have all angles equal, each measuring 90°. Both also have two pairs of parallel sides. They differ in their sides.

- A **square** has all four sides equal. It has four lines of symmetry, and its diagonals bisect each other at a right angle.
- A **rectangle** has opposite sides equal: its two longer sides carry one tick each, and its two shorter sides carry two ticks each. It has two lines of symmetry, and its diagonals bisect each other but not at a right angle.

So the rectangle's four sides are not all equal, while the square's four sides are equal.

blocks.caption: Square: a right-angle mark at each corner, a single tick on each of the four sides. Rectangle: a right-angle mark at each corner, a single tick on each of the two longer sides and a double tick on each of the two shorter sides.

blocks.text:
Finally, compare the parallelogram and the trapezium in fig-03.

- A **parallelogram** has two pairs of opposite sides equal and parallel. Its opposite angles are equal. It has no line of symmetry, and its diagonals divide it into two equal triangles.
- A **trapezium** has only one pair of parallel sides. Its opposite angles are not equal. It has no line of symmetry, and its diagonal divides it into two unequal triangles.

The great difference is the number of parallel sides: a parallelogram has two pairs, while a trapezium has only one pair.

blocks.caption: Parallelogram: a single arrow on each of the two horizontal sides, a double arrow on each of the two slanted sides. Trapezium: a single arrow on each of the two parallel sides, and one diagonal drawn in.

blocks.text:
Polygons come in many forms, and each is named by its number of straight sides. The table below lists common polygons, how many sides each has, and how many triangles each can be divided into by drawing diagonals from one vertex to all the non-adjacent vertices.

| Name of polygon | Number of sides ($n$) | Number of triangles ($n-2$) |
|---|---|---|
| Triangle | 3 | 1 |
| Quadrilateral | 4 | 2 |
| Pentagon | 5 | 3 |
| Hexagon | 6 | 4 |
| Heptagon | 7 | 5 |
| Octagon | 8 | 6 |
| Nonagon | 9 | 7 |
| Decagon | 10 | 8 |
| Hendecagon (or undecagon) | 11 | 9 |
| Dodecagon | 12 | 10 |

Now notice the trap in this table. An octagon has **8 sides**, so its row reads Octagon | 8 | 6. If a question asks, “How many triangles can an octagon be divided into?”, a common slip is to answer 8 because 8 is the number of sides. But the triangle count is in the last column: $n - 2 = 8 - 2 = 6$. For every polygon in the table, the number of triangles is two less than the number of sides.

**Worked example — triangles in an octagon**

How many triangles can an octagon be divided into if you draw diagonals from one vertex to all the non-adjacent vertices?

**Solution**

1. An octagon has **8 sides**, so $n = 8$.
2. Use the rule from the table: number of triangles $= n - 2$.
3. Substitute: $8 - 2 = 6$.

So an octagon divides into **6 triangles**. The tempting answer 8 is the number of sides, not the number of triangles.

practice.prompt: How many triangles can a pentagon be divided into if you draw diagonals from one vertex to all the non-adjacent vertices?
practice.worked_solution: A pentagon has 5 sides, so $n = 5$. Number of triangles $= n - 2 = 5 - 2 = 3$.

practice.prompt: A hexagon has how many sides, and into how many triangles can it be divided from one vertex?
practice.answer: A hexagon has 6 sides and divides into 4 triangles.
practice.worked_solution: Use the hexagon row in the table: sides = 6, triangles = $6 - 2 = 4$.

practice.prompt: Name the triangle whose three sides are all equal, and state the size of each of its angles.
practice.worked_solution: All three sides equal means the triangle is equilateral. Its three angles are all equal, and the angles of a triangle add to 180°, so each angle is 180° ÷ 3 = 60°.

practice.prompt: Which has more lines of symmetry: a square or a rectangle? State how many each has.
practice.answer: A square has more lines of symmetry: a square has 4, while a rectangle has 2.
practice.worked_solution: The square has 4 lines of symmetry. The rectangle has 2 lines of symmetry.

practice.prompt: State one difference between a parallelogram and a trapezium.
practice.answer: A parallelogram has two pairs of parallel sides, while a trapezium has only one pair of parallel sides.
practice.worked_solution: Parallelogram: two pairs of opposite sides are parallel. Trapezium: only one pair of sides is parallel.

blocks.text:
A circle is a plane shape with no corners: every point on its boundary is the same distance from its centre. The curved line that forms the round boundary of the circle is its **circumference**. fig-04 shows two labelled circles so you can see each part sitting on a real circle.

- The **centre** is the point in the middle of the circle.
- The **radius** (plural *radii*) is any straight line joining the centre to the circumference. In the second circle of fig-04 a radius is drawn from the centre out to the circumference, and the right-hand bounding line of the sector below is also a radius.
- A **chord** is any straight line joining two points on the circumference. The second circle in fig-04 has a chord drawn near the top.
- The **diameter** is any chord that passes through the centre of the circle. In the first circle of fig-04 the diameter is drawn straight across through the centre. Because it goes through the centre, it is the longest chord a circle can have, and it is twice as long as the radius.
- An **arc** is a curved part of the circumference. In the first circle of fig-04 a part of the circumference is marked and named the arc.

The figure also shows three more parts:
- A **segment** is the region of the circle cut off by a chord — the shaded part above the chord in the second circle.
- A **sector** is the region bounded by two radii and the arc between them — the shaded part below in the second circle, whose two straight sides are both radii.
- A **tangent** is a straight line that touches the circle at exactly one point, as shown touching the right side of the second circle.

blocks.caption: Two labelled circles. The first has the diameter drawn across it and a radius from its centre to the circumference, with the arc and the circumference labelled. The second has a chord near the top with the segment above it shaded, a shaded sector below with its right-hand bounding line labelled Radius, and a tangent touching it on the right.

sections.title: Finding the Perimeter of Plane Shapes

blocks.text:
Perimeter is the distance all the way round a plane shape. For a shape with straight sides, find it by adding the length of every side once. For a circle, that distance is called the circumference, and you use the radius or diameter together with $\pi$ (about $\frac{22}{7}$ or 3.14). Because some shapes have equal sides, we can write short formulas:

- Square: $P = 4L$, where $L$ is one side.
- Rectangle: $P = L + L + b + b = 2L + 2b = 2(L + b)$.
- Parallelogram: $P = a + a + b + b = 2(a + b)$.
- Trapezium: add all four sides: $P = a + b + c + d$.
- Any regular polygon with $n$ equal sides: $P = n \times$ side length.

A key point: every formula counts each side exactly once. In a rectangle, $2L$ and $2b$ are already the doubled sides. Once you have them, add them once: if $L = 7$ cm and $b = 4$ cm, then $2L = 14$ cm and $2b = 8$ cm, so $P = 14 + 8 = 22$ cm. A common slip is to double again and write $2(14 + 8)$, which gives 44 — twice the real perimeter.

Check adding too. For a square of side 8 cm, $8 + 8 + 8 + 8 = 32$ cm. Add in steps: $8 + 8 = 16$, $16 + 8 = 24$, $24 + 8 = 32$. The perimeter is 32 cm, not 316 cm.

**Example 1 — a square.** In fig-05, each side of the square is marked $L$ and measures 15 cm. There are four equal sides, so
$$P = L + L + L + L = 4L = 4(15) = 60\text{ cm}.$$
Adding directly: $15 + 15 + 15 + 15 = 30 + 30 = 60$.

**Example 2 — a rectangle.** In fig-06, $L = 10$ cm and $b = 7$ cm. Count the sides: one $L$, one $b$, another $L$, another $b$.
$$P = L + b + L + b = 2L + 2b = 2(L + b).$$
Using the lengths:
$$P = 2(10) + 2(7) = 20 + 14 = 34\text{ cm}.$$
The 20 and 14 are already $2L$ and $2b$. Add them once to finish. Do not then find $2(20 + 14)$; that would give 68 cm, twice the real perimeter.

**Example 3 — finding a missing side.** In fig-07, a rectangle has perimeter 60 cm and length 17 cm. Start from $P = 2L + 2b$:
$$60 = 2(17) + 2b = 34 + 2b.$$
Subtract 34 from both sides:
$$60 - 34 = 2b \quad\Rightarrow\quad 26 = 2b.$$
Divide both sides by 2:
$$b = 13\text{ cm}.$$

blocks.caption: A rectangle with both long sides marked $L = 17$cm and both short sides marked $b$.
A rectangle with both long sides marked $L$, the top one also 10cm, and both short sides marked $b$, the right-hand one also 7cm.
A square, named *Square* at its left, with all four sides marked twice — $L$ and 15cm.

blocks.text:
**Example 4 — a trapezium.** In fig-08, the four labelled sides are $a = 11$ cm, $b = 9$ cm, $c = 5$ cm and $d = 4$ cm. A trapezium can have four different sides, so write each labelled side once and add:
$$P = a + b + c + d = 11 + 9 + 5 + 4 = 29\text{ cm}.$$
If no working is shown, listing the four side lengths first is the best starting point.

**Example 5 — a parallelogram.** In fig-09, a parallelogram has two sides of length $a = 9$ cm and two of length $b = 5$ cm. Opposite sides are equal, so
$$P = a + a + b + b = 2a + 2b = 2(a + b).$$
$$P = 2(9) + 2(5) = 18 + 10 = 28\text{ cm}.$$
Here $18 + 10$ is already the sum of the doubled sides; adding them gives the perimeter. A common slip is to double again and write $2(18 + 10)$, getting 56 cm — twice the real perimeter.

**Example 6 — a regular hexagon.** In fig-10, a regular hexagon has six equal sides, each 5.2 cm. Instead of adding six numbers, multiply:
$$P = 6 \times 5.2 = 31.2\text{ cm}.$$

blocks.caption: A regular hexagon, named above the drawing, with each of its six sides marked 5.2cm.

A parallelogram with a single arrow on each of its four sides: the two horizontal ones both lettered $a$, the lower also measured 9cm, and the two slanted ones both lettered $b$, the right-hand one also measured 5cm.
A trapezium with each side lettered and measured: the top $c$, 5cm; the left $b$, 9cm; the right $d$, 4cm; the base $a$, 11cm.

blocks.text:
**Example 7 — a circle.** The perimeter of a circle is its circumference, found by one formula:
$$C = 2\pi r \quad\text{or}\quad C = \pi d.$$
In fig-11, the radius is 7 cm. Using $\pi = \frac{22}{7}$:
$$C = 2 \times \frac{22}{7} \times 7 = 2 \times 22 = 44\text{ cm}.$$
Since $d = 2r = 2 \times 7 = 14$ cm, the second version gives $C = \frac{22}{7} \times 14 = 44$ cm too. The formula contains $r$, not $r^2$; a common slip is to write $2\pi r^2$, which is not the circumference.

**Example 8 — a rope wound round a cylinder.** One turn round the cylinder is one circumference. With radius 25 cm and $\pi = 3.14$:
$$C = 2\pi r = 2 \times 3.14 \times 25 = 157\text{ cm}.$$
Fifty turns use $157 \times 50 = 7850$ cm of rope.

**Example 9 — the radius from the circumference.** Suppose the circumference is 440 cm. Find $r$, using $\pi = \frac{22}{7}$.
$$440 = 2\pi r = 2 \times \frac{22}{7} \times r = \frac{44r}{7}.$$
Cross-multiply:
$$440 \times 7 = 44r \quad\Rightarrow\quad 3080 = 44r.$$
Divide both sides by 44:
$$r = \frac{3080}{44} = 70\text{ cm}.$$
Do not simply halve 440: the formula has $2\pi$, not just 2. Quick check with a circumference of 22 cm: half of 22 is 11 cm, but the correct radius is 3.5 cm because $2 \times \frac{22}{7} \times 3.5 = 22$ cm.

blocks.caption: A circle with a radius drawn from the centre to the right of the circumference, marked 7cm.

blocks.text:
**Example 10 — a quarter circle.** The shape in fig-14 is made of two straight sides of 4.9 cm each and a curved part that is one quarter of a full circle. So its perimeter is the two straight sides plus that curved part.

First find the curved part:
$$\frac{1}{4} \times 2\pi r = \frac{1}{4} \times 2 \times \frac{22}{7} \times 4.9.$$
Work carefully step by step:
$$= \frac{1}{4} \times \frac{44}{7} \times \frac{49}{10} = \frac{11}{7} \times \frac{49}{10} = \frac{77}{10} = 7.7\text{ cm}.$$
Then add the curved part to the two straight sides:
$$P = 4.9 + 4.9 + 7.7 = 17.5\text{ cm}.$$

blocks.caption: A quarter circle: an upright side and a base meeting at a right angle, each marked 4.9cm, with an arc closing them from the top of the upright to the end of the base.
An upright cylinder with a rope wound round it, drawn as a series of turns spiralling down the body from the top face to the base.
A circle with a radius drawn from the centre to the right of the circumference, marked $r$.

practice.prompt: Find the perimeter of a square with side 6 cm.
practice.worked_solution: A square has 4 equal sides. Add in steps: $6 + 6 = 12$, $12 + 6 = 18$, $18 + 6 = 24$ cm. Or use $P = 4 \times 6 = 24$ cm.

practice.prompt: Find the perimeter of a rectangle of length 8 cm and breadth 3 cm.
practice.worked_solution: Use $P = 2L + 2b = 2(8) + 2(3) = 16 + 6 = 22$ cm. The 16 and 6 are already the doubled sides, so stop at 22 cm; do not double $16 + 6$ again.

practice.prompt: Find the perimeter of a regular pentagon with sides of 3 cm.
practice.worked_solution: A regular pentagon has five equal sides. $P = 5 \times 3 = 15$ cm, or add $3 + 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 15$ cm.

practice.prompt: A parallelogram has a base of 8 cm and a sloping side of 5 cm. Find its perimeter.
practice.worked_solution: Opposite sides are equal, so there are two sides of 8 cm and two sides of 5 cm. $P = 2(8) + 2(5) = 16 + 10 = 26$ cm. The 16 and 10 are already the doubled sides; do not double them again.

practice.prompt: A trapezium has sides 5 cm, 4 cm, 3 cm and 2 cm. Find its perimeter.
practice.worked_solution: A trapezium's sides are usually all different, so add each side once: $P = 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 = 14$ cm.

practice.prompt: The radius of a circle is 7 cm. Taking $\pi = \frac{22}{7}$, find its circumference.
practice.worked_solution: Use $C = 2\pi r = 2 \times \frac{22}{7} \times 7 = 44$ cm.

practice.prompt: The circumference of a circle is 88 cm. Taking $\pi = \frac{22}{7}$, find its radius.
practice.worked_solution: Use $C = 2\pi r$. Then $88 = 2 \times \frac{22}{7} \times r = \frac{44r}{7}$. Multiply both sides by 7: $616 = 44r$. Divide by 44: $r = 14$ cm. Check: $2 \times \frac{22}{7} \times 14 = 88$ cm. Do not just halve 88; divide by $2\pi$.

practice.prompt: Find the perimeter of a regular hexagon with sides of 4 cm.
practice.worked_solution: A regular hexagon has six equal sides. $P = 6 \times 4 = 24$ cm, or add 4 six times to get 24 cm.

blocks.text: Plane shapes are shapes that lie flat on a surface, so they are also called two-dimensional shapes (2-D shapes). The plane shapes you will meet include the triangle, the square, the rectangle, the parallelogram, the trapezium, the circle and other polygons. A polygon is any closed shape that has three or more straight sides. Let us look at each family of plane shapes, its properties, and how the shapes are similar to or different from one another.

Look at the three triangles in fig-01: the isosceles, the scalene and the equilateral. Their names tell you how their sides compare. - An isosceles triangle has two adjacent sides equal (the two slanted sides carry a single tick each). Its base angles are equal, and it has one line of symmetry. - A scalene triangle has no side equal to another — each side carries a different number of ticks (one, two, three). No angle is equal to another, and it has no line of symmetry. - An equilateral triangle has all three sides equal (a single tick on each side). All three angles are equal, each measuring $60^\circ$, and it has three lines of symmetry. blocks.text: Now compare the square and the rectangle in fig-02. It has four lines of symmetry, and its diagonals bisect each other at a right angle. - A rectangle has only two opposite sides equal — the two longer sides carry a single tick each and the two shorter sides a double tick each. Its opposite angles are not equal, it has no line of symmetry, and its diagonal divides it into two unequal triangles. blocks.text:

|---|---|---|

| Pentagon | 5 | 3 |

Use the rule: number of triangles $= n-2 = 7-2 = 5$. So a heptagon divides into 5 triangles, which matches the table.

sections.title: Finding the Perimeter of Plane Shapes

blocks.text:
The perimeter of a shape is the distance all the way round it. To find it you simply add the lengths of every side. For a straight-sided shape, this means adding each side once. For a circle, the perimeter has a special name — the circumference — and you find it using the radius (or diameter) and the number π (pi), which is about $\frac{22}{7}$ or 3.14.

Because some shapes have equal sides, you can often write a short formula instead of adding each side separately. Work through the examples below to see how each shape's perimeter is found.

Example 1 — a square. A square has four equal sides. In fig-05 each side is marked $L$ and measures 15cm. Its perimeter is four lengths added together: $$L + L + L + L = 4L$$ $$= 15 + 15 + 15 + 15 = 4(15) = 60\text{cm}.$$ Example 2 — a rectangle. A rectangle has two long sides $L$ and two short sides $b$. In fig-06, $L = 10\text{cm}$ and $b = 7\text{cm}$. Adding all four sides: $$P = L + b + L + b = 2L + 2b = 2(L + b)$$ $$= 2(10 + 7) = 2(17) = 34\text{cm}.$$ Example 3 — a missing side. Sometimes you are given the perimeter and one side and must find the other. Suppose a rectangle has perimeter 60cm and length 17cm (fig-07). Write the perimeter formula and solve for $b$: $$P = 2L + 2b$$ $$60 = 2(17) + 2b$$ $$60 = 34 + 2b$$ Collect like terms: $$60 - 34 = 2b$$ $$2b = 26$$ Divide both sides by 2: $$b = 13\text{cm}.$$

blocks.caption: A rectangle with both long sides marked $L = 17$cm and both short sides marked $b$.
A rectangle with both long sides marked $L$, the top one also 10cm, and both short sides marked $b$, the right-hand one also 7cm.
A square, named *Square* at its left, with all four sides marked twice — $L$ and 15cm.

blocks.text: Example 4 — a trapezium. A trapezium has four sides, usually of different lengths. In fig-08 they are $a = 11\text{cm}$, $b = 9\text{cm}$, $c = 5\text{cm}$ and $d = 4\text{cm}$. The perimeter is all four added: $$P = a + b + c + d$$ $$= 11 + 9 + 5 + 4 = 29\text{cm}.$$ Example 5 — a parallelogram. A parallelogram has opposite sides equal: two of length $a$ and two of length $b$ (fig-09, where $a = 9\text{cm}$ and $b = 5\text{cm}$). So $$P = a + a + b + b = 2a + 2b = 2(a + b)$$ $$= 2(9 + 5) = 2(14) = 28\text{cm}.$$ Example 6 — a regular hexagon. A regular hexagon has six equal sides. In fig-10 each side is 5.2cm, so $$P = 6 \times 5.2 = 31.2\text{cm}.$$

blocks.caption: A regular hexagon, named above the drawing, with each of its six sides marked 5.2cm.

A parallelogram with a single arrow on each of its four sides: the two horizontal ones both lettered $a$, the lower also measured 9cm, and the two slanted ones both lettered $b$, the right-hand one also measured 5cm.
A trapezium with each side lettered and measured: the top $c$, 5cm; the left $b$, 9cm; the right $d$, 4cm; the base $a$, 11cm.

blocks.text: Example 7 — a circle. The perimeter of a circle is its circumference, found with either formula: $$C = 2\pi r \quad\text{or}\quad C = \pi d.$$ In fig-11 the radius is 7cm, using $\pi = \frac{22}{7}$: $$C = 2 \times \frac{22}{7} \times 7 = 2 \times 22 = 44\text{cm}.$$ Using $\pi d$ instead: since $d = 2r = 2 \times 7 = 14\text{cm}$, $$C = \frac{22}{7} \times 14 = 22 \times 2 = 44\text{cm}.$$ Example 8 — a rope wound round a cylinder. One turn round the cylinder is one circumference. With radius 25cm and $\pi = 3.14$, $$C = 2\pi r = 2 \times 3.14 \times 25 = 157\text{cm}.$$ Wound 50 times, the rope's total length is $$157 \times 50 = 7850\text{cm}.$$ Example 9 — the radius from the circumference. If the circumference is 440cm, find $r$ ($\pi = \frac{22}{7}$): $$440 = 2\pi r = 2 \times \frac{22}{7} \times r = \frac{44r}{7}.$$ Cross-multiply: $$440 \times 7 = 44r \quad\Rightarrow\quad 3080 = 44r.$$ Divide both sides by 44: $$r = \frac{3080}{44} = 70\text{cm}.$$

blocks.caption: A circle with a radius drawn from the centre to the right of the circumference, marked 7cm.

blocks.text: Example 10 — a quarter circle. The shape in fig-14 is made of two straight sides of 4.9cm each and a curved part that is one quarter of a full circle. Its perimeter is the two straight sides plus that curved part. First find the curved part. It is $\frac{1}{4}$ of a full circumference: $$\frac{1}{4} \times 2\pi r = \frac{1}{4} \times 2 \times \frac{22}{7} \times 4.9$$ $$= \frac{1}{4} \times \frac{44}{7} \times 4.9 = \frac{11}{7} \times \frac{49}{10}$$ $$= \frac{11 \times 7}{10} = \frac{77}{10} = 7.7\text{cm}.$$ Now add the straight sides and the curved part: $$P = 4.9 + 4.9 + 7.7 = 17.5\text{cm}.$$

blocks.caption: A quarter circle: an upright side and a base meeting at a right angle, each marked 4.9cm, with an arc closing them from the top of the upright to the end of the base.
An upright cylinder with a rope wound round it, drawn as a series of turns spiralling down the body from the top face to the base.
A circle with a radius drawn from the centre to the right of the circumference, marked $r$.

sections.title: Plane Shapes: Their Types, Properties, Similarities and Differences

blocks.text: Plane shapes are shapes that lie flat on a surface, so they are also called two-dimensional shapes (**2-D shapes**). The plane shapes you will meet include the triangle, the square, the rectangle, the parallelogram, the trapezium, the circle, and other polygons. A **polygon** is any closed shape that has three or more straight sides. As you study each family, keep two questions in mind: *How many sides are equal?* and *How many pairs of sides are parallel?* These two questions explain most of the similarities and differences between the shapes.

Look at the three triangles in fig-01: the isosceles, the scalene and the equilateral. The ticks on the sides tell you which sides are equal.

- An **isosceles** triangle has **two adjacent sides equal** (the two slanted sides carry a single tick each). Its **base angles are equal**, and it has **one line of symmetry**.
- A **scalene** triangle has **no side equal** to another (one, two and three ticks on different sides). No angle is equal to another, and it has **no line of symmetry**.
- An **equilateral** triangle has **all three sides equal** (a single tick on every side). All three angles are equal, each measuring $60^\circ$, and it has **three lines of symmetry**.

So compare triangles by counting equal sides: an equilateral triangle has three equal sides, an isosceles has two, and a scalene has none.

blocks.caption: Isosceles: a single tick on each of the two slanted sides, an arc at each base angle. Scalene: one, two and three ticks on the three sides, an arc at each vertex. Equilateral: a single tick on each of the three sides, an arc at each vertex.

blocks.text:
Now compare the square and the rectangle in fig-02. Both have a right-angle mark at every corner, so all angles are equal (each measuring $90^\circ$), and both have **two pairs of parallel sides**.

- A **square** has **all four sides equal**. It has **four lines of symmetry**, and its diagonals bisect each other at a right angle.
- A **rectangle** has **only opposite sides equal** - the two longer sides are equal to each other and the two shorter sides are equal to each other. It has **two lines of symmetry**, and its diagonals bisect each other but not at a right angle.

So the square and the rectangle share equal angles and parallel sides; the difference is that the square has all four sides equal, while the rectangle has only opposite sides equal.

blocks.caption: Square: a right-angle mark at each corner, a single tick on each of the four sides. Rectangle: a right-angle mark at each corner, a single tick on each of the two longer sides and a double tick on each of the two shorter sides.

blocks.text:
Finally, compare the parallelogram and the trapezium in fig-03.

- A **parallelogram** has **two pairs of opposite sides equal and parallel**. Its **opposite angles are equal**, it has **no line of symmetry**, and its diagonals divide it into **two equal triangles**.
- A **trapezium** has **only one pair of parallel sides**. Its opposite angles are **not** equal, it has **no line of symmetry**, and its diagonal divides it into **two unequal triangles**.

The great difference is the number of parallel sides: a parallelogram has **two pairs**, while a trapezium has only **one pair**.

blocks.caption: Parallelogram: a single arrow on each of the two horizontal sides, a double arrow on each of the two slanted sides. Trapezium: a single arrow on each of the two parallel sides, and one diagonal drawn in.

blocks.text:
Polygons come in many forms, and each is named by its number of straight sides. The table below lists common polygons, their number of sides, and the number of triangles they can be divided into.

| Name of polygon | Number of sides | Number of triangles ($n-2$) |
|---|---|---|
| Triangle | 3 | 1 |
| Quadrilateral | 4 | 2 |
| Pentagon | 5 | 3 |
| Hexagon | 6 | 4 |
| Heptagon | 7 | 5 |
| Octagon | 8 | 6 |
| Nonagon | 9 | 7 |
| Decagon | 10 | 8 |
| Hendecagon (or undecagon) | 11 | 9 |
| Dodecagon | 12 | 10 |

The rule in the third column is simple: take the number of sides $n$ and subtract $2$. A hexagon has 6 sides, so it divides into $6-2=4$ triangles; a pentagon has 5 sides, so it divides into $5-2=3$ triangles.

Read the octagon row with care: an octagon has 8 sides, and $8-2=6$. A common slip is to use $n-1$ and write 7 for an octagon, but the table's heading is $n-2$, so the number of triangles is **6**, not 7.

**Worked example - triangles in an octagon**

**Question.** How many triangles can an octagon be divided into?

**Solution.**
1. An octagon has $n=8$ sides.
2. Use the rule: number of triangles $= n-2$.
3. Substitute: $8-2=6$.

So an octagon divides into **6 triangles**.

**Check.** Look at the octagon row of the table: 8 sides and 6 triangles. If a calculation gives 7, check the formula again - it is $n-2$, not $n-1$.

practice.prompt: How many triangles can a pentagon be divided into?
practice.worked_solution: A pentagon has 5 sides. Using the rule $n-2$: $5-2=3$.

practice.prompt: Name the triangle whose three sides are all equal, and state the size of each angle.
practice.answer: It is an equilateral triangle, and each of its angles measures $60^\circ$.
practice.worked_solution: The word equilateral tells you all three sides are equal. From the triangle table, when all sides are equal, all angles are also equal and each measures $60^\circ$.

practice.prompt: How many lines of symmetry does a square have? How many lines of symmetry does a rectangle have?
practice.answer: A square has 4 lines of symmetry, and a rectangle has 2 lines of symmetry.
practice.worked_solution: For a square all four sides are equal, so it folds in 4 ways. For a rectangle only opposite sides are equal, so it folds in 2 ways.

practice.prompt: State one difference between a parallelogram and a trapezium.
practice.answer: A parallelogram has two pairs of parallel sides, while a trapezium has only one pair of parallel sides.
practice.worked_solution: Count the pairs of parallel sides. The parallelogram has two pairs, so both pairs of opposite sides are parallel. The trapezium has only one pair of parallel sides.

practice.prompt: An octagon has 8 sides. How many triangles can it be divided into, and why is the answer not 7?
practice.answer: It can be divided into 6 triangles, because the rule is $n-2=8-2=6$, not $n-1$.
practice.worked_solution:
Step 1: Write the number of sides, $n=8$.
Step 2: Use the table's rule: number of triangles $=n-2$.
Step 3: Substitute: $8-2=6$.
So an octagon gives 6 triangles. The common slip is to subtract only 1 and get 7, but the formula subtracts 2.

blocks.text:
A circle is a plane shape with no corners: every point on its boundary is the same distance from its centre. The curved line that forms the round boundary of the circle is its **circumference**. fig-04 shows two labelled circles so you can see each part sitting on a real circle.

- The **centre** is the point in the middle of the circle.
- The **radius** (plural *radii*) is any straight line joining the centre to the circumference. In the second circle of fig-04 a radius is drawn from the centre out to the circumference, and the right-hand bounding line of the sector below is also a radius.
- A **chord** is any straight line joining two points on the circumference. The second circle in fig-04 has a chord drawn near the top.
- The **diameter** is any chord that passes through the centre of the circle. In the first circle of fig-04 the diameter is drawn straight across through the centre. Because it goes through the centre, it is the longest chord a circle can have, and it is twice as long as the radius.
- An **arc** is a curved part of the circumference. In the first circle of fig-04 a part of the circumference is marked and named the arc.

The figure also shows three more parts:
- A **segment** is the region of the circle cut off by a chord — the shaded part above the chord in the second circle.
- A **sector** is the region bounded by two radii and the arc between them — the shaded part below in the second circle, whose two straight sides are both radii.
- A **tangent** is a straight line that touches the circle at exactly one point, as shown touching the right side of the second circle.

blocks.caption: Two labelled circles. The first has the diameter drawn across it and a radius from its centre to the circumference, with the arc and the circumference labelled. The second has a chord near the top with the segment above it shaded, a shaded sector below with its right-hand bounding line labelled Radius, and a tangent touching it on the right.

blocks.text:
**What is perimeter?**

The **perimeter** of a shape is the total distance all the way round its boundary — the length you would walk if you went once around the outside. To find it you simply **add up the lengths of all the sides**.

For many plane shapes we can turn that adding into a short formula, because some shapes have sides that are equal.

- **Square** — all four sides equal. If each side is $L$, then
  $$\text{Perimeter} = L + L + L + L = 4L$$
  A square is one kind of **regular polygon**: a shape whose sides are all equal and whose angles are all equal.
- **Rectangle** — the two opposite long sides are equal (call each $L$) and the two opposite short sides are equal (call each $b$).
  $$\text{Perimeter} = L + b + L + b = 2L + 2b = 2(L + b)$$
- **Regular polygon** (pentagon, hexagon, and so on) — a regular shape with $n$ equal sides of length $s$ has
  $$\text{Perimeter} = n \times s$$
  so a regular pentagon has 5 equal sides and a regular hexagon has 6.
- **Trapezium** — four sides, generally all different, so just add all four:
  $$\text{Perimeter} = a + b + c + d$$
- **Parallelogram** — two pairs of equal sides (call each longer side $a$ and each slanted side $b$):
  $$\text{Perimeter} = a + a + b + b = 2(a + b)$$
- **Circle** — its perimeter has a special name, the **circumference**:
  $$\text{Circumference} = 2\pi r = \pi d$$
  where $r$ is the radius, $d = 2r$ is the diameter, and $\pi$ is the number $\frac{22}{7}$ or $3.14$ (as the question tells you to use).

> **One caution.** Each formula belongs to its own shape. The parallelogram rule $2(a+b)$ only counts four sides — two of $a$ and two of $b$. A regular pentagon has **five** equal sides, so its perimeter is $5 \times s$, not $2(a+b)$. Always count the sides the shape actually has before you choose your rule.

**Example 1 — square.** Calculate the perimeter of a square of side $15$ cm.

Since all four sides are equal, each is $15$ cm:
$$\text{Perimeter} = 4L = 4 \times 15 = 60\ \text{cm}.$$

So the perimeter is $60$ cm.

**Example 2 — rectangle.** Find the perimeter of a rectangle of length $10$ cm and breadth $7$ cm.

There are two lengths of $10$ cm and two breadths of $7$ cm:
$$P = 2L + 2b = 2(10) + 2(7) = 20 + 14 = 34\ \text{cm}.$$

Or add the sides straight round: $10 + 7 + 10 + 7 = 34$ cm. The perimeter is $34$ cm.

**Example 3 — rectangle, finding a missing side.** If the perimeter of a rectangle is $60$ cm and its length is $17$ cm, find its breadth $b$.

Write the perimeter rule and fill in what we know:
$$P = 2L + 2b$$
$$60 = 2(17) + 2b$$
$$60 = 34 + 2b$$

Collect like terms (take $34$ from both sides):
$$60 - 34 = 2b$$
$$26 = 2b$$

Divide both sides by $2$:
$$b = \frac{26}{2} = 13\ \text{cm}.$$

The breadth is $13$ cm. Check: $2(17) + 2(13) = 34 + 26 = 60$ cm. ✓

**Example 4 — trapezium.** Find the perimeter of a trapezium whose sides are $11$ cm, $9$ cm, $5$ cm and $4$ cm.

A trapezium has four sides, usually all different, so just add them:
$$\text{Perimeter} = a + b + c + d = 11 + 9 + 5 + 4 = 29\ \text{cm}.$$

The perimeter is $29$ cm.

**Example 5 — parallelogram.** Find the perimeter of a parallelogram with each longer side $9$ cm and each slanted side $5$ cm.

A parallelogram has two sides of $a = 9$ cm and two sides of $b = 5$ cm:
$$P = 2(a + b) = 2(9 + 5) = 2(14) = 28\ \text{cm}.$$

The perimeter is $28$ cm.

**Example 6 — regular hexagon.** Find the perimeter of a regular hexagon of side $5.2$ cm.

A hexagon has **6** equal sides, so multiply the side by the number of sides:
$$P = 6 \times 5.2 = 31.2\ \text{cm}.$$

The perimeter is $31.2$ cm.

**Example 7 — circle.** Calculate the circumference of a circle of radius $7$ cm. Use $\pi = \frac{22}{7}$.

$$\text{Circumference} = 2\pi r = 2 \times \frac{22}{7} \times 7 = 2 \times 22 = 44\ \text{cm}.$$

The $\frac{22}{7} \times 7$ cancels to $22$, leaving $2 \times 22 = 44$ cm. The circumference is $44$ cm.

**Example 8 — circle, finding the radius.** The circumference of a circle is $440$ cm. Find its radius. Use $\pi = \frac{22}{7}$.

Start from the circumference rule and substitute $C = 440$:
$$C = 2\pi r$$
$$440 = 2 \times \frac{22}{7} \times r = \frac{44r}{7}$$

Multiply both sides by $7$ (cross-multiply):
$$440 \times 7 = 44r$$
$$3080 = 44r$$

Divide both sides by $44$:
$$r = \frac{3080}{44} = 70\ \text{cm}.$$

The radius is $70$ cm.

**Example 9 — putting perimeter to work.** A rope is wound $50$ times around a cylinder of radius $25$ cm. How long is the rope? Use $\pi = 3.14$.

One complete turn of the rope goes once around the circle, so one turn equals one circumference:
$$C = 2\pi r = 2 \times 3.14 \times 25 = 157\ \text{cm}.$$

For $50$ turns, multiply:
$$50 \times 157 = 7850\ \text{cm}.$$

The rope is $7850$ cm long.

**Example 10 — a quarter circle.** A shape is a quarter of a circle: its two straight sides are each $4.9$ cm and they meet at a right angle. Find its perimeter. Use $\pi = \frac{22}{7}$.

The perimeter is made of two straight sides and one curved part (the quarter arc).

The full circumference of a circle of radius $4.9$ cm is $2\pi r$, and a quarter circle keeps one quarter of that arc:
$$\text{arc} = \frac14 \times 2\pi r = \frac14 \times 2 \times \frac{22}{7} \times 4.9$$
$$= \frac14 \times \frac{44}{7} \times \frac{49}{10} = \frac{11}{7} \times \frac{49}{10} = \frac{77}{10} = 7.7\ \text{cm}.$$

Now add the two straight sides and the arc:
$$\text{Perimeter} = 4.9 + 4.9 + 7.7 = 17.5\ \text{cm}.$$

The perimeter is $17.5$ cm.

sections.title: Plane Shapes: Their Types, Properties, Similarities and Differences

blocks.text: Plane shapes are shapes that lie flat on a surface, so they are also called two-dimensional shapes (2-D shapes). The plane shapes you will meet include the triangle, the square, the rectangle, the parallelogram, the trapezium, the circle and other polygons. A polygon is any closed shape that has three or more straight sides. Let us look at each family of plane shapes, its properties, and how the shapes are similar to or different from one another.

Look at the three triangles in fig-01: the isosceles, the scalene and the equilateral. Their names tell you how their sides compare. - An isosceles triangle has two adjacent sides equal (the two slanted sides carry a single tick each). Its base angles are equal, and it has one line of symmetry. - A scalene triangle has no side equal to another — each side carries a different number of ticks (one, two, three). No angle is equal to another, and it has no line of symmetry. - An equilateral triangle has all three sides equal (a single tick on each side). All three angles are equal, each measuring $60^\circ$, and it has three lines of symmetry. So the key differences come down to how many sides are equal: an equilateral has three equal sides, an isosceles has two, and a scalene has none.

blocks.caption: Isosceles: a single tick on each of the two slanted sides, an arc at each base angle. Scalene: one, two and three ticks on the three sides, an arc at each vertex. Equilateral: a single tick on each of the three sides, an arc at each vertex.

blocks.text: Now compare the square and the rectangle in fig-02. Each has a right-angle mark at every corner, so both have all angles equal, each measuring $90^\circ$, and both have two pairs of parallel sides. The difference lies in the sides. - A square has all four sides equal (a single tick on every side). It has four lines of symmetry, and its diagonals bisect each other at a right angle. - A rectangle has only two opposite sides equal — the two longer sides carry a single tick each and the two shorter sides a double tick each. It has two lines of symmetry, and its diagonals bisect each other but not at a right angle.

blocks.caption: Square: a right-angle mark at each corner, a single tick on each of the four sides. Rectangle: a right-angle mark at each corner, a single tick on each of the two longer sides and a double tick on each of the two shorter sides.

blocks.text: Finally, compare the parallelogram and the trapezium in fig-03. - A parallelogram has two pairs of opposite sides equal and parallel (its two horizontal sides carry a single arrow and its two slanted sides a double arrow). Its opposite angles are equal, it has no line of symmetry, and its diagonals divide it into two equal triangles. - A trapezium has only one pair of parallel sides (the two parallel sides carry a single arrow each, and one diagonal is drawn in). Its opposite angles are not equal, it has no line of symmetry, and its diagonal divides it into two unequal triangles. The great difference between them is the number of parallel sides: a parallelogram has two pairs, a trapezium has only one pair.

blocks.caption: Parallelogram: a single arrow on each of the two horizontal sides, a double arrow on each of the two slanted sides. Trapezium: a single arrow on each of the two parallel sides, and one diagonal drawn in.

blocks.text:
Polygons come in many forms, and each is named by its number of straight sides. The table below lists the common polygons, their number of sides, and how many triangles each can be divided into by drawing diagonals from one vertex to all the non-adjacent vertices.

| Name of polygon | Number of sides | Number of triangles ($n-2$) |
|---|---|---|
| Triangle | 3 | 1 |
| Quadrilateral | 4 | 2 |
| Pentagon | 5 | 3 |
| Hexagon | 6 | 4 |
| Heptagon | 7 | 5 |
| Octagon | 8 | 6 |
| Nonagon | 9 | 7 |
| Decagon | 10 | 8 |
| Hendecagon (or undecagon) | 11 | 9 |
| Dodecagon | 12 | 10 |

The rule that produces the third column is simple: take the number of sides $n$ and subtract $2$. A hexagon has 6 sides, so it divides into $6-2=4$ triangles; a pentagon has 5 sides, so it divides into $5-2=3$ triangles.

Worked example — triangles in a polygon How many triangles can a heptagon be divided into if you draw diagonals from one vertex to all the non-adjacent vertices? Solution. A heptagon has 7 sides. Use the rule: number of triangles $= n-2 = 7-2 = 5$. So a heptagon divides into 5 triangles, which matches the table.

practice.prompt: How many triangles can an octagon be divided into if you draw diagonals from one vertex to all the non-adjacent vertices?
practice.worked_solution: An octagon has 8 sides. Number of triangles $= n-2 = 8-2 = 6$.

practice.prompt: Name the triangle whose three sides are all equal, and state the size of each of its angles.
practice.answer: It is an equilateral triangle, and each of its three angles measures 60°.

practice.answer: The square has four lines of symmetry; the rectangle has two.

practice.prompt: State one difference between a parallelogram and a trapezium.
practice.answer: A parallelogram has two pairs of parallel sides, while a trapezium has only one pair of parallel sides.

practice.prompt: How many sides does a dodecagon have, and into how many triangles can it be divided?
practice.answer: A dodecagon has 12 sides and divides into 10 triangles.

blocks.text:
A circle is a plane shape with no corners: every point on its boundary is the same distance from its centre. The curved line that forms the round boundary of the circle is its **circumference**. fig-04 shows two labelled circles so you can see each part sitting on a real circle.

- The **centre** is the point in the middle of the circle.
- The **radius** (plural *radii*) is any straight line joining the centre to the circumference. In the second circle of fig-04 a radius is drawn from the centre out to the circumference, and the right-hand bounding line of the sector below is also a radius.
- A **chord** is any straight line joining two points on the circumference. The second circle in fig-04 has a chord drawn near the top.
- The **diameter** is any chord that passes through the centre of the circle. In the first circle of fig-04 the diameter is drawn straight across through the centre. Because it goes through the centre, it is the longest chord a circle can have, and it is twice as long as the radius.
- An **arc** is a curved part of the circumference. In the first circle of fig-04 a part of the circumference is marked and named the arc.

The figure also shows three more parts:
- A **segment** is the region of the circle cut off by a chord — the shaded part above the chord in the second circle.
- A **sector** is the region bounded by two radii and the arc between them — the shaded part below in the second circle, whose two straight sides are both radii.
- A **tangent** is a straight line that touches the circle at exactly one point, as shown touching the right side of the second circle.

The second has a chord near the top with the segment above it shaded, a shaded sector below with its right-hand bounding line labelled Radius, and a tangent touching it on the right.

sections.title: Finding the Perimeter of Plane Shapes

blocks.text:
The perimeter of a shape is the distance all the way round it. To find it you simply add the lengths of every side. For a straight-sided shape, this means adding each side once. For a circle, the perimeter has a special name — the circumference — and you find it using the radius (or diameter) and the number π (pi), which is about $\frac{22}{7}$ or 3.14.

Because some shapes have equal sides, you can often write a short formula instead of adding each side separately. Work through the examples below to see how each shape's perimeter is found.

Example 1 — a square. A square has four equal sides. In fig-05 each side is marked $L$ and measures 15cm. Its perimeter is four lengths added together: $$L + L + L + L = 4L$$ $$= 15 + 15 + 15 + 15 = 4(15) = 60\text{cm}.$$ Example 2 — a rectangle. A rectangle has two long sides $L$ and two short sides $b$. In fig-06, $L = 10\text{cm}$ and $b = 7\text{cm}$. Adding all four sides: $$P = L + b + L + b = 2L + 2b = 2(L + b)$$ $$= 2(10 + 7) = 2(17) = 34\text{cm}.$$ Example 3 — a missing side. Sometimes you are given the perimeter and one side and must find the other. Suppose a rectangle has perimeter 60cm and length 17cm (fig-07). Write the perimeter formula and solve for $b$: $$P = 2L + 2b$$ $$60 = 2(17) + 2b$$ $$60 = 34 + 2b$$ Collect like terms: $$60 - 34 = 2b$$ $$2b = 26$$ Divide both sides by 2: $$b = 13\text{cm}.$$

blocks.caption: A rectangle with both long sides marked $L = 17$cm and both short sides marked $b$.
A rectangle with both long sides marked $L$, the top one also 10cm, and both short sides marked $b$, the right-hand one also 7cm.
A square, named *Square* at its left, with all four sides marked twice — $L$ and 15cm.

blocks.text: Example 4 — a trapezium. A trapezium has four sides, usually of different lengths. In fig-08 they are $a = 11\text{cm}$, $b = 9\text{cm}$, $c = 5\text{cm}$ and $d = 4\text{cm}$. The perimeter is all four added: $$P = a + b + c + d$$ $$= 11 + 9 + 5 + 4 = 29\text{cm}.$$ Example 5 — a parallelogram. A parallelogram has opposite sides equal: two of length $a$ and two of length $b$ (fig-09, where $a = 9\text{cm}$ and $b = 5\text{cm}$). So $$P = a + a + b + b = 2a + 2b = 2(a + b)$$ $$= 2(9 + 5) = 2(14) = 28\text{cm}.$$ Example 6 — a regular hexagon. A regular hexagon has six equal sides. In fig-10 each side is 5.2cm, so $$P = 6 \times 5.2 = 31.2\text{cm}.$$

blocks.caption: A regular hexagon, named above the drawing, with each of its six sides marked 5.2cm.

A parallelogram with a single arrow on each of its four sides: the two horizontal ones both lettered $a$, the lower also measured 9cm, and the two slanted ones both lettered $b$, the right-hand one also measured 5cm.
A trapezium with each side lettered and measured: the top $c$, 5cm; the left $b$, 9cm; the right $d$, 4cm; the base $a$, 11cm.

blocks.text: Example 7 — a circle. The perimeter of a circle is its circumference, found with either formula: $$C = 2\pi r \quad\text{or}\quad C = \pi d.$$ In fig-11 the radius is 7cm, using $\pi = \frac{22}{7}$: $$C = 2 \times \frac{22}{7} \times 7 = 2 \times 22 = 44\text{cm}.$$ Using $\pi d$ instead: since $d = 2r = 2 \times 7 = 14\text{cm}$, $$C = \frac{22}{7} \times 14 = 22 \times 2 = 44\text{cm}.$$ Example 8 — a rope wound round a cylinder. One turn round the cylinder is one circumference. With radius 25cm and $\pi = 3.14$, $$C = 2\pi r = 2 \times 3.14 \times 25 = 157\text{cm}.$$ Wound 50 times, the rope's total length is $$157 \times 50 = 7850\text{cm}.$$ Example 9 — the radius from the circumference. If the circumference is 440cm, find $r$ ($\pi = \frac{22}{7}$): $$440 = 2\pi r = 2 \times \frac{22}{7} \times r = \frac{44r}{7}.$$ Cross-multiply: $$440 \times 7 = 44r \quad\Rightarrow\quad 3080 = 44r.$$ Divide both sides by 44: $$r = \frac{3080}{44} = 70\text{cm}.$$

blocks.caption: A circle with a radius drawn from the centre to the right of the circumference, marked 7cm.

blocks.text: Example 10 — a quarter circle. The shape in fig-14 is made of two straight sides of 4.9cm each and a curved part that is one quarter of a full circle. Its perimeter is the two straight sides plus that curved part. First find the curved part. It is $\frac{1}{4}$ of a full circumference: $$\frac{1}{4} \times 2\pi r = \frac{1}{4} \times 2 \times \frac{22}{7} \times 4.9$$ $$= \frac{1}{4} \times \frac{44}{7} \times 4.9 = \frac{11}{7} \times \frac{49}{10}$$ $$= \frac{11 \times 7}{10} = \frac{77}{10} = 7.7\text{cm}.$$ Now add the straight sides and the curved part: $$P = 4.9 + 4.9 + 7.7 = 17.5\text{cm}.$$

blocks.caption: A quarter circle: an upright side and a base meeting at a right angle, each marked 4.9cm, with an arc closing them from the top of the upright to the end of the base.
An upright cylinder with a rope wound round it, drawn as a series of turns spiralling down the body from the top face to the base.
A circle with a radius drawn from the centre to the right of the circumference, marked $r$.

practice.prompt: Find the perimeter of a square with sides of 8cm.
practice.worked_solution: A square has four equal sides, so $P = 4 \times 8 = 32\text{cm}$.

practice.prompt: Find the perimeter of a rectangle of length 7cm and breadth 4cm.
What is the perimeter of a regular pentagon with sides of 5cm?
practice.worked_solution: A regular pentagon has five equal sides, so $P = 5 \times 5 = 25\text{cm}$.

practice.prompt: Find the perimeter of a parallelogram whose base is 6cm and whose sides are 5cm.
practice.worked_solution: Opposite sides are equal, so $P = 2a + 2b = 2(6) + 2(5) = 12 + 10 = 22\text{cm}$.

practice.prompt: The circumference of a circle is 22cm. Find its radius $(\pi = \frac{22}{7})$.
practice.worked_solution: $C = 2\pi r$, so $22 = 2 \times \frac{22}{7} \times r = \frac{44r}{7}$. Cross-multiply: $22 \times 7 = 44r$, so $154 = 44r$, giving $r = \frac{154}{44} = 3.5\text{cm}$.

practice.prompt: A rectangle is such that its length is twice its breadth. If the breadth is $d$, find the total length of the sides of the rectangle.
practice.worked_solution: Length $= 2d$ and breadth $= d$. Perimeter $= 2(\text{length} + \text{breadth}) = 2(2d + d) = 2(3d) = 6d$.

practice.prompt: Find the perimeter of a regular hexagon with sides of 5cm.
practice.worked_solution: A regular hexagon has six equal sides, so $P = 6 \times 5 = 30\text{cm}$.
