sections.title: Plane Shapes: What They Are and How They Differ

blocks.text:
**Plane shapes** are also called **two-dimensional (2-D) shapes** — shapes that lie flat on a single surface. They include triangles, squares, rectangles, parallelograms, trapeziums, circles and many other polygons. In this section you will learn to recognise each of these shapes, state their properties, and see how they are similar to and different from one another.

The common shapes come in a few families. We will look at them family by family, and for each one we will list its properties so you can compare one shape with the next.

**Triangles** are closed shapes with three straight sides. They are grouped by whether their sides and angles are equal. Look at fig-01.

| Isosceles | Scalene | Equilateral |
|---|---|---|
| (i) 2 adjacent sides are equal | No side is equal | 3 sides are equal |
| (ii) base angles are equal | No angle equals another | All angles are equal, $60^\circ$ each |
| (iii) one line of symmetry | No line of symmetry | 3 lines of symmetry |

So the *isosceles* triangle has two equal sides and two equal base angles, and one line of symmetry. The *scalene* triangle has all three sides different, all three angles different, and no line of symmetry. The *equilateral* triangle has all three sides equal, all three angles equal to $60^\circ$, and three lines of symmetry.

blocks.caption: Isosceles: a single tick on each of the two slanted sides, an arc at each base angle. Scalene: one, two and three ticks on the three sides, an arc at each vertex. Equilateral: a single tick on each of the three sides, an arc at each vertex.

blocks.text:
**Squares and rectangles** are both four-sided shapes whose corners are all right angles ($90^\circ$). The difference is in their sides. Look at fig-02.

| Squares | Rectangles |
|---|---|
| (i) All sides are equal | Only the 2 opposite sides are equal |
| (ii) 2 pairs of parallel sides | 2 pairs of parallel sides |
| (iii) All angles are equal, $90^\circ$ each | All angles are equal, $90^\circ$ each |
| (iv) Four lines of symmetry | Two lines of symmetry |
| (v) Diagonals bisect it at a right angle | Diagonals bisect it but not at a right angle |

A square is really a special rectangle: it has everything a rectangle has, and on top of that *all four sides are equal* and its diagonals meet at a right angle.

blocks.caption: Square: a right-angle mark at each corner, a single tick on each of the four sides. Rectangle: a right-angle mark at each corner, a single tick on each of the two longer sides and a double tick on each of the two shorter sides.

blocks.text:
**Parallelograms and trapeziums** are also four-sided, but their sides are not all right angles. Look at fig-03.

| Parallelogram | Trapezium |
|---|---|
| (i) 2 pairs of opposite sides are equal and parallel | Only one pair of sides is parallel |
| (ii) opposite angles are equal | opposite angles are not equal |
| (iii) No line of symmetry | No line of symmetry |
| (iv) Diagonals divide it into equal triangles | A diagonal divides it into two unequal triangles |

The key difference is the parallel sides. A *parallelogram* has two pairs of parallel sides (opposite sides equal and parallel), while a *trapezium* has only one pair of parallel sides. Neither has a line of symmetry.

blocks.caption: Parallelogram: a single arrow on each of the two horizontal sides, a double arrow on each of the two slanted sides. Trapezium: a single arrow on each of the two parallel sides, and one diagonal drawn in.

blocks.text:
**Polygons** are closed shapes with three or more straight sides. A polygon with $n$ sides can be split into $n-2$ triangles by drawing diagonals from one vertex to all the non-adjacent vertices.

| Name of Polygon | Number of sides | Number of triangles $(n-2)$ |
|---|---|---|
| Triangle | 3 | 1 |
| Quadrilateral | 4 | 2 |
| Pentagon | 5 | 3 |
| Hexagon | 6 | 4 |
| Heptagon | 7 | 5 |
| Octagon | 8 | 6 |
| Nonagon | 9 | 7 |
| Decagon | 10 | 8 |
| Hendecagon (undecagon) | 11 | 9 |
| Dodecagon | 12 | 10 |

Notice the pattern: the number of triangles is always two less than the number of sides. A pentagon (5 sides) splits into $5-2=3$ triangles, a hexagon (6 sides) into $6-2=4$, and so on.

Now let's pull the properties together and compare shapes side by side.

**Square versus parallelogram** — Both have two pairs of parallel sides and their diagonals divide them into equal triangles. But a square has all four angles equal to $90^\circ$ and four lines of symmetry, while a parallelogram has no line of symmetry and its angles are not all right angles.

**Equilateral triangle versus scalene triangle** — Both are triangles with three straight sides. But an equilateral triangle has three equal sides, three equal angles ($60^\circ$ each) and three lines of symmetry, while a scalene triangle has all three sides and angles different and no line of symmetry.

**Worked example — comparing a rectangle and a trapezium**

A learner is asked: *State two ways a rectangle is different from a trapezium.*

- A rectangle has **two pairs** of parallel sides and all its angles are $90^\circ$; a trapezium has only **one pair** of parallel sides.
- A rectangle has two lines of symmetry; a trapezium has no line of symmetry.

So the two differences we could name are the number of parallel sides and the presence or absence of lines of symmetry.

practice.prompt: How many triangles can an octagon be divided into if you draw diagonals from one vertex to all the non-adjacent vertices?
practice.answer: An octagon has 8 sides, so it divides into $8 - 2 = 6$ triangles.

practice.prompt: Name two ways an isosceles triangle is different from an equilateral triangle.
practice.answer: Any two of: an isosceles triangle has only 2 equal sides while an equilateral has all 3 sides equal; an isosceles has only 2 equal (base) angles while an equilateral has all 3 angles equal at $60^\circ$; an isosceles has one line of symmetry while an equilateral has three.

practice.prompt: State the one key difference between a parallelogram and a trapezium when it comes to their parallel sides.
practice.answer: A parallelogram has two pairs of parallel sides, while a trapezium has only one pair of parallel sides.

- The **centre** is the point in the middle of the circle.
- The **radius** (plural *radii*) is any straight line joining the centre to the circumference. In the second circle of fig-04 a radius is drawn from the centre out to the circumference, and the right-hand bounding line of the sector below is also a radius.
- A **chord** is any straight line joining two points on the circumference. The second circle in fig-04 has a chord drawn near the top.

sections.title: Finding the Perimeter of Plane Shapes

blocks.text:
**Perimeter** is the total distance round the outside of a shape. To find it, you add up the lengths of all the shape's sides. For shapes whose sides are equal, you can multiply instead of adding.

The perimeter of a **regular polygon** (a shape with all sides equal, like a square, an equilateral triangle or a regular hexagon) is easy: multiply the length of one side by the number of sides.

For a **rectangle**, opposite sides are equal, so the two long sides are equal and the two short sides are equal. If the length is $L$ and the breadth (short side) is $b$:

$$\text{Perimeter} = L + b + L + b = 2L + 2b = 2(L + b)$$

A **square** is a rectangle whose four sides are all equal, so if its side is $L$:

$$\text{Perimeter} = L + L + L + L = 4L$$

A **parallelogram** has two pairs of equal, opposite sides, so like a rectangle:

$$\text{Perimeter} = 2(a + b)$$

where $a$ is the base and $b$ is one of the slanted sides. A **trapezium** has four sides that are generally all different, so you simply add all four:

$$\text{Perimeter} = a + b + c + d$$

The perimeter of a **circle** has its own name — the **circumference** — and it depends on the radius $r$ (the distance from the centre to the edge) or the diameter $d$ (twice the radius):

$$\text{Circumference} = 2\pi r = \pi d$$

where $\pi$ is about $3.14$ or $\frac{22}{7}$.

**Worked example — perimeter of a square**

A square has side $15\text{cm}$. Find its perimeter.

The square has four equal sides, so its perimeter is $4$ times one side:

$$\text{Perimeter} = 4L = 4 \times 15 = 60\text{cm}$$

**Worked example — perimeter of a rectangle**

A rectangle has length $10\text{cm}$ and breadth $7\text{cm}$. Find its perimeter.

$$\text{Perimeter} = 2(L + b) = 2(10 + 7) = 2(17) = 34\text{cm}$$

You get the same answer by adding the four sides: $10 + 7 + 10 + 7 = 34\text{cm}$.

**Worked example — finding a missing breadth**

The perimeter of a rectangle is $60\text{cm}$ and its length is $17\text{cm}$. Find its breadth $b$.

$$\text{Perimeter} = 2(L + b)$$

$$60 = 2(17 + b)$$

Expand the bracket:

$$60 = 34 + 2b$$

Collect like terms — take $34$ away from both sides:

$$60 - 34 = 2b$$

$$26 = 2b$$

Divide both sides by $2$:

$$b = 13\text{cm}$$

So the breadth is $13\text{cm}$.

**Worked example — perimeter of a trapezium**

A trapezium has sides $11\text{cm}$, $9\text{cm}$, $5\text{cm}$ and $4\text{cm}$. Find its perimeter.

The four sides are all different, so add them all:

$$\text{Perimeter} = 11 + 9 + 5 + 4 = 29\text{cm}$$

**Worked example — perimeter of a parallelogram**

A parallelogram has base $9\text{cm}$ and slanted side $5\text{cm}$. Find its perimeter.

A parallelogram has two pairs of equal sides, so:

$$\text{Perimeter} = 2(a + b) = 2(9 + 5) = 2(14) = 28\text{cm}$$

**Worked example — perimeter of a regular hexagon**

A regular hexagon has sides $5.2\text{cm}$. Find its perimeter.

A hexagon has $6$ sides, all equal:

$$\text{Perimeter} = 6 \times 5.2 = 31.2\text{cm}$$

**Worked example — circumference of a circle**

A circle has radius $7\text{cm}$. Calculate its perimeter (circumference), using $\pi = \frac{22}{7}$.

$$\text{Circumference} = 2\pi r = 2 \times \frac{22}{7} \times 7 = 2 \times 22 = 44\text{cm}$$

You can use the diameter instead. Since $d = 2r = 2 \times 7 = 14\text{cm}$:

$$\text{Circumference} = \pi d = \frac{22}{7} \times 14 = 22 \times 2 = 44\text{cm}$$

Both ways give the same answer.

**Worked example — finding the radius from the circumference**

The circumference of a circle is $440\text{cm}$. Find its radius, using $\pi = \frac{22}{7}$.

$$\text{Circumference} = 2\pi r$$

$$440 = 2 \times \frac{22}{7} \times r = \frac{44r}{7}$$

Cross-multiply:

$$440 \times 7 = 44r$$

$$3080 = 44r$$

Divide both sides by $44$:

$$r = \frac{3080}{44} = 70\text{cm}$$

So the radius is $70\text{cm}$.

**Worked example — perimeter of a quarter circle**

The shape below is a quarter circle: two straight sides each $4.9\text{cm}$ meeting at a right angle, closed by a curved arc (fig-14). Calculate its perimeter.

A quarter circle has $\frac{1}{4}$ of a full circumference as its curved part:

$$\text{curved part} = \frac{1}{4} \times 2\pi r = \frac{1}{4} \times 2 \times \frac{22}{7} \times 4.9 = 7.7\text{cm}$$

The perimeter is the two straight sides plus the curved part:

$$\text{Perimeter} = 4.9 + 4.9 + 7.7 = 17.5\text{cm}$$

Notice that the straight sides of a quarter circle are the two radii of the circle, each equal to $4.9\text{cm}$.

**Worked example — applying the circumference**

A rope is wound $50$ times round a cylinder of radius $25\text{cm}$. How long is the rope, using $\pi = 3.14$?

Each turn of the rope goes round once, so one turn is one circumference:

$$\text{Circumference} = 2\pi r = 2 \times 3.14 \times 25 = 157\text{cm}$$

Fifty turns give:

$$\text{Total length} = 157 \times 50 = 7850\text{cm}$$

practice.worked_solution: $\text{Perimeter} = 2(L + b) = 2(7 + 4) = 2(11) = 22\text{cm}$.

practice.prompt: What is the perimeter of a regular pentagon with sides $5\text{cm}$?
practice.worked_solution: A pentagon has $5$ equal sides, so $\text{Perimeter} = 5 \times 5 = 25\text{cm}$.

practice.prompt: Find the perimeter of a parallelogram whose base is $6\text{cm}$ and slanted sides are $5\text{cm}$.
practice.worked_solution: $\text{Perimeter} = 2(a + b) = 2(6 + 5) = 2(11) = 22\text{cm}$.

practice.prompt: The circumference of a circle is $22\text{cm}$. Find its radius, using $\pi = \frac{22}{7}$.
practice.worked_solution: $\text{Circumference} = 2\pi r$, so $22 = 2 \times \frac{22}{7} \times r = \frac{44r}{7}$. Cross-multiplying: $22 \times 7 = 44r$, so $154 = 44r$, and $r = \frac{154}{44} = \frac{7}{2} = 3.5\text{cm}$.

practice.prompt: A rectangle is such that its length is twice its breadth. If the breadth is $d$, find the total length of the sides of the rectangle.
practice.worked_solution: Breadth $= d$, length $= 2d$. There are two breadths and two lengths, so total $= 2d + 2(2d) = 2d + 4d = 6d$.

sections.title: Plane Shapes: Their Types, Properties, Similarities and Differences

blocks.text: Plane shapes are shapes that lie flat on a surface, so they are also called two-dimensional shapes (2-D shapes). The plane shapes you will meet include the triangle, the square, the rectangle, the parallelogram, the trapezium, the circle and other polygons. A polygon is any closed shape that has three or more straight sides. Let us look at each family of plane shapes, its properties, and how the shapes are similar to or different from one another.

Look at the three triangles in fig-01: the isosceles, the scalene and the equilateral. Their names tell you how their sides compare. - An isosceles triangle has two adjacent sides equal (the two slanted sides carry a single tick each). Its base angles are equal, and it has one line of symmetry. - A scalene triangle has no side equal to another — each side carries a different number of ticks (one, two, three). No angle is equal to another, and it has no line of symmetry. - An equilateral triangle has all three sides equal (a single tick on each side). All three angles are equal, each measuring $60^\circ$, and it has three lines of symmetry. So the key differences come down to how many sides are equal: an equilateral has three equal sides, an isosceles has two, and a scalene has none.

blocks.caption: Isosceles: a single tick on each of the two slanted sides, an arc at each base angle. Scalene: one, two and three ticks on the three sides, an arc at each vertex. Equilateral: a single tick on each of the three sides, an arc at each vertex.

blocks.text: Now compare the square and the rectangle in fig-02. Each has a right-angle mark at every corner, so both have all angles equal, each measuring $90^\circ$, and both have two pairs of parallel sides. The difference lies in the sides. - A square has all four sides equal (a single tick on every side). It has four lines of symmetry, and its diagonals bisect each other at a right angle. - A rectangle has only two opposite sides equal — the two longer sides carry a single tick each and the two shorter sides a double tick each. It has two lines of symmetry, and its diagonals bisect each other but not at a right angle.

blocks.caption: Square: a right-angle mark at each corner, a single tick on each of the four sides. Rectangle: a right-angle mark at each corner, a single tick on each of the two longer sides and a double tick on each of the two shorter sides.

blocks.text: Finally, compare the parallelogram and the trapezium in fig-03. - A parallelogram has two pairs of opposite sides equal and parallel (its two horizontal sides carry a single arrow and its two slanted sides a double arrow). Its opposite angles are equal, it has no line of symmetry, and its diagonals divide it into two equal triangles. - A trapezium has only one pair of parallel sides (the two parallel sides carry a single arrow each, and one diagonal is drawn in). Its opposite angles are not equal, it has no line of symmetry, and its diagonal divides it into two unequal triangles. The great difference between them is the number of parallel sides: a parallelogram has two pairs, a trapezium has only one pair.

blocks.caption: Parallelogram: a single arrow on each of the two horizontal sides, a double arrow on each of the two slanted sides. Trapezium: a single arrow on each of the two parallel sides, and one diagonal drawn in.

blocks.text:
Polygons come in many forms, and each is named by its number of straight sides. The table below lists the common polygons, their number of sides, and how many triangles each can be divided into by drawing diagonals from one vertex to all the non-adjacent vertices.

| Name of polygon | Number of sides | Number of triangles ($n-2$) |
|---|---|---|
| Triangle | 3 | 1 |
| Quadrilateral | 4 | 2 |
| Pentagon | 5 | 3 |
| Hexagon | 6 | 4 |
| Heptagon | 7 | 5 |
| Octagon | 8 | 6 |
| Nonagon | 9 | 7 |
| Decagon | 10 | 8 |
| Hendecagon (or undecagon) | 11 | 9 |
| Dodecagon | 12 | 10 |

The rule that produces the third column is simple: take the number of sides $n$ and subtract $2$. A hexagon has 6 sides, so it divides into $6-2=4$ triangles; a pentagon has 5 sides, so it divides into $5-2=3$ triangles.

Worked example — triangles in a polygon How many triangles can a heptagon be divided into if you draw diagonals from one vertex to all the non-adjacent vertices? Solution. A heptagon has 7 sides. Use the rule: number of triangles $= n-2 = 7-2 = 5$. So a heptagon divides into 5 triangles, which matches the table.

practice.prompt: How many triangles can an octagon be divided into if you draw diagonals from one vertex to all the non-adjacent vertices?
practice.worked_solution: An octagon has 8 sides. Number of triangles $= n-2 = 8-2 = 6$.

practice.prompt: Name the triangle whose three sides are all equal, and state the size of each of its angles.
practice.answer: It is an equilateral triangle, and each of its three angles measures 60°.

practice.prompt: Which of the square and the rectangle has four lines of symmetry?
practice.answer: The square has four lines of symmetry; the rectangle has two.

practice.prompt: State one difference between a parallelogram and a trapezium.
practice.answer: A parallelogram has two pairs of parallel sides, while a trapezium has only one pair of parallel sides.

practice.prompt: How many sides does a dodecagon have, and into how many triangles can it be divided?
practice.answer: A dodecagon has 12 sides and divides into 10 triangles.
practice.worked_solution: Number of triangles $= n-2 = 12-2 = 10$.

blocks.text:
A circle is a plane shape with no corners: every point on its boundary is the same distance from its centre. The curved line that forms the round boundary of the circle is its **circumference**. fig-04 shows two labelled circles so you can see each part sitting on a real circle.

- The **centre** is the point in the middle of the circle.
- The **radius** (plural *radii*) is any straight line joining the centre to the circumference. In the second circle of fig-04 a radius is drawn from the centre out to the circumference, and the right-hand bounding line of the sector below is also a radius.
- A **chord** is any straight line joining two points on the circumference. The second circle in fig-04 has a chord drawn near the top.
- The **diameter** is any chord that passes through the centre of the circle. In the first circle of fig-04 the diameter is drawn straight across through the centre. Because it goes through the centre, it is the longest chord a circle can have, and it is twice as long as the radius.
- An **arc** is a curved part of the circumference. In the first circle of fig-04 a part of the circumference is marked and named the arc.

The figure also shows three more parts:
- A **segment** is the region of the circle cut off by a chord — the shaded part above the chord in the second circle.
- A **sector** is the region bounded by two radii and the arc between them — the shaded part below in the second circle, whose two straight sides are both radii.
- A **tangent** is a straight line that touches the circle at exactly one point, as shown touching the right side of the second circle.

The second has a chord near the top with the segment above it shaded, a shaded sector below with its right-hand bounding line labelled Radius, and a tangent touching it on the right.

sections.title: Finding the Perimeter of Plane Shapes

blocks.text:
The perimeter of a shape is the distance all the way round it. To find it you simply add the lengths of every side. For a straight-sided shape, this means adding each side once. For a circle, the perimeter has a special name — the circumference — and you find it using the radius (or diameter) and the number π (pi), which is about $\frac{22}{7}$ or 3.14.

Because some shapes have equal sides, you can often write a short formula instead of adding each side separately. Work through the examples below to see how each shape's perimeter is found.

Example 1 — a square. A square has four equal sides. In fig-05 each side is marked $L$ and measures 15cm. Its perimeter is four lengths added together: $$L + L + L + L = 4L$$ $$= 15 + 15 + 15 + 15 = 4(15) = 60\text{cm}.$$ Example 2 — a rectangle. A rectangle has two long sides $L$ and two short sides $b$. In fig-06, $L = 10\text{cm}$ and $b = 7\text{cm}$. Adding all four sides: $$P = L + b + L + b = 2L + 2b = 2(L + b)$$ $$= 2(10 + 7) = 2(17) = 34\text{cm}.$$ Example 3 — a missing side. Sometimes you are given the perimeter and one side and must find the other. Suppose a rectangle has perimeter 60cm and length 17cm (fig-07). Write the perimeter formula and solve for $b$: $$P = 2L + 2b$$ $$60 = 2(17) + 2b$$ $$60 = 34 + 2b$$ Collect like terms: $$60 - 34 = 2b$$ $$2b = 26$$ Divide both sides by 2: $$b = 13\text{cm}.$$

blocks.caption: A rectangle with both long sides marked $L = 17$cm and both short sides marked $b$.
A rectangle with both long sides marked $L$, the top one also 10cm, and both short sides marked $b$, the right-hand one also 7cm.
A square, named *Square* at its left, with all four sides marked twice — $L$ and 15cm.

blocks.text: Example 4 — a trapezium. A trapezium has four sides, usually of different lengths. In fig-08 they are $a = 11\text{cm}$, $b = 9\text{cm}$, $c = 5\text{cm}$ and $d = 4\text{cm}$. The perimeter is all four added: $$P = a + b + c + d$$ $$= 11 + 9 + 5 + 4 = 29\text{cm}.$$ Example 5 — a parallelogram. A parallelogram has opposite sides equal: two of length $a$ and two of length $b$ (fig-09, where $a = 9\text{cm}$ and $b = 5\text{cm}$). So $$P = a + a + b + b = 2a + 2b = 2(a + b)$$ $$= 2(9 + 5) = 2(14) = 28\text{cm}.$$ Example 6 — a regular hexagon. A regular hexagon has six equal sides. In fig-10 each side is 5.2cm, so $$P = 6 \times 5.2 = 31.2\text{cm}.$$

blocks.caption: A regular hexagon, named above the drawing, with each of its six sides marked 5.2cm.

A parallelogram with a single arrow on each of its four sides: the two horizontal ones both lettered $a$, the lower also measured 9cm, and the two slanted ones both lettered $b$, the right-hand one also measured 5cm.
A trapezium with each side lettered and measured: the top $c$, 5cm; the left $b$, 9cm; the right $d$, 4cm; the base $a$, 11cm.

blocks.text: Example 7 — a circle. The perimeter of a circle is its circumference, found with either formula: $$C = 2\pi r \quad\text{or}\quad C = \pi d.$$ In fig-11 the radius is 7cm, using $\pi = \frac{22}{7}$: $$C = 2 \times \frac{22}{7} \times 7 = 2 \times 22 = 44\text{cm}.$$ Using $\pi d$ instead: since $d = 2r = 2 \times 7 = 14\text{cm}$, $$C = \frac{22}{7} \times 14 = 22 \times 2 = 44\text{cm}.$$ Example 8 — a rope wound round a cylinder. One turn round the cylinder is one circumference. With radius 25cm and $\pi = 3.14$, $$C = 2\pi r = 2 \times 3.14 \times 25 = 157\text{cm}.$$ Wound 50 times, the rope's total length is $$157 \times 50 = 7850\text{cm}.$$ Example 9 — the radius from the circumference. If the circumference is 440cm, find $r$ ($\pi = \frac{22}{7}$): $$440 = 2\pi r = 2 \times \frac{22}{7} \times r = \frac{44r}{7}.$$ Cross-multiply: $$440 \times 7 = 44r \quad\Rightarrow\quad 3080 = 44r.$$ Divide both sides by 44: $$r = \frac{3080}{44} = 70\text{cm}.$$

blocks.caption: A circle with a radius drawn from the centre to the right of the circumference, marked 7cm.

blocks.text: Example 10 — a quarter circle. The shape in fig-14 is made of two straight sides of 4.9cm each and a curved part that is one quarter of a full circle. Its perimeter is the two straight sides plus that curved part. First find the curved part. It is $\frac{1}{4}$ of a full circumference: $$\frac{1}{4} \times 2\pi r = \frac{1}{4} \times 2 \times \frac{22}{7} \times 4.9$$ $$= \frac{1}{4} \times \frac{44}{7} \times 4.9 = \frac{11}{7} \times \frac{49}{10}$$ $$= \frac{11 \times 7}{10} = \frac{77}{10} = 7.7\text{cm}.$$ Now add the straight sides and the curved part: $$P = 4.9 + 4.9 + 7.7 = 17.5\text{cm}.$$

blocks.caption: A quarter circle: an upright side and a base meeting at a right angle, each marked 4.9cm, with an arc closing them from the top of the upright to the end of the base.
An upright cylinder with a rope wound round it, drawn as a series of turns spiralling down the body from the top face to the base.
A circle with a radius drawn from the centre to the right of the circumference, marked $r$.

blocks.text: Plane shapes lie flat on a surface, so they are also called **two-dimensional shapes (2-D shapes)**. The families you will compare are triangles, squares, rectangles, parallelograms, trapeziums, the circle, and other polygons. A **polygon** is any closed shape with three or more straight sides. As you compare shapes, keep two questions in mind: *How many sides are equal?* and *How many pairs of sides are parallel?* These two comparisons separate almost every shape in this section.

Look at the three triangles in **fig-01**: the isosceles, the scalene and the equilateral. Tick marks on the sides carry the classification.

- An **isosceles** triangle has two adjacent sides equal (a single tick on each slanted side). Its base angles are equal, and it has one line of symmetry.
- A **scalene** triangle has no two sides equal (one, two and three ticks on its sides). None of its angles equals another, and it has no line of symmetry.
- An **equilateral** triangle has all three sides equal (a single tick on each side). All its angles are equal, each $60^\circ$, and it has three lines of symmetry.

So the family difference is the number of equal sides: three, two, or none.

blocks.caption: Isosceles: a single tick on each of the two slanted sides, an arc at each base angle. Scalene: one, two and three ticks on the three sides, an arc at each vertex. Equilateral: a single tick on each of the three sides, an arc at each vertex.

blocks.text:
Compare the square and the rectangle in **fig-02**. Every corner carries a right-angle mark, so both have all angles equal, each measuring $90^\circ$, and both have two pairs of parallel sides. The differences are:

- A **square** has all four sides equal (a single tick on each side). It has four lines of symmetry, and its diagonals bisect each other at a right angle.
- A **rectangle** has only opposite sides equal: the two longer sides carry a single tick each and the two shorter sides a double tick each. It has two lines of symmetry, and its diagonals bisect each other but not at a right angle.

blocks.caption: Square: a right-angle mark at each corner, a single tick on each of the four sides. Rectangle: a right-angle mark at each corner, a single tick on each of the two longer sides and a double tick on each of the two shorter sides.

blocks.text:
Finally, compare the parallelogram and the trapezium in **fig-03**.

- A **parallelogram** has two pairs of opposite sides equal and parallel. Its opposite angles are equal, it has no line of symmetry, and its diagonals divide it into two equal triangles.
- A **trapezium** has only one pair of parallel sides. Its opposite angles are not equal, it has no line of symmetry, and its diagonal divides it into two unequal triangles.

The decisive difference is the number of parallel sides: a parallelogram has two pairs, while a trapezium has only one pair.

blocks.caption: Parallelogram: a single arrow on each of the two horizontal sides, a double arrow on each of the two slanted sides. Trapezium: a single arrow on each of the two parallel sides, and one diagonal drawn in.

blocks.text:
Polygons are named by their number of straight sides. The table lists common polygons and the number of triangles each can be divided into by drawing diagonals from one vertex to all non-adjacent vertices.

| Name of polygon | Number of sides | Number of triangles ($n-2$) |
|---|---|---|
| Triangle | 3 | 1 |
| Quadrilateral | 4 | 2 |
| Pentagon | 5 | 3 |
| Hexagon | 6 | 4 |
| Heptagon | 7 | 5 |
| Octagon | 8 | 6 |
| Nonagon | 9 | 7 |
| Decagon | 10 | 8 |
| Hendecagon (or undecagon) | 11 | 9 |
| Dodecagon | 12 | 10 |

The rule in the third column is: subtract 2 from the number of sides. A hexagon has $6$ sides, so it forms $6-2=4$ triangles; a dodecagon has $12$ sides, so it forms $12-2=10$ triangles.

**Worked example — comparing polygons by triangles**

How many more triangles does a dodecagon form than an octagon when diagonals are drawn from one vertex to all non-adjacent vertices?

**Solution.** A dodecagon has $12$ sides, so $12-2=10$ triangles. An octagon has $8$ sides, so $8-2=6$ triangles. The difference is $10-6=4$.

So a dodecagon forms **4 more triangles** than an octagon.

sections.title: Finding the Perimeter of Plane Shapes

blocks.text:
The **perimeter** of a shape is the total distance all the way round it. To find a perimeter you simply add up the lengths of every side that makes the outline of the shape. For a shape with equal sides — like a square, a regular polygon or a circle — you can multiply instead of adding.

Here are the shapes you will meet and how their perimeters are found:

- **Square** – all four sides equal. Perimeter $= 4 \times \text{side}$.
- **Rectangle** – two long sides (length, $L$) and two short sides (breadth, $b$). Perimeter $= 2L + 2b$.
- **Regular polygon** – all its sides equal, so Perimeter $= \text{number of sides} \times \text{length of one side}$.
- **Trapezium** – four sides, each a different length, so just add all four: $a + b + c + d$.
- **Parallelogram** – two pairs of equal sides. Perimeter $= 2a + 2b$ where $a$ and $b$ are the two different side lengths.
- **Circle** – its perimeter is called the **circumference**. Circumference $= 2\pi r$ or $\pi d$, where $r$ is the radius and $d$ the diameter. A common value to use is $\pi = \frac{22}{7}$.

**Example 1 — a square.** Calculate the perimeter of a square of side 15 cm (fig-05).

A square has four equal sides, so:
$$\text{Perimeter} = 4 \times \text{side} = 4(15) = 60\ \mathrm{cm}.$$

**Example 2 — a rectangle.** Find the perimeter of a rectangle whose length is 10 cm and breadth is 7 cm (fig-06).

Perimeter $= 2L + 2b = 2(10) + 2(7) = 20 + 14 = 34\ \mathrm{cm}$.
Another way: $2(L + b) = 2(10 + 7) = 2(17) = 34\ \mathrm{cm}$.

**Example 3 — finding a missing side.** The perimeter of a rectangle is 60 cm and its length is 17 cm (fig-07). Find its breadth.

Write the perimeter formula and put in what we know:
$$60 = 2(17) + 2b$$
$$60 = 34 + 2b$$
Collect like terms: $2b = 60 - 34 = 26$, so $b = \frac{26}{2} = 13\ \mathrm{cm}$.

**Example 4 — a trapezium.** Find the perimeter of the trapezium (fig-08) whose sides are 11 cm, 9 cm, 5 cm and 4 cm.

Just add the four sides:
$$\text{Perimeter} = 11 + 9 + 5 + 4 = 29\ \mathrm{cm}.$$

**Example 5 — a parallelogram.** Find the perimeter of the parallelogram (fig-09) whose base $a = 9$ cm and other side $b = 5$ cm.

Each length appears twice:
$$\text{Perimeter} = 2a + 2b = 2(9) + 2(5) = 18 + 10 = 28\ \mathrm{cm}.$$

**Example 6 — a regular hexagon.** Find the perimeter of a regular hexagon whose sides are 5.2 cm (fig-10).

A hexagon has 6 equal sides:
$$\text{Perimeter} = 6 \times 5.2 = 31.2\ \mathrm{cm}.$$

**Example 7 — a circle.** Calculate the circumference of a circle of radius 7 cm, using $\pi = \frac{22}{7}$ (fig-11).

$$\text{Circumference} = 2\pi r = 2 \times \frac{22}{7} \times 7 = 2 \times 22 = 44\ \mathrm{cm}.$$

**Example 8 — a quarter circle.** Calculate the perimeter of the quarter circle (fig-14) with two straight sides of 4.9 cm each.

A quarter circle takes one quarter of a full circle's circumference. The curved part is:
$$\tfrac{1}{4} \times 2\pi r = \tfrac{1}{4} \times 2 \times \tfrac{22}{7} \times 4.9 = 7.7\ \mathrm{cm}.$$
Add the two straight sides:
$$\text{Perimeter} = 4.9 + 4.9 + 7.7 = 17.5\ \mathrm{cm}.$$

blocks.caption: A quarter circle: an upright side and a base meeting at a right angle, each marked 4.9cm, with an arc closing them from the top of the upright to the end of the base.

blocks.text:
Sometimes you are given the circumference and asked to work back to the radius.

**Example 9 — finding the radius.** The circumference of a circle is 440 cm. Find its radius, using $\pi = \frac{22}{7}$ (fig-13).

$$\text{Circumference} = 2\pi r$$
$$440 = 2 \times \frac{22}{7} \times r = \frac{44r}{7}$$
Cross-multiply: $440 \times 7 = 44r$, so $3080 = 44r$.
Divide both sides by 44: $r = \frac{3080}{44} = 70\ \mathrm{cm}$.

**Example 10 — a rope round a cylinder.** A rope is wound 50 times round a cylinder of radius 25 cm. How long is the rope? Take $\pi = 3.14$.

Each turn of the rope goes once round the cylinder, so one turn is one circumference:
$$\text{Circumference} = 2\pi r = 2 \times 3.14 \times 25 = 157\ \mathrm{cm}.$$
Fifty turns give the total length of the rope:
$$\text{Total} = 157 \times 50 = 7850\ \mathrm{cm}.$$

sections.title: Plane Shapes: Their Types, Properties, Similarities and Differences

blocks.text: Plane shapes are shapes that lie flat on a surface, so they are also called two-dimensional shapes (2-D shapes). The plane shapes you will meet include the triangle, the square, the rectangle, the parallelogram, the trapezium, the circle and other polygons. A polygon is any closed shape that has three or more straight sides. Let us look at each family of plane shapes, its properties, and how the shapes are similar to or different from one another.

Look at the three triangles in fig-01: the isosceles, the scalene and the equilateral. Their names tell you how their sides compare. - An isosceles triangle has two adjacent sides equal (the two slanted sides carry a single tick each). Its base angles are equal, and it has one line of symmetry. - A scalene triangle has no side equal to another — each side carries a different number of ticks (one, two, three). No angle is equal to another, and it has no line of symmetry. - An equilateral triangle has all three sides equal (a single tick on each side). All three angles are equal, each measuring $60^\circ$, and it has three lines of symmetry. So the key differences come down to how many sides are equal: an equilateral has three equal sides, an isosceles has two, and a scalene has none.

blocks.caption: Isosceles: a single tick on each of the two slanted sides, an arc at each base angle. Scalene: one, two and three ticks on the three sides, an arc at each vertex. Equilateral: a single tick on each of the three sides, an arc at each vertex.

blocks.text: Now compare the square and the rectangle in fig-02. Each has a right-angle mark at every corner, so both have all angles equal, each measuring $90^\circ$, and both have two pairs of parallel sides. The difference lies in the sides. - A square has all four sides equal (a single tick on every side). It has four lines of symmetry, and its diagonals bisect each other at a right angle. - A rectangle has only two opposite sides equal — the two longer sides carry a single tick each and the two shorter sides a double tick each. It has two lines of symmetry, and its diagonals bisect each other but not at a right angle.

blocks.caption: Square: a right-angle mark at each corner, a single tick on each of the four sides. Rectangle: a right-angle mark at each corner, a single tick on each of the two longer sides and a double tick on each of the two shorter sides.

blocks.text: Finally, compare the parallelogram and the trapezium in fig-03. - A parallelogram has two pairs of opposite sides equal and parallel (its two horizontal sides carry a single arrow and its two slanted sides a double arrow). Its opposite angles are equal, it has no line of symmetry, and its diagonals divide it into two equal triangles. - A trapezium has only one pair of parallel sides (the two parallel sides carry a single arrow each, and one diagonal is drawn in). Its opposite angles are not equal, it has no line of symmetry, and its diagonal divides it into two unequal triangles. The great difference between them is the number of parallel sides: a parallelogram has two pairs, a trapezium has only one pair.

blocks.caption: Parallelogram: a single arrow on each of the two horizontal sides, a double arrow on each of the two slanted sides. Trapezium: a single arrow on each of the two parallel sides, and one diagonal drawn in.

blocks.text:
Polygons come in many forms, and each is named by its number of straight sides. The table below lists the common polygons, their number of sides, and how many triangles each can be divided into by drawing diagonals from one vertex to all the non-adjacent vertices.

| Name of polygon | Number of sides | Number of triangles ($n-2$) |
|---|---|---|
| Triangle | 3 | 1 |
| Quadrilateral | 4 | 2 |
| Pentagon | 5 | 3 |
| Hexagon | 6 | 4 |
| Heptagon | 7 | 5 |
| Octagon | 8 | 6 |
| Nonagon | 9 | 7 |
| Decagon | 10 | 8 |
| Hendecagon (or undecagon) | 11 | 9 |
| Dodecagon | 12 | 10 |

The rule that produces the third column is simple: take the number of sides $n$ and subtract $2$. A hexagon has 6 sides, so it divides into $6-2=4$ triangles; a pentagon has 5 sides, so it divides into $5-2=3$ triangles.

Worked example — triangles in a polygon How many triangles can a heptagon be divided into if you draw diagonals from one vertex to all the non-adjacent vertices? Solution. A heptagon has 7 sides. Use the rule: number of triangles $= n-2 = 7-2 = 5$. So a heptagon divides into 5 triangles, which matches the table.

practice.prompt: How many triangles can an octagon be divided into if you draw diagonals from one vertex to all the non-adjacent vertices?
practice.worked_solution: An octagon has 8 sides. Number of triangles $= n-2 = 8-2 = 6$.

practice.answer: It is an equilateral triangle, and each of its three angles measures 60°.

practice.answer: The square has four lines of symmetry; the rectangle has two.

practice.answer: A parallelogram has two pairs of parallel sides, while a trapezium has only one pair of parallel sides.

practice.prompt: How many sides does a dodecagon have, and into how many triangles can it be divided?
practice.answer: A dodecagon has 12 sides and divides into 10 triangles.
practice.worked_solution: Number of triangles $= n-2 = 12-2 = 10$.

blocks.text:
A circle is a plane shape with no corners: every point on its boundary is the same distance from its centre. The curved line that forms the round boundary of the circle is its **circumference**. fig-04 shows two labelled circles so you can see each part sitting on a real circle.

- The **centre** is the point in the middle of the circle.
- The **radius** (plural *radii*) is any straight line joining the centre to the circumference. In the second circle of fig-04 a radius is drawn from the centre out to the circumference, and the right-hand bounding line of the sector below is also a radius.
- A **chord** is any straight line joining two points on the circumference. The second circle in fig-04 has a chord drawn near the top.
- The **diameter** is any chord that passes through the centre of the circle. In the first circle of fig-04 the diameter is drawn straight across through the centre. Because it goes through the centre, it is the longest chord a circle can have, and it is twice as long as the radius.
- An **arc** is a curved part of the circumference. In the first circle of fig-04 a part of the circumference is marked and named the arc.

The figure also shows three more parts:
- A **segment** is the region of the circle cut off by a chord — the shaded part above the chord in the second circle.
- A **sector** is the region bounded by two radii and the arc between them — the shaded part below in the second circle, whose two straight sides are both radii.
- A **tangent** is a straight line that touches the circle at exactly one point, as shown touching the right side of the second circle.

The second has a chord near the top with the segment above it shaded, a shaded sector below with its right-hand bounding line labelled Radius, and a tangent touching it on the right.

sections.title: Finding the Perimeter of Plane Shapes

blocks.text:
The perimeter of a shape is the distance all the way round it. To find it you simply add the lengths of every side. For a straight-sided shape, this means adding each side once. For a circle, the perimeter has a special name — the circumference — and you find it using the radius (or diameter) and the number π (pi), which is about $\frac{22}{7}$ or 3.14.

Because some shapes have equal sides, you can often write a short formula instead of adding each side separately. Work through the examples below to see how each shape's perimeter is found.

Example 1 — a square. A square has four equal sides. In fig-05 each side is marked $L$ and measures 15cm. Its perimeter is four lengths added together: $$L + L + L + L = 4L$$ $$= 15 + 15 + 15 + 15 = 4(15) = 60\text{cm}.$$ Example 2 — a rectangle. A rectangle has two long sides $L$ and two short sides $b$. In fig-06, $L = 10\text{cm}$ and $b = 7\text{cm}$. Adding all four sides: $$P = L + b + L + b = 2L + 2b = 2(L + b)$$ $$= 2(10 + 7) = 2(17) = 34\text{cm}.$$ Example 3 — a missing side. Sometimes you are given the perimeter and one side and must find the other. Suppose a rectangle has perimeter 60cm and length 17cm (fig-07). Write the perimeter formula and solve for $b$: $$P = 2L + 2b$$ $$60 = 2(17) + 2b$$ $$60 = 34 + 2b$$ Collect like terms: $$60 - 34 = 2b$$ $$2b = 26$$ Divide both sides by 2: $$b = 13\text{cm}.$$

blocks.caption: A rectangle with both long sides marked $L = 17$cm and both short sides marked $b$.
A rectangle with both long sides marked $L$, the top one also 10cm, and both short sides marked $b$, the right-hand one also 7cm.
A square, named *Square* at its left, with all four sides marked twice — $L$ and 15cm.

blocks.text: Example 4 — a trapezium. A trapezium has four sides, usually of different lengths. In fig-08 they are $a = 11\text{cm}$, $b = 9\text{cm}$, $c = 5\text{cm}$ and $d = 4\text{cm}$. The perimeter is all four added: $$P = a + b + c + d$$ $$= 11 + 9 + 5 + 4 = 29\text{cm}.$$ Example 5 — a parallelogram. A parallelogram has opposite sides equal: two of length $a$ and two of length $b$ (fig-09, where $a = 9\text{cm}$ and $b = 5\text{cm}$). So $$P = a + a + b + b = 2a + 2b = 2(a + b)$$ $$= 2(9 + 5) = 2(14) = 28\text{cm}.$$ Example 6 — a regular hexagon. A regular hexagon has six equal sides. In fig-10 each side is 5.2cm, so $$P = 6 \times 5.2 = 31.2\text{cm}.$$

blocks.caption: A regular hexagon, named above the drawing, with each of its six sides marked 5.2cm.

A parallelogram with a single arrow on each of its four sides: the two horizontal ones both lettered $a$, the lower also measured 9cm, and the two slanted ones both lettered $b$, the right-hand one also measured 5cm.
A trapezium with each side lettered and measured: the top $c$, 5cm; the left $b$, 9cm; the right $d$, 4cm; the base $a$, 11cm.

blocks.text: Example 7 — a circle. The perimeter of a circle is its circumference, found with either formula: $$C = 2\pi r \quad\text{or}\quad C = \pi d.$$ In fig-11 the radius is 7cm, using $\pi = \frac{22}{7}$: $$C = 2 \times \frac{22}{7} \times 7 = 2 \times 22 = 44\text{cm}.$$ Using $\pi d$ instead: since $d = 2r = 2 \times 7 = 14\text{cm}$, $$C = \frac{22}{7} \times 14 = 22 \times 2 = 44\text{cm}.$$ Example 8 — a rope wound round a cylinder. One turn round the cylinder is one circumference. With radius 25cm and $\pi = 3.14$, $$C = 2\pi r = 2 \times 3.14 \times 25 = 157\text{cm}.$$ Wound 50 times, the rope's total length is $$157 \times 50 = 7850\text{cm}.$$ Example 9 — the radius from the circumference. If the circumference is 440cm, find $r$ ($\pi = \frac{22}{7}$): $$440 = 2\pi r = 2 \times \frac{22}{7} \times r = \frac{44r}{7}.$$ Cross-multiply: $$440 \times 7 = 44r \quad\Rightarrow\quad 3080 = 44r.$$ Divide both sides by 44: $$r = \frac{3080}{44} = 70\text{cm}.$$

blocks.caption: A circle with a radius drawn from the centre to the right of the circumference, marked 7cm.

blocks.text: Example 10 — a quarter circle. The shape in fig-14 is made of two straight sides of 4.9cm each and a curved part that is one quarter of a full circle. Its perimeter is the two straight sides plus that curved part. First find the curved part. It is $\frac{1}{4}$ of a full circumference: $$\frac{1}{4} \times 2\pi r = \frac{1}{4} \times 2 \times \frac{22}{7} \times 4.9$$ $$= \frac{1}{4} \times \frac{44}{7} \times 4.9 = \frac{11}{7} \times \frac{49}{10}$$ $$= \frac{11 \times 7}{10} = \frac{77}{10} = 7.7\text{cm}.$$ Now add the straight sides and the curved part: $$P = 4.9 + 4.9 + 7.7 = 17.5\text{cm}.$$

blocks.caption: A quarter circle: an upright side and a base meeting at a right angle, each marked 4.9cm, with an arc closing them from the top of the upright to the end of the base.
An upright cylinder with a rope wound round it, drawn as a series of turns spiralling down the body from the top face to the base.
A circle with a radius drawn from the centre to the right of the circumference, marked $r$.

sections.title: Plane Shapes: Types, Properties, Similarities and Differences

blocks.text: Plane shapes lie flat on a surface, so they are also called two-dimensional (2-D) shapes. They include triangles, squares, rectangles, parallelograms, trapeziums, the circle, and other polygons. A polygon is any closed shape with three or more straight sides. The review below concentrates on the properties that make these shapes the same or different, because those properties are exactly what you use to identify them.

Look at fig-01 and read the tick marks on the sides.

- **Isosceles triangle** — two adjacent sides are equal. Its base angles are equal, and it has one line of symmetry.
- **Scalene triangle** — no side is equal to another. No two angles are equal, and it has no line of symmetry.
- **Equilateral triangle** — all three sides are equal. All three angles are equal, each measuring $60^\circ$, and it has three lines of symmetry.

The real difference is the number of equal sides: an equilateral triangle has three, an isosceles triangle has two, and a scalene triangle has none.

blocks.caption: Isosceles: a single tick on each of the two slanted sides, an arc at each base angle. Scalene: one, two and three ticks on the three sides, an arc at each vertex. Equilateral: a single tick on each of the three sides, an arc at each vertex.

blocks.text:
Compare the square and rectangle in fig-02. They agree on two facts: every corner is a right angle, so all angles measure $90^\circ$, and each has two pairs of parallel sides. The difference is in the sides.

- **Square** — all four sides are equal. It has four lines of symmetry, and its diagonals bisect each other at a right angle.
- **Rectangle** — opposite sides are equal in pairs: the two longer sides match, and the two shorter sides match. It has two lines of symmetry, and its diagonals bisect each other but not at a right angle.

The key contrast is the number of equal sides: all four sides in the square, but only opposite sides in the rectangle.

blocks.caption: Square: a right-angle mark at each corner, a single tick on each of the four sides. Rectangle: a right-angle mark at each corner, a single tick on each of the two longer sides and a double tick on each of the two shorter sides.

blocks.text:
Now compare the parallelogram and trapezium in fig-03.

- **Parallelogram** — it has two pairs of opposite sides equal and parallel. Its opposite angles are equal, it has no line of symmetry, and its diagonals divide it into two equal triangles.
- **Trapezium** — it has only one pair of parallel sides. Its opposite angles are not equal, it has no line of symmetry, and its diagonal divides it into two unequal triangles.

The main difference is the number of parallel sides: a parallelogram has two pairs, while a trapezium has only one pair.

blocks.caption: Parallelogram: a single arrow on each of the two horizontal sides, a double arrow on each of the two slanted sides. Trapezium: a single arrow on each of the two parallel sides, and one diagonal drawn in.

blocks.text:
The family of polygons is named by its number of straight sides. With $n$ sides, the number of triangles obtained by drawing diagonals from one vertex to all non-adjacent vertices is $n-2$.

| Polygon | Number of sides ($n$) | Number of triangles ($n-2$) |
|---|---|---|
| Triangle | 3 | 1 |
| Quadrilateral | 4 | 2 |
| Pentagon | 5 | 3 |
| Hexagon | 6 | 4 |
| Heptagon | 7 | 5 |
| Octagon | 8 | 6 |
| Nonagon | 9 | 7 |
| Decagon | 10 | 8 |
| Hendecagon (or undecagon) | 11 | 9 |
| Dodecagon | 12 | 10 |

**Worked example — using the polygon rule in reverse**

A polygon is divided into 8 triangles when diagonals are drawn from one vertex to all non-adjacent vertices. How many sides does it have, and what is it called?

**Solution.** The rule is: number of triangles $= n - 2$. Here $8 = n - 2$, so $n = 10$. A polygon with 10 sides is called a **decagon**. The table confirms this: a decagon has 10 sides, and $10 - 2 = 8$.

practice.prompt: A polygon is divided into 9 triangles when diagonals are drawn from one vertex to every non-adjacent vertex. How many sides does it have, and what is the polygon called?
practice.answer: It has 11 sides and is called a hendecagon (or undecagon).
practice.worked_solution: Number of triangles $= n - 2$. So $9 = n - 2$, giving $n = 11$. From the polygon table, an 11-sided polygon is a hendecagon (or undecagon).

practice.prompt: Using fig-02, write one property that the square and rectangle share and one property that the square has but the rectangle does not.
practice.answer: Shared: all angles are $90^\circ$ (equivalently, both have two pairs of parallel sides). Square only: all four sides are equal (equivalently, four lines of symmetry, or diagonals bisect at a right angle).
practice.worked_solution: A square and a rectangle both have four right angles and two pairs of parallel sides. The square also has all four sides equal, four lines of symmetry, and diagonals that bisect at a right angle; the rectangle has opposite sides equal in pairs, two lines of symmetry, and diagonals that do not bisect at a right angle.

practice.prompt: A shape has two pairs of parallel sides and its diagonals divide it into two equal triangles. Which shape is it? Could a trapezium also fit this description? Give the reason.
practice.answer: It is a parallelogram. A trapezium cannot fit the description because a trapezium has only one pair of parallel sides, and its single diagonal divides it into two unequal triangles.
practice.worked_solution: A parallelogram has two pairs of opposite sides equal and parallel, and its diagonals divide it into two equal triangles. A trapezium has only one pair of parallel sides, and its diagonal divides it into two unequal triangles.

practice.prompt: A triangle has exactly one line of symmetry. Can it be a scalene triangle? Name the kind of triangle it is.
practice.answer: No. A scalene triangle has no line of symmetry; a triangle with exactly one line of symmetry is an isosceles triangle.
practice.worked_solution: A scalene triangle has no equal sides and no line of symmetry. An equilateral triangle has three lines of symmetry, so exactly one line of symmetry identifies an isosceles triangle.

practice.prompt: Which gives more triangles when its diagonals are drawn from one vertex: a nonagon or a dodecagon? How many more?

blocks.text:
A circle is a plane shape with no corners: every point on its boundary is the same distance from its centre. The curved line that forms the round boundary of the circle is its **circumference**. fig-04 shows two labelled circles so you can see each part sitting on a real circle.

- The **centre** is the point in the middle of the circle.
- The **radius** (plural *radii*) is any straight line joining the centre to the circumference. In the second circle of fig-04 a radius is drawn from the centre out to the circumference, and the right-hand bounding line of the sector below is also a radius.
- A **chord** is any straight line joining two points on the circumference. The second circle in fig-04 has a chord drawn near the top.
- The **diameter** is any chord that passes through the centre of the circle. In the first circle of fig-04 the diameter is drawn straight across through the centre. Because it goes through the centre, it is the longest chord a circle can have, and it is twice as long as the radius.
- An **arc** is a curved part of the circumference. In the first circle of fig-04 a part of the circumference is marked and named the arc.

The figure also shows three more parts:
- A **segment** is the region of the circle cut off by a chord — the shaded part above the chord in the second circle.
- A **sector** is the region bounded by two radii and the arc between them — the shaded part below in the second circle, whose two straight sides are both radii.
- A **tangent** is a straight line that touches the circle at exactly one point, as shown touching the right side of the second circle.

blocks.caption: Two labelled circles. The first has the diameter drawn across it and a radius from its centre to the circumference, with the arc and the circumference labelled. The second has a chord near the top with the segment above it shaded, a shaded sector below with its right-hand bounding line labelled Radius, and a tangent touching it on the right.

blocks.text:
**Perimeter** is the total distance all the way round a shape. To find it, you add up the lengths of every side that makes the shape's boundary.

You already know a lot about shapes and the angles inside them. Now we use that idea of "going all the way round" to measure how long each shape's outline is. The perimeter is always measured in units of length — centimetres (cm), metres (m), and so on.

Because some shapes have sides that are equal, we can often use a short cut instead of adding every side one by one:

- **Square:** all four sides are equal. If one side is $L$, the perimeter is
$$P = L + L + L + L = 4L.$$
- **Rectangle:** the two long sides (length $L$) are equal and the two short sides (breadth $b$) are equal. Going round you meet $L + b + L + b$, which is
$$P = 2L + 2b = 2(L + b).$$
- **Parallelogram:** the two long sides (base $a$) are equal and the two slanted sides ($b$) are equal, so just like the rectangle,
$$P = 2a + 2b = 2(a + b).$$
- **Trapezium:** its four sides can all be different, so add all four:
$$P = a + b + c + d.$$
- **Regular polygon:** a regular polygon has all its sides equal. If it has $n$ sides each of length $s$,
$$P = n \times s.$$
  A square is a regular polygon with $n = 4$ (which is why $P = 4L$), and a regular hexagon has $n = 6$.
- **Circle:** the perimeter of a circle has its own name — the **circumference** — and it uses $\pi$ (a number close to $3.14$ or $\frac{22}{7}$):
$$C = 2\pi r \quad\text{or}\quad C = \pi d,$$
  where $r$ is the radius (halfway across) and $d$ is the diameter (all the way across, so $d = 2r$).

We'll work through each of these in turn.

**Worked example — square.** A square has each side $15$ cm. Find its perimeter.

A square has four equal sides, so multiply one side by $4$:

$$P = 4L = 4 \times 15\text{ cm} = 60\text{ cm}.$$

The perimeter of the square is $60$ cm.

**Worked example — rectangle.** A rectangle has length $10$ cm and breadth $7$ cm. Find its perimeter.

Going all the way round, you meet the two lengths and the two breadths:

$$P = L + b + L + b.$$

Put the two lengths together and the two breadths together:

$$P = 2L + 2b = 2(L + b).$$

Now substitute $L = 10$ cm and $b = 7$ cm:

$$P = 2(10 + 7) = 2 \times 17 = 34\text{ cm}.$$

The perimeter of the rectangle is $34$ cm.

**Worked example — using the perimeter to find a missing side.** The perimeter of a rectangle is $60$ cm and its length is $17$ cm. Find its breadth.

Start from the perimeter formula $P = 2(L + b)$ and put in what we know:

$$60 = 2(17 + b).$$

Divide both sides by $2$:

$$30 = 17 + b.$$

Subtract $17$ from both sides:

$$b = 30 - 17 = 13\text{ cm}.$$

So the breadth is $13$ cm. Check: $2(17 + 13) = 2 \times 30 = 60$ cm. ✔

**Worked example — trapezium.** A trapezium has sides $11$ cm, $9$ cm, $5$ cm and $4$ cm (its four sides, labelled $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$). Find its perimeter.

The four sides of a trapezium can all be different, so just add them:

$$P = a + b + c + d = 11 + 9 + 5 + 4 = 29\text{ cm}.$$

The perimeter of the trapezium is $29$ cm.

**Worked example — parallelogram.** A parallelogram has base $9$ cm and slanted side $5$ cm. Find its perimeter.

A parallelogram has two equal long sides ($a$) and two equal slanted sides ($b$), so:

$$P = a + a + b + b = 2a + 2b = 2(a + b).$$

Put in $a = 9$ cm and $b = 5$ cm:

$$P = 2(9 + 5) = 2 \times 14 = 28\text{ cm}.$$

The perimeter of the parallelogram is $28$ cm.

**Worked example — regular hexagon.** A regular hexagon has each side $5.2$ cm. Find its perimeter.

A regular hexagon has $6$ equal sides, so multiply one side by $6$:

$$P = 6 \times 5.2\text{ cm} = 31.2\text{ cm}.$$

The perimeter of the hexagon is $31.2$ cm.

**Worked example — circle.** A circle has radius $7$ cm. Find its circumference, using $\pi = \frac{22}{7}$.

Use $C = 2\pi r$ with $r = 7$ cm:

$$C = 2 \times \frac{22}{7} \times 7 = 2 \times 22 = 44\text{ cm}.$$

The same result comes from $C = \pi d$, since the diameter is $d = 2 \times 7 = 14$ cm:

$$C = \frac{22}{7} \times 14 = 22 \times 2 = 44\text{ cm}.$$

The circumference of the circle is $44$ cm.

**Worked example — from circumference back to radius.** The circumference of a circle is $440$ cm. Find its radius, using $\pi = \frac{22}{7}$.

Use $C = 2\pi r$ and put in $C = 440$ cm:

$$440 = 2 \times \frac{22}{7} \times r = \frac{44r}{7}.$$

Multiply both sides by $7$:

$$440 \times 7 = 44r \quad\Rightarrow\quad 3080 = 44r.$$

Divide both sides by $44$:

$$r = \frac{3080}{44} = 70\text{ cm}.$$

The radius of the circle is $70$ cm.

**Worked example — a rope round a cylinder.** A rope is wound $50$ times round a cylinder of radius $25$ cm. How long is the rope? Use $\pi = 3.14$.

Each turn of the rope goes right round the cylinder, so one turn is as long as the circumference of the circular end:

$$\text{one turn} = 2\pi r = 2 \times 3.14 \times 25 = 157\text{ cm}.$$

Wound $50$ times, the total length is:

$$50 \times 157 = 7850\text{ cm}.$$

The rope is $7850$ cm long.

**Worked example — a quarter-circle shape.** A shape is a quarter of a circle: two straight sides, each $4.9$ cm, meeting at a right angle, closed by the curved arc. Find its perimeter. Use $\pi = \frac{22}{7}$.

The perimeter is the two straight sides plus the curved arc. The arc is a quarter of a full circumference, and the radius here is $4.9$ cm, so:

$$\text{arc} = \frac{1}{4} \times 2\pi r = \frac{1}{4} \times 2 \times \frac{22}{7} \times 4.9.$$

Simplify step by step:

$$\text{arc} = \frac{1}{4} \times \frac{44}{7} \times 4.9 = \frac{11}{7} \times 4.9.$$

Since $4.9 = \frac{49}{10}$:

$$\text{arc} = \frac{11}{7} \times \frac{49}{10} = \frac{11 \times 7}{10} = \frac{77}{10} = 7.7\text{ cm}.$$

Now add the two straight sides and the arc:

$$P = 4.9 + 4.9 + 7.7 = 17.5\text{ cm}.$$

The perimeter of the shape is $17.5$ cm.

sections.title: Plane Shapes: Their Types, Properties, Similarities and Differences

blocks.text: Plane shapes are shapes that lie flat on a surface, so they are also called two-dimensional shapes (2-D shapes). The plane shapes you will meet include the triangle, the square, the rectangle, the parallelogram, the trapezium, the circle and other polygons. A polygon is any closed shape that has three or more straight sides. Let us look at each family of plane shapes, its properties, and how the shapes are similar to or different from one another.

Look at the three triangles in fig-01: the isosceles, the scalene and the equilateral. Their names tell you how their sides compare. - An isosceles triangle has two adjacent sides equal (the two slanted sides carry a single tick each). Its base angles are equal, and it has one line of symmetry. - A scalene triangle has no side equal to another — each side carries a different number of ticks (one, two, three). No angle is equal to another, and it has no line of symmetry. - An equilateral triangle has all three sides equal (a single tick on each side). All three angles are equal, each measuring $60^\circ$, and it has three lines of symmetry. So the key differences come down to how many sides are equal: an equilateral has three equal sides, an isosceles has two, and a scalene has none.

blocks.caption: Isosceles: a single tick on each of the two slanted sides, an arc at each base angle. Scalene: one, two and three ticks on the three sides, an arc at each vertex. Equilateral: a single tick on each of the three sides, an arc at each vertex.

blocks.text: Now compare the square and the rectangle in fig-02. Each has a right-angle mark at every corner, so both have all angles equal, each measuring $90^\circ$, and both have two pairs of parallel sides. The difference lies in the sides. - A square has all four sides equal (a single tick on every side). It has four lines of symmetry, and its diagonals bisect each other at a right angle. - A rectangle has only two opposite sides equal — the two longer sides carry a single tick each and the two shorter sides a double tick each. It has two lines of symmetry, and its diagonals bisect each other but not at a right angle.

blocks.caption: Square: a right-angle mark at each corner, a single tick on each of the four sides. Rectangle: a right-angle mark at each corner, a single tick on each of the two longer sides and a double tick on each of the two shorter sides.

blocks.text: Finally, compare the parallelogram and the trapezium in fig-03. - A parallelogram has two pairs of opposite sides equal and parallel (its two horizontal sides carry a single arrow and its two slanted sides a double arrow). Its opposite angles are equal, it has no line of symmetry, and its diagonals divide it into two equal triangles. - A trapezium has only one pair of parallel sides (the two parallel sides carry a single arrow each, and one diagonal is drawn in). Its opposite angles are not equal, it has no line of symmetry, and its diagonal divides it into two unequal triangles. The great difference between them is the number of parallel sides: a parallelogram has two pairs, a trapezium has only one pair.

blocks.caption: Parallelogram: a single arrow on each of the two horizontal sides, a double arrow on each of the two slanted sides. Trapezium: a single arrow on each of the two parallel sides, and one diagonal drawn in.

blocks.text:
Polygons come in many forms, and each is named by its number of straight sides. The table below lists the common polygons, their number of sides, and how many triangles each can be divided into by drawing diagonals from one vertex to all the non-adjacent vertices.

| Name of polygon | Number of sides | Number of triangles ($n-2$) |
|---|---|---|
| Triangle | 3 | 1 |
| Quadrilateral | 4 | 2 |
| Pentagon | 5 | 3 |
| Hexagon | 6 | 4 |
| Heptagon | 7 | 5 |
| Octagon | 8 | 6 |
| Nonagon | 9 | 7 |
| Decagon | 10 | 8 |
| Hendecagon (or undecagon) | 11 | 9 |
| Dodecagon | 12 | 10 |

The rule that produces the third column is simple: take the number of sides $n$ and subtract $2$. A hexagon has 6 sides, so it divides into $6-2=4$ triangles; a pentagon has 5 sides, so it divides into $5-2=3$ triangles.

Worked example — triangles in a polygon How many triangles can a heptagon be divided into if you draw diagonals from one vertex to all the non-adjacent vertices? Solution. A heptagon has 7 sides. Use the rule: number of triangles $= n-2 = 7-2 = 5$. So a heptagon divides into 5 triangles, which matches the table.

practice.prompt: How many triangles can an octagon be divided into if you draw diagonals from one vertex to all the non-adjacent vertices?
practice.worked_solution: An octagon has 8 sides. Number of triangles $= n-2 = 8-2 = 6$.

practice.prompt: Name the triangle whose three sides are all equal, and state the size of each of its angles.
practice.answer: It is an equilateral triangle, and each of its three angles measures 60°.

practice.prompt: Which of the square and the rectangle has four lines of symmetry?
practice.answer: The square has four lines of symmetry; the rectangle has two.

practice.prompt: State one difference between a parallelogram and a trapezium.
practice.answer: A parallelogram has two pairs of parallel sides, while a trapezium has only one pair of parallel sides.

practice.prompt: How many sides does a dodecagon have, and into how many triangles can it be divided?
practice.answer: A dodecagon has 12 sides and divides into 10 triangles.
practice.worked_solution: Number of triangles $= n-2 = 12-2 = 10$.

blocks.text:
A circle is a plane shape with no corners: every point on its boundary is the same distance from its centre. The curved line that forms the round boundary of the circle is its **circumference**. fig-04 shows two labelled circles so you can see each part sitting on a real circle.

- The **centre** is the point in the middle of the circle.
- The **radius** (plural *radii*) is any straight line joining the centre to the circumference. In the second circle of fig-04 a radius is drawn from the centre out to the circumference, and the right-hand bounding line of the sector below is also a radius.
- A **chord** is any straight line joining two points on the circumference. The second circle in fig-04 has a chord drawn near the top.
- The **diameter** is any chord that passes through the centre of the circle. In the first circle of fig-04 the diameter is drawn straight across through the centre. Because it goes through the centre, it is the longest chord a circle can have, and it is twice as long as the radius.
- An **arc** is a curved part of the circumference. In the first circle of fig-04 a part of the circumference is marked and named the arc.

The figure also shows three more parts:
- A **segment** is the region of the circle cut off by a chord — the shaded part above the chord in the second circle.
- A **sector** is the region bounded by two radii and the arc between them — the shaded part below in the second circle, whose two straight sides are both radii.
- A **tangent** is a straight line that touches the circle at exactly one point, as shown touching the right side of the second circle.

blocks.caption: Two labelled circles. The first has the diameter drawn across it and a radius from its centre to the circumference, with the arc and the circumference labelled. The second has a chord near the top with the segment above it shaded, a shaded sector below with its right-hand bounding line labelled Radius, and a tangent touching it on the right.

practice.prompt: Name the straight line that joins the centre of a circle to its circumference.
What do we call a chord that passes through the centre of the circle?
A straight line drawn across a circle joining two points on its circumference is called a ______.
The curved part of the circumference between two points on a circle is called an ______.
If a circle has a radius of 5 cm, how long is its diameter?
practice.worked_solution: The diameter is twice the radius, so 2 × 5 cm = 10 cm.

practice.prompt: Which part of a circle is the region bounded by two radii and the arc between them? Which part is the region cut off by a chord?
practice.answer: The region bounded by two radii and the arc between them is a sector; the region cut off by a chord is a segment.

sections.title: Finding the Perimeter of Plane Shapes

blocks.text:
The perimeter of a shape is the distance all the way round it. To find it you simply add the lengths of every side. For a straight-sided shape, this means adding each side once. For a circle, the perimeter has a special name — the circumference — and you find it using the radius (or diameter) and the number π (pi), which is about $\frac{22}{7}$ or 3.14.

Because some shapes have equal sides, you can often write a short formula instead of adding each side separately. Work through the examples below to see how each shape's perimeter is found.

Example 1 — a square. A square has four equal sides. In fig-05 each side is marked $L$ and measures 15cm. Its perimeter is four lengths added together: $$L + L + L + L = 4L$$ $$= 15 + 15 + 15 + 15 = 4(15) = 60\text{cm}.$$ Example 2 — a rectangle. A rectangle has two long sides $L$ and two short sides $b$. In fig-06, $L = 10\text{cm}$ and $b = 7\text{cm}$. Adding all four sides: $$P = L + b + L + b = 2L + 2b = 2(L + b)$$ $$= 2(10 + 7) = 2(17) = 34\text{cm}.$$ Example 3 — a missing side. Sometimes you are given the perimeter and one side and must find the other. Suppose a rectangle has perimeter 60cm and length 17cm (fig-07). Write the perimeter formula and solve for $b$: $$P = 2L + 2b$$ $$60 = 2(17) + 2b$$ $$60 = 34 + 2b$$ Collect like terms: $$60 - 34 = 2b$$ $$2b = 26$$ Divide both sides by 2: $$b = 13\text{cm}.$$

blocks.caption: A rectangle with both long sides marked $L = 17$cm and both short sides marked $b$.
A rectangle with both long sides marked $L$, the top one also 10cm, and both short sides marked $b$, the right-hand one also 7cm.
A square, named *Square* at its left, with all four sides marked twice — $L$ and 15cm.

blocks.text: Example 4 — a trapezium. A trapezium has four sides, usually of different lengths. In fig-08 they are $a = 11\text{cm}$, $b = 9\text{cm}$, $c = 5\text{cm}$ and $d = 4\text{cm}$. The perimeter is all four added: $$P = a + b + c + d$$ $$= 11 + 9 + 5 + 4 = 29\text{cm}.$$ Example 5 — a parallelogram. A parallelogram has opposite sides equal: two of length $a$ and two of length $b$ (fig-09, where $a = 9\text{cm}$ and $b = 5\text{cm}$). So $$P = a + a + b + b = 2a + 2b = 2(a + b)$$ $$= 2(9 + 5) = 2(14) = 28\text{cm}.$$ Example 6 — a regular hexagon. A regular hexagon has six equal sides. In fig-10 each side is 5.2cm, so $$P = 6 \times 5.2 = 31.2\text{cm}.$$

blocks.caption: A regular hexagon, named above the drawing, with each of its six sides marked 5.2cm.

A parallelogram with a single arrow on each of its four sides: the two horizontal ones both lettered $a$, the lower also measured 9cm, and the two slanted ones both lettered $b$, the right-hand one also measured 5cm.
A trapezium with each side lettered and measured: the top $c$, 5cm; the left $b$, 9cm; the right $d$, 4cm; the base $a$, 11cm.

blocks.text: Example 7 — a circle. The perimeter of a circle is its circumference, found with either formula: $$C = 2\pi r \quad\text{or}\quad C = \pi d.$$ In fig-11 the radius is 7cm, using $\pi = \frac{22}{7}$: $$C = 2 \times \frac{22}{7} \times 7 = 2 \times 22 = 44\text{cm}.$$ Using $\pi d$ instead: since $d = 2r = 2 \times 7 = 14\text{cm}$, $$C = \frac{22}{7} \times 14 = 22 \times 2 = 44\text{cm}.$$ Example 8 — a rope wound round a cylinder. One turn round the cylinder is one circumference. With radius 25cm and $\pi = 3.14$, $$C = 2\pi r = 2 \times 3.14 \times 25 = 157\text{cm}.$$ Wound 50 times, the rope's total length is $$157 \times 50 = 7850\text{cm}.$$ Example 9 — the radius from the circumference. If the circumference is 440cm, find $r$ ($\pi = \frac{22}{7}$): $$440 = 2\pi r = 2 \times \frac{22}{7} \times r = \frac{44r}{7}.$$ Cross-multiply: $$440 \times 7 = 44r \quad\Rightarrow\quad 3080 = 44r.$$ Divide both sides by 44: $$r = \frac{3080}{44} = 70\text{cm}.$$

blocks.caption: A circle with a radius drawn from the centre to the right of the circumference, marked 7cm.

blocks.text: Example 10 — a quarter circle. The shape in fig-14 is made of two straight sides of 4.9cm each and a curved part that is one quarter of a full circle. Its perimeter is the two straight sides plus that curved part. First find the curved part. It is $\frac{1}{4}$ of a full circumference: $$\frac{1}{4} \times 2\pi r = \frac{1}{4} \times 2 \times \frac{22}{7} \times 4.9$$ $$= \frac{1}{4} \times \frac{44}{7} \times 4.9 = \frac{11}{7} \times \frac{49}{10}$$ $$= \frac{11 \times 7}{10} = \frac{77}{10} = 7.7\text{cm}.$$ Now add the straight sides and the curved part: $$P = 4.9 + 4.9 + 7.7 = 17.5\text{cm}.$$

blocks.caption: A quarter circle: an upright side and a base meeting at a right angle, each marked 4.9cm, with an arc closing them from the top of the upright to the end of the base.
An upright cylinder with a rope wound round it, drawn as a series of turns spiralling down the body from the top face to the base.
A circle with a radius drawn from the centre to the right of the circumference, marked $r$.

practice.prompt: Find the perimeter of a parallelogram whose base is 6cm and whose sides are 5cm.
practice.worked_solution: Opposite sides are equal, so $P = 2a + 2b = 2(6) + 2(5) = 12 + 10 = 22\text{cm}$.

practice.worked_solution: $C = 2\pi r$, so $22 = 2 \times \frac{22}{7} \times r = \frac{44r}{7}$. Cross-multiply: $22 \times 7 = 44r$, so $154 = 44r$, giving $r = \frac{154}{44} = 3.5\text{cm}$.

practice.worked_solution: Length $= 2d$ and breadth $= d$. Perimeter $= 2(\text{length} + \text{breadth}) = 2(2d + d) = 2(3d) = 6d$.

practice.worked_solution: A regular hexagon has six equal sides, so $P = 6 \times 5 = 30\text{cm}$.

sections.title: Plane Shapes: Their Types, Properties, Similarities and Differences

blocks.text: Plane shapes are shapes that lie flat on a surface, so they are also called **two-dimensional (2-D) shapes**. The plane shapes to know are the triangle, the square, the rectangle, the parallelogram, the trapezium, the circle and other polygons. A **polygon** is any closed shape with three or more straight sides — the polygons in this section are named by their number of sides.

**Triangles — see fig-01.** The name of a triangle tells you how its sides compare, and that drives the rest of its properties.

- An **equilateral** triangle has all three sides equal, all three angles equal ($60^\circ$ each), and three lines of symmetry.
- An **isosceles** triangle has two adjacent sides equal, equal base angles, and one line of symmetry.
- A **scalene** triangle has no equal sides, no equal angles, and no line of symmetry.

So the three triangle families differ in how many sides are equal: three, two, or none.

blocks.caption: Isosceles: a single tick on each of the two slanted sides, an arc at each base angle. Scalene: one, two and three ticks on the three sides, an arc at each vertex. Equilateral: a single tick on each of the three sides, an arc at each vertex.

blocks.text:
**Squares and rectangles — see fig-02.** Both shapes have all angles equal ($90^\circ$ each) and two pairs of parallel sides. The difference is in the sides and symmetry:

- A **square** has all four sides equal, four lines of symmetry, and its diagonals cut each other at a right angle.
- A **rectangle** has opposite sides equal (the two longer sides equal and the two shorter sides equal), two lines of symmetry, and its diagonals cut each other but not at a right angle.

The tick marks in fig-02 show exactly which sides are equal.

blocks.caption: Square: a right-angle mark at each corner, a single tick on each of the four sides. Rectangle: a right-angle mark at each corner, a single tick on each of the two longer sides and a double tick on each of the two shorter sides.

blocks.text:
**Parallelograms and trapezium — see fig-03.**

- A **parallelogram** has two pairs of opposite sides equal and parallel, opposite angles equal, no line of symmetry, and its diagonals divide it into two equal triangles.
- A **trapezium** has only one pair of parallel sides, opposite angles not equal, no line of symmetry, and its diagonal divides it into two unequal triangles.

The big difference is the number of parallel sides: a parallelogram has two pairs, but a trapezium has only one.

blocks.caption: Parallelogram: a single arrow on each of the two horizontal sides, a double arrow on each of the two slanted sides. Trapezium: a single arrow on each of the two parallel sides, and one diagonal drawn in.

blocks.text:
**Polygon names and triangle count.** Every polygon is named by its number of straight sides. The last column of the table below gives the number of triangles by the $n-2$ rule, where $n$ is the number of sides.

| Name of polygon | Number of sides | Number of triangles ($n-2$) |
|---|---|---|
| Triangle | 3 | 1 |
| Quadrilateral | 4 | 2 |
| Pentagon | 5 | 3 |
| Hexagon | 6 | 4 |
| Heptagon | 7 | 5 |
| Octagon | 8 | 6 |
| Nonagon | 9 | 7 |
| Decagon | 10 | 8 |
| Hendecagon (undecagon) | 11 | 9 |
| Dodecagon | 12 | 10 |

The pattern is always the same: subtract 2 from the number of sides.

**Worked example — working backwards from the triangle count.**

A polygon is divided into 7 triangles using the $n-2$ rule. Name the polygon.

**Solution.** The rule says triangles $= n-2$. So $7=n-2$, which means $n=7+2=9$. A polygon with 9 sides is a **nonagon**. The table confirms it: nonagon has $9-2=7$ triangles.

practice.prompt: A polygon is divided into 8 triangles using the $n-2$ rule. What is the polygon called, and how many sides does it have?
practice.answer: It is a decagon, with 10 sides.
practice.worked_solution: Number of triangles $= n-2$. Here $n-2=8$, so $n=10$. The 10-sided polygon is the decagon.

practice.prompt: An octagon and a dodecagon are each divided into triangles using the $n-2$ rule. How many more triangles does the dodecagon form than the octagon?
practice.worked_solution: Octagon: $n-2 = 8-2=6$. Dodecagon: $n-2=12-2=10$. Difference: $10-6=4$.

practice.prompt: Give one property shared by an equilateral triangle and a square, and one property in which they differ.
practice.answer: Shared: all sides are equal. Differ: an equilateral triangle has 3 sides, while a square has 4 sides.
practice.worked_solution: From the properties: an equilateral triangle has 3 equal sides and a square has 4 equal sides. The angle size also differs: $60^\circ$ each for the triangle, $90^\circ$ each for the square.

practice.prompt: Which shape has diagonals that cut each other at a right angle: the square or the rectangle? State how many lines of symmetry that shape has.
practice.answer: The square; it has four lines of symmetry.

practice.prompt: Using the properties in fig-03, explain why a trapezium cannot correctly be described as a parallelogram.
