blocks.text:
A circle is a plane shape with no corners: every point on its boundary is the same distance from its centre. The curved line that forms the round boundary of the circle is its **circumference**. fig-04 shows two labelled circles so you can see each part sitting on a real circle.

- The **centre** is the point in the middle of the circle.
- The **radius** (plural *radii*) is any straight line joining the centre to the circumference. In the second circle of fig-04 a radius is drawn from the centre out to the circumference, and the right-hand bounding line of the sector below is also a radius.
- A **chord** is any straight line joining two points on the circumference. The second circle in fig-04 has a chord drawn near the top.
- The **diameter** is any chord that passes through the centre of the circle. In the first circle of fig-04 the diameter is drawn straight across through the centre. Because it goes through the centre, it is the longest chord a circle can have, and it is twice as long as the radius.
- An **arc** is a curved part of the circumference. In the first circle of fig-04 a part of the circumference is marked and named the arc.

The figure also shows three more parts:
- A **segment** is the region of the circle cut off by a chord — the shaded part above the chord in the second circle.
- A **sector** is the region bounded by two radii and the arc between them — the shaded part below in the second circle, whose two straight sides are both radii.
- A **tangent** is a straight line that touches the circle at exactly one point, as shown touching the right side of the second circle.

blocks.caption: Two labelled circles. The first has the diameter drawn across it and a radius from its centre to the circumference, with the arc and the circumference labelled. The second has a chord near the top with the segment above it shaded, a shaded sector below with its right-hand bounding line labelled Radius, and a tangent touching it on the right.

practice.answer: The region bounded by two radii and the arc between them is a sector; the region cut off by a chord is a segment.

blocks.text:
The **perimeter** of a shape is the total distance around it. To find it, you add up the lengths of all the sides that make up the boundary of the shape.

For a **circle**, the perimeter has a special name: the **circumference**. You find it with $2\pi r$ (twice the radius times $\pi$) or $\pi d$ (the diameter times $\pi$), where $d = 2r$.

Because some shapes have equal sides, there are quick ways to add. A square has four equal sides, so its perimeter is $4L$ where $L$ is one side. A rectangle has two equal lengths $L$ and two equal breadths $b$, so its perimeter is $2L + 2b$ or $2(L + b)$. Opposite sides of a parallelogram are equal, so its perimeter is $2(a + b)$ where $a$ and $b$ are the two different side lengths. A **regular** polygon has all its sides equal, so you multiply the number of sides by the length of one side.

**Example 1 — Square.** Calculate the perimeter of a square of side $15\text{ cm}$ (see fig-05).

Every side of a square is equal, so:
$$P = L + L + L + L = 4L$$
$$P = 4 \times 15\text{ cm} = 60\text{ cm}$$

The perimeter of the square is $60\text{ cm}$.

blocks.caption: A square, named *Square* at its left, with all four sides marked twice — $L$ and 15cm.

blocks.text:
**Example 2 — Rectangle.** Find the perimeter of a rectangle whose length is $10\text{ cm}$ and breadth $7\text{ cm}$ (see fig-06).

A rectangle has two equal lengths and two equal breadths:
$$P = L + b + L + b = 2L + 2b = 2(L + b)$$
$$P = 2(10\text{ cm} + 7\text{ cm}) = 2(17\text{ cm}) = 34\text{ cm}$$

The perimeter of the rectangle is $34\text{ cm}$.

**Example 3 — Rectangle (finding a missing side).** If the perimeter of a rectangle is $60\text{ cm}$ and its length is $17\text{ cm}$, calculate its breadth (see fig-07).

$$P = 2L + 2b$$
$$60 = 2(17) + 2b$$
$$60 = 34 + 2b$$

Subtract $34$ from both sides:
$$60 - 34 = 2b$$
$$2b = 26$$

Divide both sides by $2$:
$$b = 13\text{ cm}$$

The breadth is $13\text{ cm}$.

blocks.caption: A rectangle with both long sides marked $L = 17$cm and both short sides marked $b$.
A rectangle with both long sides marked $L$, the top one also 10cm, and both short sides marked $b$, the right-hand one also 7cm.

blocks.text:
**Example 4 — Trapezium.** Find the perimeter of the trapezium with sides $a = 11\text{ cm}$, $b = 9\text{ cm}$, $c = 5\text{ cm}$ and $d = 4\text{ cm}$ (see fig-08).

A trapezium has four sides, not usually equal, so simply add all of them:
$$P = a + b + c + d$$
$$P = 11 + 9 + 5 + 4 = 29\text{ cm}$$

The perimeter of the trapezium is $29\text{ cm}$.

**Example 5 — Parallelogram.** Find the perimeter of a parallelogram with base $a = 9\text{ cm}$ and slanted side $b = 5\text{ cm}$ (see fig-09).

Opposite sides of a parallelogram are equal, so there are two of length $a$ and two of length $b$:
$$P = a + a + b + b = 2a + 2b = 2(a + b)$$
$$P = 2(9 + 5) = 2(14) = 28\text{ cm}$$

The perimeter of the parallelogram is $28\text{ cm}$.

blocks.caption: A parallelogram with a single arrow on each of its four sides: the two horizontal ones both lettered $a$, the lower also measured 9cm, and the two slanted ones both lettered $b$, the right-hand one also measured 5cm.
A trapezium with each side lettered and measured: the top $c$, 5cm; the left $b$, 9cm; the right $d$, 4cm; the base $a$, 11cm.

blocks.text:
**Example 6 — Regular hexagon.** Find the perimeter of a regular hexagon with sides $5.2\text{ cm}$ (see fig-10).

A regular hexagon has $6$ equal sides. Multiply the number of sides by the length of one side:
$$P = 6 \times 5.2\text{ cm} = 31.2\text{ cm}$$

The perimeter of the hexagon is $31.2\text{ cm}$.

**Example 7 — Circle.** Calculate the circumference of a circle of radius $7\text{ cm}$, using $\pi = \frac{22}{7}$ (see fig-11).

The perimeter of a circle is its circumference:
$$C = 2\pi r$$
$$C = 2 \times \frac{22}{7} \times 7\text{ cm} = 2 \times 22 = 44\text{ cm}$$

The circumference is $44\text{ cm}$. We could also use $\pi d$: since $d = 2 \times 7 = 14\text{ cm}$, then $\frac{22}{7} \times 14 = 22 \times 2 = 44\text{ cm}$, the same answer.

blocks.caption: A circle with a radius drawn from the centre to the right of the circumference, marked 7cm.
A regular hexagon, named above the drawing, with each of its six sides marked 5.2cm.

blocks.text:
**Example 8 — Finding the radius from the circumference.** The circumference of a circle is $440\text{ cm}$. Find its radius, using $\pi = \frac{22}{7}$ (see fig-13).

$$C = 2\pi r$$
$$440 = 2 \times \frac{22}{7} \times r$$
$$440 = \frac{44r}{7}$$

Cross-multiply:
$$440 \times 7 = 44r$$
$$3080 = 44r$$

Divide both sides by $44$:
$$r = \frac{3080}{44} = 70\text{ cm}$$

The radius is $70\text{ cm}$.

**Example 9 — Rope around a cylinder.** A rope is wound $50$ times round a cylinder of radius $25\text{ cm}$. How long is the rope? Use $\pi = 3.14$ (see fig-12).

One full turn of the rope goes round once, so its length for one turn is the circumference:
$$C = 2\pi r = 2 \times 3.14 \times 25 = 157\text{ cm}$$

For $50$ turns, multiply by $50$:
$$157 \times 50 = 7850\text{ cm}$$

The rope is $7850\text{ cm}$ long.

blocks.caption: A circle with a radius drawn from the centre to the right of the circumference, marked $r$.
An upright cylinder with a rope wound round it, drawn as a series of turns spiralling down the body from the top face to the base.

blocks.text:
**Example 10 — Quarter circle.** Calculate the perimeter of the quarter-circle shape below, whose two straight sides are each $4.9\text{ cm}$ (see fig-14).

The curved part is one quarter of a full circle of the same radius, $r = 4.9\text{ cm}$:
$$\text{curved part} = \frac{1}{4} \times 2\pi r = \frac{1}{4} \times 2 \times \frac{22}{7} \times 4.9$$
$$= \frac{1}{4} \times \frac{44}{7} \times 4.9 = \frac{11}{7} \times \frac{49}{10} = \frac{77}{10} = 7.7\text{ cm}$$

The perimeter is the curved part plus the two straight sides:
$$P = 4.9 + 4.9 + 7.7 = 17.5\text{ cm}$$

The perimeter of the shape is $17.5\text{ cm}$.

blocks.caption: A quarter circle: an upright side and a base meeting at a right angle, each marked 4.9cm, with an arc closing them from the top of the upright to the end of the base.

sections.title: Plane Shapes: Their Types, Properties, Similarities and Differences

blocks.text: Plane shapes are shapes that lie flat on a surface, so they are also called two-dimensional shapes (2-D shapes). The plane shapes you will meet include the triangle, the square, the rectangle, the parallelogram, the trapezium, the circle and other polygons. A polygon is any closed shape that has three or more straight sides. Let us look at each family of plane shapes, its properties, and how the shapes are similar to or different from one another.

Look at the three triangles in fig-01: the isosceles, the scalene and the equilateral. Their names tell you how their sides compare. - An isosceles triangle has two adjacent sides equal (the two slanted sides carry a single tick each). Its base angles are equal, and it has one line of symmetry. - A scalene triangle has no side equal to another — each side carries a different number of ticks (one, two, three). No angle is equal to another, and it has no line of symmetry. - An equilateral triangle has all three sides equal (a single tick on each side). All three angles are equal, each measuring $60^\circ$, and it has three lines of symmetry. So the key differences come down to how many sides are equal: an equilateral has three equal sides, an isosceles has two, and a scalene has none.

blocks.caption: Isosceles: a single tick on each of the two slanted sides, an arc at each base angle. Scalene: one, two and three ticks on the three sides, an arc at each vertex. Equilateral: a single tick on each of the three sides, an arc at each vertex.

blocks.text: Now compare the square and the rectangle in fig-02. Each has a right-angle mark at every corner, so both have all angles equal, each measuring $90^\circ$, and both have two pairs of parallel sides. The difference lies in the sides. - A square has all four sides equal (a single tick on every side). It has four lines of symmetry, and its diagonals bisect each other at a right angle. - A rectangle has only two opposite sides equal — the two longer sides carry a single tick each and the two shorter sides a double tick each. It has two lines of symmetry, and its diagonals bisect each other but not at a right angle.

blocks.caption: Square: a right-angle mark at each corner, a single tick on each of the four sides. Rectangle: a right-angle mark at each corner, a single tick on each of the two longer sides and a double tick on each of the two shorter sides.

blocks.text: Finally, compare the parallelogram and the trapezium in fig-03. - A parallelogram has two pairs of opposite sides equal and parallel (its two horizontal sides carry a single arrow and its two slanted sides a double arrow). Its opposite angles are equal, it has no line of symmetry, and its diagonals divide it into two equal triangles. - A trapezium has only one pair of parallel sides (the two parallel sides carry a single arrow each, and one diagonal is drawn in). Its opposite angles are not equal, it has no line of symmetry, and its diagonal divides it into two unequal triangles. The great difference between them is the number of parallel sides: a parallelogram has two pairs, a trapezium has only one pair.

blocks.caption: Parallelogram: a single arrow on each of the two horizontal sides, a double arrow on each of the two slanted sides. Trapezium: a single arrow on each of the two parallel sides, and one diagonal drawn in.

blocks.text:
Polygons come in many forms, and each is named by its number of straight sides. The table below lists the common polygons, their number of sides, and how many triangles each can be divided into by drawing diagonals from one vertex to all the non-adjacent vertices.

| Name of polygon | Number of sides | Number of triangles ($n-2$) |
|---|---|---|
| Triangle | 3 | 1 |
| Quadrilateral | 4 | 2 |
| Pentagon | 5 | 3 |
| Hexagon | 6 | 4 |
| Heptagon | 7 | 5 |
| Octagon | 8 | 6 |
| Nonagon | 9 | 7 |
| Decagon | 10 | 8 |
| Hendecagon (or undecagon) | 11 | 9 |
| Dodecagon | 12 | 10 |

The rule that produces the third column is simple: take the number of sides $n$ and subtract $2$. A hexagon has 6 sides, so it divides into $6-2=4$ triangles; a pentagon has 5 sides, so it divides into $5-2=3$ triangles.

Worked example — triangles in a polygon How many triangles can a heptagon be divided into if you draw diagonals from one vertex to all the non-adjacent vertices? Solution. A heptagon has 7 sides. Use the rule: number of triangles $= n-2 = 7-2 = 5$. So a heptagon divides into 5 triangles, which matches the table.

sections.title: Finding the Perimeter of Plane Shapes

blocks.text:
The perimeter of a shape is the distance all the way round it. To find it you simply add the lengths of every side. For a straight-sided shape, this means adding each side once. For a circle, the perimeter has a special name — the circumference — and you find it using the radius (or diameter) and the number π (pi), which is about $\frac{22}{7}$ or 3.14.

Because some shapes have equal sides, you can often write a short formula instead of adding each side separately. Work through the examples below to see how each shape's perimeter is found.

Example 1 — a square. A square has four equal sides. In fig-05 each side is marked $L$ and measures 15cm. Its perimeter is four lengths added together: $$L + L + L + L = 4L$$ $$= 15 + 15 + 15 + 15 = 4(15) = 60\text{cm}.$$ Example 2 — a rectangle. A rectangle has two long sides $L$ and two short sides $b$. In fig-06, $L = 10\text{cm}$ and $b = 7\text{cm}$. Adding all four sides: $$P = L + b + L + b = 2L + 2b = 2(L + b)$$ $$= 2(10 + 7) = 2(17) = 34\text{cm}.$$ Example 3 — a missing side. Sometimes you are given the perimeter and one side and must find the other. Suppose a rectangle has perimeter 60cm and length 17cm (fig-07). Write the perimeter formula and solve for $b$: $$P = 2L + 2b$$ $$60 = 2(17) + 2b$$ $$60 = 34 + 2b$$ Collect like terms: $$60 - 34 = 2b$$ $$2b = 26$$ Divide both sides by 2: $$b = 13\text{cm}.$$

blocks.caption: A rectangle with both long sides marked $L = 17$cm and both short sides marked $b$.
A rectangle with both long sides marked $L$, the top one also 10cm, and both short sides marked $b$, the right-hand one also 7cm.
A square, named *Square* at its left, with all four sides marked twice — $L$ and 15cm.

blocks.text: Example 4 — a trapezium. A trapezium has four sides, usually of different lengths. In fig-08 they are $a = 11\text{cm}$, $b = 9\text{cm}$, $c = 5\text{cm}$ and $d = 4\text{cm}$. The perimeter is all four added: $$P = a + b + c + d$$ $$= 11 + 9 + 5 + 4 = 29\text{cm}.$$ Example 5 — a parallelogram. A parallelogram has opposite sides equal: two of length $a$ and two of length $b$ (fig-09, where $a = 9\text{cm}$ and $b = 5\text{cm}$). So $$P = a + a + b + b = 2a + 2b = 2(a + b)$$ $$= 2(9 + 5) = 2(14) = 28\text{cm}.$$ Example 6 — a regular hexagon. A regular hexagon has six equal sides. In fig-10 each side is 5.2cm, so $$P = 6 \times 5.2 = 31.2\text{cm}.$$

blocks.caption: A regular hexagon, named above the drawing, with each of its six sides marked 5.2cm.

A parallelogram with a single arrow on each of its four sides: the two horizontal ones both lettered $a$, the lower also measured 9cm, and the two slanted ones both lettered $b$, the right-hand one also measured 5cm.
A trapezium with each side lettered and measured: the top $c$, 5cm; the left $b$, 9cm; the right $d$, 4cm; the base $a$, 11cm.

blocks.text: Example 7 — a circle. The perimeter of a circle is its circumference, found with either formula: $$C = 2\pi r \quad\text{or}\quad C = \pi d.$$ In fig-11 the radius is 7cm, using $\pi = \frac{22}{7}$: $$C = 2 \times \frac{22}{7} \times 7 = 2 \times 22 = 44\text{cm}.$$ Using $\pi d$ instead: since $d = 2r = 2 \times 7 = 14\text{cm}$, $$C = \frac{22}{7} \times 14 = 22 \times 2 = 44\text{cm}.$$ Example 8 — a rope wound round a cylinder. One turn round the cylinder is one circumference. With radius 25cm and $\pi = 3.14$, $$C = 2\pi r = 2 \times 3.14 \times 25 = 157\text{cm}.$$ Wound 50 times, the rope's total length is $$157 \times 50 = 7850\text{cm}.$$ Example 9 — the radius from the circumference. If the circumference is 440cm, find $r$ ($\pi = \frac{22}{7}$): $$440 = 2\pi r = 2 \times \frac{22}{7} \times r = \frac{44r}{7}.$$ Cross-multiply: $$440 \times 7 = 44r \quad\Rightarrow\quad 3080 = 44r.$$ Divide both sides by 44: $$r = \frac{3080}{44} = 70\text{cm}.$$

blocks.caption: A circle with a radius drawn from the centre to the right of the circumference, marked 7cm.

blocks.text: Example 10 — a quarter circle. The shape in fig-14 is made of two straight sides of 4.9cm each and a curved part that is one quarter of a full circle. Its perimeter is the two straight sides plus that curved part. First find the curved part. It is $\frac{1}{4}$ of a full circumference: $$\frac{1}{4} \times 2\pi r = \frac{1}{4} \times 2 \times \frac{22}{7} \times 4.9$$ $$= \frac{1}{4} \times \frac{44}{7} \times 4.9 = \frac{11}{7} \times \frac{49}{10}$$ $$= \frac{11 \times 7}{10} = \frac{77}{10} = 7.7\text{cm}.$$ Now add the straight sides and the curved part: $$P = 4.9 + 4.9 + 7.7 = 17.5\text{cm}.$$

blocks.caption: A quarter circle: an upright side and a base meeting at a right angle, each marked 4.9cm, with an arc closing them from the top of the upright to the end of the base.
An upright cylinder with a rope wound round it, drawn as a series of turns spiralling down the body from the top face to the base.
A circle with a radius drawn from the centre to the right of the circumference, marked $r$.

sections.title: Plane Shapes: Types, Properties, Similarities and Differences

blocks.text: Plane shapes lie flat on a surface, which is why they are also called **two-dimensional (2-D) shapes**. The 2-D shapes here are the triangle, square, rectangle, parallelogram, trapezium, circle, and other polygons. A **polygon** is any closed shape with three or more straight sides. As you revise, compare shapes by four questions: Which sides are equal? Which angles are equal? How many pairs of sides are parallel? What do the symmetry and diagonals show?

**Triangles (fig-01).** Read the tick marks: sides with the same tick are equal.

- **Isosceles:** two adjacent sides equal; base angles equal; one line of symmetry.
- **Scalene:** no side equal; no angle equal; no line of symmetry.
- **Equilateral:** all three sides equal; each angle $60^\circ$; three lines of symmetry.

So the families differ by exactly how many sides are equal: equilateral has three, isosceles has two, scalene has none.

blocks.caption: Isosceles: a single tick on each of the two slanted sides, an arc at each base angle. Scalene: one, two and three ticks on the three sides, an arc at each vertex. Equilateral: a single tick on each of the three sides, an arc at each vertex.

blocks.text:
**Squares and rectangles (fig-02).** Both have right angles at all four corners, each $90^\circ$, and both have two pairs of parallel sides.

- **Square:** all four sides equal; four lines of symmetry; diagonals bisect each other at a right angle.
- **Rectangle:** only opposite sides equal; two lines of symmetry; diagonals bisect each other but **not** at a right angle.

The decisive difference is **all four sides equal** versus **opposite sides equal only**.

blocks.caption: Square: a right-angle mark at each corner, a single tick on each of the four sides. Rectangle: a right-angle mark at each corner, a single tick on each of the two longer sides and a double tick on each of the two shorter sides.

blocks.text:
**Parallelogram and trapezium (fig-03).** Use the arrow marks and the drawn diagonal to compare them.

- **Parallelogram:** two pairs of opposite sides are equal and parallel; opposite angles are equal; no line of symmetry; diagonals divide it into two equal triangles.
- **Trapezium:** only one pair of parallel sides; opposite angles are not equal; no line of symmetry; its diagonal divides it into two unequal triangles.

The sharpest difference is the number of parallel sides: a parallelogram has two pairs, while a trapezium has only one pair.

blocks.caption: Parallelogram: a single arrow on each of the two horizontal sides, a double arrow on each of the two slanted sides. Trapezium: a single arrow on each of the two parallel sides, and one diagonal drawn in.

blocks.text:
**Polygons.** Each polygon is named by its number of straight sides. Drawing diagonals from one vertex to every non-adjacent vertex divides an $n$-sided polygon into $n-2$ triangles.

| Name of polygon | Number of sides | Number of triangles ($n-2$) |
|---|---|---|
| Triangle | 3 | 1 |
| Quadrilateral | 4 | 2 |
| Pentagon | 5 | 3 |
| Hexagon | 6 | 4 |
| Heptagon | 7 | 5 |
| Octagon | 8 | 6 |
| Nonagon | 9 | 7 |
| Decagon | 10 | 8 |
| Hendecagon (or undecagon) | 11 | 9 |
| Dodecagon | 12 | 10 |

**Worked example — naming a polygon from its triangles**

A polygon is divided into **10 triangles** by drawing diagonals from one vertex to all non-adjacent vertices. Name the polygon.

**Solution.** Use the table rule: number of triangles $= n - 2$. Here, $10 = n - 2$, so $n = 12$. A polygon with 12 sides is a **dodecagon**, which matches the table.

practice.prompt: A polygon is divided into **9 triangles** by drawing diagonals from one vertex to all the non-adjacent vertices. Name the polygon and write the number sentence you used.
practice.worked_solution: Use triangles $= n - 2$. Since $9 = n - 2$, $n = 11$. An 11-sided polygon is a hendecagon, also called an undecagon.

practice.prompt: Which two polygons in the table produce **6** and **7** triangles respectively? State their names and their numbers of sides.
practice.answer: Octagon (8 sides) produces 6 triangles; nonagon (9 sides) produces 7 triangles.
practice.worked_solution: For an octagon, $8 - 2 = 6$. For a nonagon, $9 - 2 = 7$.

practice.prompt: A quadrilateral has two pairs of parallel sides and all angles equal to $90^\circ$, but **not all four sides are equal**. Which shape in fig-02 is it, and what is its diagonal property?
practice.answer: It is a rectangle, and its diagonals bisect each other but not at a right angle.
practice.worked_solution: A square is ruled out because all four sides of a square are equal. In the rectangle, only opposite sides are equal, and its diagonals bisect each other but do not meet at a right angle.

practice.prompt: From fig-03, which shape has **no line of symmetry** and a diagonal that divides it into **two unequal triangles**? How many pairs of parallel sides does it have?
practice.answer: A trapezium; it has only one pair of parallel sides.
practice.worked_solution: The trapezium has no line of symmetry, its diagonal divides it into two unequal triangles, and only one pair of its sides is parallel.

practice.prompt: A dodecagon produces 10 triangles and a heptagon produces 5. Write the number sentence for each, then find how many more triangles the dodecagon produces.
practice.answer: $12 - 2 = 10$ and $7 - 2 = 5$, so the dodecagon produces 5 more triangles.
practice.worked_solution: Dodecagon: $n - 2 = 12 - 2 = 10$. Heptagon: $n - 2 = 7 - 2 = 5$. Difference: $10 - 5 = 5$ more triangles.

blocks.text:
A circle is a plane shape with no corners: every point on its boundary is the same distance from its centre. The curved line that forms the round boundary of the circle is its **circumference**. fig-04 shows two labelled circles so you can see each part sitting on a real circle.

- The **centre** is the point in the middle of the circle.
- The **radius** (plural *radii*) is any straight line joining the centre to the circumference. In the second circle of fig-04 a radius is drawn from the centre out to the circumference, and the right-hand bounding line of the sector below is also a radius.
- A **chord** is any straight line joining two points on the circumference. The second circle in fig-04 has a chord drawn near the top.
- The **diameter** is any chord that passes through the centre of the circle. In the first circle of fig-04 the diameter is drawn straight across through the centre. Because it goes through the centre, it is the longest chord a circle can have, and it is twice as long as the radius.
- An **arc** is a curved part of the circumference. In the first circle of fig-04 a part of the circumference is marked and named the arc.

The figure also shows three more parts:
- A **segment** is the region of the circle cut off by a chord — the shaded part above the chord in the second circle.
- A **sector** is the region bounded by two radii and the arc between them — the shaded part below in the second circle, whose two straight sides are both radii.
- A **tangent** is a straight line that touches the circle at exactly one point, as shown touching the right side of the second circle.

sections.title: Finding the Perimeter of a Shape

blocks.text:
**Perimeter** is the total distance round the outside of a shape. To find it, you add up the lengths of all the sides. So the first job is always to know how many sides your shape has and whether those sides are equal.

Some shapes are *regular* — every side has the same length. For a regular polygon with $n$ equal sides each of length $s$, the perimeter is

$$P = n \times s$$

because you simply add the same side length $n$ times. A square, for example, has 4 equal sides, so its perimeter is $4L$ where $L$ is one side. A regular hexagon has 6 equal sides, so its perimeter is $6 \times s$.

A **rectangle** has two long sides and two short sides. The long side is its **length** and the short side its **breadth**. Opposite sides are equal, so the perimeter is

$$P = \text{length} + \text{breadth} + \text{length} + \text{breadth} = 2(\text{length} + \text{breadth})$$

A **trapezium** is a four-sided shape with just two opposite sides parallel, and its sides are usually all different. So its perimeter is simply the sum of its four sides $a$, $b$, $c$ and $d$:

$$P = a + b + c + d$$

A **parallelogram** is a four-sided shape whose opposite sides are both parallel *and* equal. Calling the two horizontal sides $a$ and the two slanted sides $b$, its perimeter is

$$P = a + a + b + b = 2(a + b)$$

A **circle** has no straight sides, so we use a special name for its perimeter: the **circumference**. It is found using the radius $r$ (the distance from the centre to the edge) or the diameter $d$ (twice the radius):

$$C = 2\pi r \qquad\text{or}\qquad C = \pi d$$

Since $d = 2r$, both formulae give the same answer. In many questions you will be told to use $\pi = \frac{22}{7}$ or $\pi = 3.14$ — check which value you are given and use it.

Sometimes the shape is only part of a circle, such as a quarter circle. Then you find a fraction of the circumference — a quarter circle has $\frac{1}{4} \times 2\pi r$ as its curved edge — and add that to the straight sides.

**Example 1 — Square.** Find the perimeter of a square with side 15 cm.

A square has 4 equal sides, so

$$P = 4L = 4 \times 15 = 60\ \text{cm}$$

The perimeter is **60 cm**.

**Example 2 — Rectangle.** Find the perimeter of a rectangle of length 10 cm and breadth 7 cm.

$$P = 2(\text{length} + \text{breadth}) = 2(10 + 7) = 2(17) = 34\ \text{cm}$$

The perimeter is **34 cm**.

**Example 3 — Rectangle, finding the breadth.** The perimeter of a rectangle is 60 cm and its length is 17 cm. Find its breadth.

Write $P = 2(\text{length} + \text{breadth})$, let the breadth be $b$:

$$60 = 2(17 + b) = 34 + 2b$$

Collect the like terms:

$$60 - 34 = 2b \qquad \Rightarrow \qquad 26 = 2b$$

Divide both sides by 2:

$$b = \frac{26}{2} = 13\ \text{cm}$$

The breadth is **13 cm**.

**Example 4 — Trapezium.** Find the perimeter of a trapezium with sides 11 cm, 9 cm, 5 cm and 4 cm.

$$P = a + b + c + d = 11 + 9 + 5 + 4 = 29\ \text{cm}$$

The perimeter is **29 cm**.

**Example 5 — Parallelogram.** Find the perimeter of a parallelogram whose base is 9 cm and whose slanted sides are 5 cm.

The opposite sides are equal, so there are two sides of 9 cm and two of 5 cm:

$$P = 2(9 + 5) = 2(14) = 28\ \text{cm}$$

The perimeter is **28 cm**.

**Example 6 — Regular hexagon.** Find the perimeter of a regular hexagon with sides 5.2 cm.

A hexagon has 6 sides, all equal:

$$P = 6 \times 5.2 = 31.2\ \text{cm}$$

The perimeter is **31.2 cm**.

**Example 7 — Circle.** Calculate the circumference of a circle of radius 7 cm, using $\pi = \frac{22}{7}$.

$$C = 2\pi r = 2 \times \frac{22}{7} \times 7$$

The 7 cancels with the 7 in the denominator:

$$C = 2 \times 22 = 44\ \text{cm}$$

The circumference is **44 cm**. Checked the other way, with the diameter $d = 2 \times 7 = 14$ cm:

$$C = \pi d = \frac{22}{7} \times 14 = 22 \times 2 = 44\ \text{cm}$$

Both give the same result.

**Example 8 — Circle, finding the radius.** The circumference of a circle is 440 cm. Find its radius, using $\pi = \frac{22}{7}$.

$$C = 2\pi r \qquad \Rightarrow \qquad 440 = 2 \times \frac{22}{7} \times r = \frac{44r}{7}$$

Cross-multiply:

$$440 \times 7 = 44r \qquad \Rightarrow \qquad 3080 = 44r$$

Divide both sides by 44:

$$r = \frac{3080}{44} = 70\ \text{cm}$$

The radius is **70 cm**.

**Example 9 — Rope wound round a cylinder.** A rope is wound 50 times round a cylinder of radius 25 cm. How long is the rope? Use $\pi = 3.14$.

One turn of the rope goes round the circle once, so one turn equals the circumference:

$$C = 2\pi r = 2 \times 3.14 \times 25 = 157\ \text{cm}$$

Fifty turns give:

$$157 \times 50 = 7850\ \text{cm}$$

The rope is **7850 cm** long.

**Example 10 — A quarter circle.** Calculate the perimeter of a quarter circle whose two straight sides are each 4.9 cm. Use $\pi = \frac{22}{7}$.

The curved edge is one quarter of the full circumference, so its length is

$$\frac{1}{4} \times 2\pi r = \frac{1}{4} \times 2 \times \frac{22}{7} \times 4.9$$

Here the radius $r = 4.9$ cm. Simplifying:

$$\frac{1}{4} \times \frac{44}{7} \times 4.9 = \frac{11}{7} \times 4.9 = 11 \times 0.7 = 7.7\ \text{cm}$$

The perimeter is the curved edge plus the two straight sides:

$$P = 4.9 + 4.9 + 7.7 = 17.5\ \text{cm}$$

The perimeter is **17.5 cm**.

practice.prompt: Find the perimeter of a square whose side is 8 cm.
practice.worked_solution: A square has 4 equal sides, so $P = 4 \times 8 = 32$ cm.

practice.prompt: Find the perimeter of a rectangle of length 7 cm and breadth 4 cm.
practice.worked_solution: $P = 2(\text{length} + \text{breadth}) = 2(7 + 4) = 22$ cm.

practice.prompt: What is the perimeter of a regular pentagon whose side is 5 cm? (A pentagon has 5 sides.)
practice.worked_solution: A regular pentagon has 5 equal sides, so $P = 5 \times 5 = 25$ cm.

practice.prompt: Find the perimeter of a parallelogram whose base is 6 cm and whose slanted sides are 5 cm.
practice.worked_solution: There are two sides of 6 cm and two of 5 cm, so $P = 2(6 + 5) = 22$ cm.

practice.prompt: The circumference of a circle is 22 cm. Find its radius, using $\pi = \frac{22}{7}$.
practice.worked_solution: $C = 2\pi r$, so $22 = 2 \times \frac{22}{7} \times r = \frac{44r}{7}$. Cross-multiplying: $22 \times 7 = 44r \Rightarrow 154 = 44r$, so $r = \frac{154}{44} = 3.5$ cm.

practice.prompt: A rectangle is such that its length is twice its breadth. If the breadth is $d$, find, in terms of $d$, the total length of the sides of the rectangle.
practice.worked_solution: Breadth is $d$ and length is twice the breadth, so length $= 2d$. The perimeter is $2(\text{length} + \text{breadth}) = 2(2d + d) = 2(3d) = 6d$.

practice.prompt: Find the perimeter of a regular hexagon whose side is 5 cm. (A hexagon has 6 sides.)
practice.worked_solution: A regular hexagon has 6 equal sides, so $P = 6 \times 5 = 30$ cm.

practice.prompt: The perimeter of a rectangle is 34 cm and its length is 12 cm. Find its breadth.
practice.worked_solution: $P = 2(\text{length} + b)$, so $34 = 2(12 + b) = 24 + 2b$. Then $34 - 24 = 2b \Rightarrow 10 = 2b$, so $b = 5$ cm.

sections.title: Plane Shapes: Their Types, Properties, Similarities and Differences

blocks.text: Plane shapes are shapes that lie flat on a surface, so they are also called two-dimensional shapes (2-D shapes). The plane shapes you will meet include the triangle, the square, the rectangle, the parallelogram, the trapezium, the circle and other polygons. A polygon is any closed shape that has three or more straight sides. Let us look at each family of plane shapes, its properties, and how the shapes are similar to or different from one another.

Look at the three triangles in fig-01: the isosceles, the scalene and the equilateral. Their names tell you how their sides compare. - An isosceles triangle has two adjacent sides equal (the two slanted sides carry a single tick each). Its base angles are equal, and it has one line of symmetry. - A scalene triangle has no side equal to another — each side carries a different number of ticks (one, two, three). No angle is equal to another, and it has no line of symmetry. - An equilateral triangle has all three sides equal (a single tick on each side). All three angles are equal, each measuring $60^\circ$, and it has three lines of symmetry. So the key differences come down to how many sides are equal: an equilateral has three equal sides, an isosceles has two, and a scalene has none.

blocks.caption: Isosceles: a single tick on each of the two slanted sides, an arc at each base angle. Scalene: one, two and three ticks on the three sides, an arc at each vertex. Equilateral: a single tick on each of the three sides, an arc at each vertex.

blocks.text: Now compare the square and the rectangle in fig-02. Each has a right-angle mark at every corner, so both have all angles equal, each measuring $90^\circ$, and both have two pairs of parallel sides. The difference lies in the sides. - A square has all four sides equal (a single tick on every side). It has four lines of symmetry, and its diagonals bisect each other at a right angle. - A rectangle has only two opposite sides equal — the two longer sides carry a single tick each and the two shorter sides a double tick each. It has two lines of symmetry, and its diagonals bisect each other but not at a right angle.

blocks.caption: Square: a right-angle mark at each corner, a single tick on each of the four sides. Rectangle: a right-angle mark at each corner, a single tick on each of the two longer sides and a double tick on each of the two shorter sides.

blocks.text: Finally, compare the parallelogram and the trapezium in fig-03. - A parallelogram has two pairs of opposite sides equal and parallel (its two horizontal sides carry a single arrow and its two slanted sides a double arrow). Its opposite angles are equal, it has no line of symmetry, and its diagonals divide it into two equal triangles. - A trapezium has only one pair of parallel sides (the two parallel sides carry a single arrow each, and one diagonal is drawn in). Its opposite angles are not equal, it has no line of symmetry, and its diagonal divides it into two unequal triangles. The great difference between them is the number of parallel sides: a parallelogram has two pairs, a trapezium has only one pair.

blocks.caption: Parallelogram: a single arrow on each of the two horizontal sides, a double arrow on each of the two slanted sides. Trapezium: a single arrow on each of the two parallel sides, and one diagonal drawn in.

blocks.text:
Polygons come in many forms, and each is named by its number of straight sides. The table below lists the common polygons, their number of sides, and how many triangles each can be divided into by drawing diagonals from one vertex to all the non-adjacent vertices.

| Name of polygon | Number of sides | Number of triangles ($n-2$) |
|---|---|---|
| Triangle | 3 | 1 |
| Quadrilateral | 4 | 2 |
| Pentagon | 5 | 3 |
| Hexagon | 6 | 4 |
| Heptagon | 7 | 5 |
| Octagon | 8 | 6 |
| Nonagon | 9 | 7 |
| Decagon | 10 | 8 |
| Hendecagon (or undecagon) | 11 | 9 |
| Dodecagon | 12 | 10 |

The rule that produces the third column is simple: take the number of sides $n$ and subtract $2$. A hexagon has 6 sides, so it divides into $6-2=4$ triangles; a pentagon has 5 sides, so it divides into $5-2=3$ triangles.

Worked example — triangles in a polygon How many triangles can a heptagon be divided into if you draw diagonals from one vertex to all the non-adjacent vertices? Solution. A heptagon has 7 sides. Use the rule: number of triangles $= n-2 = 7-2 = 5$. So a heptagon divides into 5 triangles, which matches the table.

sections.title: Finding the Perimeter of Plane Shapes

blocks.text:
The perimeter of a shape is the distance all the way round it. To find it you simply add the lengths of every side. For a straight-sided shape, this means adding each side once. For a circle, the perimeter has a special name — the circumference — and you find it using the radius (or diameter) and the number π (pi), which is about $\frac{22}{7}$ or 3.14.

Because some shapes have equal sides, you can often write a short formula instead of adding each side separately. Work through the examples below to see how each shape's perimeter is found.

Example 1 — a square. A square has four equal sides. In fig-05 each side is marked $L$ and measures 15cm. Its perimeter is four lengths added together: $$L + L + L + L = 4L$$ $$= 15 + 15 + 15 + 15 = 4(15) = 60\text{cm}.$$ Example 2 — a rectangle. A rectangle has two long sides $L$ and two short sides $b$. In fig-06, $L = 10\text{cm}$ and $b = 7\text{cm}$. Adding all four sides: $$P = L + b + L + b = 2L + 2b = 2(L + b)$$ $$= 2(10 + 7) = 2(17) = 34\text{cm}.$$ Example 3 — a missing side. Sometimes you are given the perimeter and one side and must find the other. Suppose a rectangle has perimeter 60cm and length 17cm (fig-07). Write the perimeter formula and solve for $b$: $$P = 2L + 2b$$ $$60 = 2(17) + 2b$$ $$60 = 34 + 2b$$ Collect like terms: $$60 - 34 = 2b$$ $$2b = 26$$ Divide both sides by 2: $$b = 13\text{cm}.$$

blocks.caption: A rectangle with both long sides marked $L = 17$cm and both short sides marked $b$.
A rectangle with both long sides marked $L$, the top one also 10cm, and both short sides marked $b$, the right-hand one also 7cm.
A square, named *Square* at its left, with all four sides marked twice — $L$ and 15cm.

blocks.text: Example 4 — a trapezium. A trapezium has four sides, usually of different lengths. In fig-08 they are $a = 11\text{cm}$, $b = 9\text{cm}$, $c = 5\text{cm}$ and $d = 4\text{cm}$. The perimeter is all four added: $$P = a + b + c + d$$ $$= 11 + 9 + 5 + 4 = 29\text{cm}.$$ Example 5 — a parallelogram. A parallelogram has opposite sides equal: two of length $a$ and two of length $b$ (fig-09, where $a = 9\text{cm}$ and $b = 5\text{cm}$). So $$P = a + a + b + b = 2a + 2b = 2(a + b)$$ $$= 2(9 + 5) = 2(14) = 28\text{cm}.$$ Example 6 — a regular hexagon. A regular hexagon has six equal sides. In fig-10 each side is 5.2cm, so $$P = 6 \times 5.2 = 31.2\text{cm}.$$

blocks.caption: A regular hexagon, named above the drawing, with each of its six sides marked 5.2cm.

A parallelogram with a single arrow on each of its four sides: the two horizontal ones both lettered $a$, the lower also measured 9cm, and the two slanted ones both lettered $b$, the right-hand one also measured 5cm.
A trapezium with each side lettered and measured: the top $c$, 5cm; the left $b$, 9cm; the right $d$, 4cm; the base $a$, 11cm.

blocks.text: Example 7 — a circle. The perimeter of a circle is its circumference, found with either formula: $$C = 2\pi r \quad\text{or}\quad C = \pi d.$$ In fig-11 the radius is 7cm, using $\pi = \frac{22}{7}$: $$C = 2 \times \frac{22}{7} \times 7 = 2 \times 22 = 44\text{cm}.$$ Using $\pi d$ instead: since $d = 2r = 2 \times 7 = 14\text{cm}$, $$C = \frac{22}{7} \times 14 = 22 \times 2 = 44\text{cm}.$$ Example 8 — a rope wound round a cylinder. One turn round the cylinder is one circumference. With radius 25cm and $\pi = 3.14$, $$C = 2\pi r = 2 \times 3.14 \times 25 = 157\text{cm}.$$ Wound 50 times, the rope's total length is $$157 \times 50 = 7850\text{cm}.$$ Example 9 — the radius from the circumference. If the circumference is 440cm, find $r$ ($\pi = \frac{22}{7}$): $$440 = 2\pi r = 2 \times \frac{22}{7} \times r = \frac{44r}{7}.$$ Cross-multiply: $$440 \times 7 = 44r \quad\Rightarrow\quad 3080 = 44r.$$ Divide both sides by 44: $$r = \frac{3080}{44} = 70\text{cm}.$$

blocks.caption: A circle with a radius drawn from the centre to the right of the circumference, marked 7cm.

blocks.text: Example 10 — a quarter circle. The shape in fig-14 is made of two straight sides of 4.9cm each and a curved part that is one quarter of a full circle. Its perimeter is the two straight sides plus that curved part. First find the curved part. It is $\frac{1}{4}$ of a full circumference: $$\frac{1}{4} \times 2\pi r = \frac{1}{4} \times 2 \times \frac{22}{7} \times 4.9$$ $$= \frac{1}{4} \times \frac{44}{7} \times 4.9 = \frac{11}{7} \times \frac{49}{10}$$ $$= \frac{11 \times 7}{10} = \frac{77}{10} = 7.7\text{cm}.$$ Now add the straight sides and the curved part: $$P = 4.9 + 4.9 + 7.7 = 17.5\text{cm}.$$

sections.title: Plane Shapes: Types, Properties, Similarities and Differences

blocks.text: Plane shapes lie flat on a surface, so they are also called **two-dimensional (2-D) shapes**. Common plane shapes include the triangle, square, rectangle, parallelogram, trapezium, circle and other polygons. A **polygon** is any closed shape with three or more straight sides. Use fig-01, fig-02 and fig-03 to compare the families below.

blocks.caption: Parallelogram: a single arrow on each of the two horizontal sides, a double arrow on each of the two slanted sides. Trapezium: a single arrow on each of the two parallel sides, and one diagonal drawn in.

Square: a right-angle mark at each corner, a single tick on each of the four sides. Rectangle: a right-angle mark at each corner, a single tick on each of the two longer sides and a double tick on each of the two shorter sides.

Isosceles: a single tick on each of the two slanted sides, an arc at each base angle. Scalene: one, two and three ticks on the three sides, an arc at each vertex. Equilateral: a single tick on each of the three sides, an arc at each vertex.

blocks.text:
**fig-01 — Triangles**

- **Isosceles triangle:** two adjacent sides are equal; the base angles are equal; one line of symmetry.
- **Scalene triangle:** no side is equal to another; no angle is equal to another; no line of symmetry.
- **Equilateral triangle:** all three sides are equal; all three angles are equal, each $60^\circ$; three lines of symmetry.

The key difference is the number of equal sides: an equilateral triangle has three, an isosceles triangle has two, and a scalene triangle has none.

**fig-02 — Squares and Rectangles**

Both shapes have **two pairs of parallel sides** and **all angles equal**, each $90^\circ$.

- **Square:** all four sides equal; four lines of symmetry; diagonals bisect each other at a right angle.
- **Rectangle:** opposite sides are equal in pairs (the two longer sides match and the two shorter sides match), but the four sides are not all equal; two lines of symmetry; diagonals bisect each other but not at a right angle.

**fig-03 — Parallelogram and Trapezium**

- **Parallelogram:** two pairs of opposite sides are equal and parallel; opposite angles are equal; no line of symmetry; the diagonals divide it into two equal triangles.
- **Trapezium:** only one pair of sides is parallel; opposite angles are not equal; no line of symmetry; the diagonal divides it into two unequal triangles.

The big difference is the number of parallel sides: a parallelogram has two pairs, while a trapezium has only one pair.

**Polygons and their names**

A polygon is named by its number of straight sides. Drawing diagonals from one vertex to all the non-adjacent vertices divides an $n$-sided polygon into $n-2$ triangles.

| Name of polygon | Number of sides | Number of triangles ($n-2$) |
|---|---|---|
| Triangle | 3 | 1 |
| Quadrilateral | 4 | 2 |
| Pentagon | 5 | 3 |
| Hexagon | 6 | 4 |
| Heptagon | 7 | 5 |
| Octagon | 8 | 6 |
| Nonagon | 9 | 7 |
| Decagon | 10 | 8 |
| Hendecagon (or undecagon) | 11 | 9 |
| Dodecagon | 12 | 10 |

**Worked example — using the rule in reverse**

A polygon forms 8 triangles when diagonals are drawn from one vertex to all non-adjacent vertices. Which polygon is it?

**Solution.** Here triangles $= n-2=8$, so $n=10$. A polygon with 10 sides is a **decagon**.

practice.prompt: A polygon forms 9 triangles when diagonals are drawn from one vertex to all the non-adjacent vertices. How many sides does it have, and what is it called?
practice.answer: 11 sides; it is a hendecagon (or undecagon).
practice.worked_solution: $n-2=9$, so $n=11$. An 11-sided polygon is a hendecagon (or undecagon).

practice.prompt: State one property that a square and a rectangle share, and state the side property that separates them.
practice.answer: Both have two pairs of parallel sides and all four angles equal, each $90^\circ$. The difference is in the sides: a square has all four sides equal, while a rectangle has opposite sides equal in pairs, so its four sides are not all equal.
practice.worked_solution: A square and a rectangle share two pairs of parallel sides and four right angles. They differ because the square has all four sides equal, while the rectangle does not.

practice.prompt: A quadrilateral has exactly one pair of parallel sides, no line of symmetry, and its diagonal divides it into two unequal triangles. Name the quadrilateral.
An unknown quadrilateral has opposite angles equal and its diagonals divide it into two equal triangles. Could it be a trapezium? Explain your answer.
practice.answer: No. Equal opposite angles and diagonals dividing the shape into equal triangles are properties of a parallelogram, not a trapezium. A trapezium has only one pair of parallel sides, opposite angles are not equal, and its diagonal divides it into two unequal triangles.
practice.worked_solution: The described properties match the parallelogram row: two pairs of equal and parallel sides, opposite angles equal, and diagonals dividing it into equal triangles. A trapezium has only one pair of parallel sides.

practice.prompt: Which polygon produces twice as many triangles as a pentagon when diagonals are drawn from one vertex? Show the rule you used.
practice.worked_solution: Pentagon: $5-2=3$; twice is $6$. For an octagon: $8-2=6$, so the octagon produces 6 triangles, twice the pentagon's 3.

blocks.text:
A circle is a plane shape with no corners: every point on its boundary is the same distance from its centre. The curved line that forms the round boundary of the circle is its **circumference**. fig-04 shows two labelled circles so you can see each part sitting on a real circle.

- The **centre** is the point in the middle of the circle.
- The **radius** (plural *radii*) is any straight line joining the centre to the circumference. In the second circle of fig-04 a radius is drawn from the centre out to the circumference, and the right-hand bounding line of the sector below is also a radius.
- A **chord** is any straight line joining two points on the circumference. The second circle in fig-04 has a chord drawn near the top.
- The **diameter** is any chord that passes through the centre of the circle. In the first circle of fig-04 the diameter is drawn straight across through the centre. Because it goes through the centre, it is the longest chord a circle can have, and it is twice as long as the radius.
- An **arc** is a curved part of the circumference. In the first circle of fig-04 a part of the circumference is marked and named the arc.

The figure also shows three more parts:
- A **segment** is the region of the circle cut off by a chord — the shaded part above the chord in the second circle.
- A **sector** is the region bounded by two radii and the arc between them — the shaded part below in the second circle, whose two straight sides are both radii.
- A **tangent** is a straight line that touches the circle at exactly one point, as shown touching the right side of the second circle.

blocks.caption: Two labelled circles. The first has the diameter drawn across it and a radius from its centre to the circumference, with the arc and the circumference labelled. The second has a chord near the top with the segment above it shaded, a shaded sector below with its right-hand bounding line labelled Radius, and a tangent touching it on the right.

practice.prompt: Name the straight line that joins the centre of a circle to its circumference.
What do we call a chord that passes through the centre of the circle?
A straight line drawn across a circle joining two points on its circumference is called a ______.
The curved part of the circumference between two points on a circle is called an ______.
If a circle has a radius of 5 cm, how long is its diameter?
practice.worked_solution: The diameter is twice the radius, so 2 × 5 cm = 10 cm.

practice.prompt: Which part of a circle is the region bounded by two radii and the arc between them? Which part is the region cut off by a chord?
practice.answer: The region bounded by two radii and the arc between them is a sector; the region cut off by a chord is a segment.

sections.title: Perimeter: the Distance Round a Plane Shape

blocks.text:
**Perimeter** is the distance right round a shape — all the way around its boundary. To find it you add up the lengths of every side that makes that boundary.

Plane shapes often have sides that repeat. A square has four equal sides, so instead of adding the same length four times you can multiply one side by four. A rectangle has two equal long sides and two equal short sides. Because of that, many perimeters have a short, tidy formula. You'll use them here for the **square**, **rectangle**, **trapezium**, **parallelogram**, a **regular polygon** such as a hexagon, and the **circle** — whose perimeter is called its **circumference**.

Always keep the unit of length, such as $\mathrm{cm}$, on your answer.

**Square and rectangle.** Let a square's side be $L$. All four sides equal $L$, so

$$\text{Perimeter of a square} = L + L + L + L = 4L.$$

For a rectangle, let the length be $L$ and the breadth be $b$. A rectangle has two lengths and two breadths, so

$$\text{Perimeter of a rectangle} = L + b + L + b = 2L + 2b = 2(L+b).$$

**Trapezium and parallelogram.** A trapezium's four sides can all be different, so you simply add all four of them. If we call them $a, b, c, d$:

$$\text{Perimeter of a trapezium} = a + b + c + d.$$

A parallelogram has two pairs of equal opposite sides. If the base is $a$ and the slanted side is $b$, then

$$\text{Perimeter of a parallelogram} = a + a + b + b = 2a + 2b = 2(a+b).$$

**Regular polygon.** A *regular* polygon has all its sides equal. A hexagon has six sides, so if each side is $s$, its perimeter is $6s$. In general, for a regular polygon with $n$ sides each of length $s$, the perimeter is $n \times s$.

**Circle.** The perimeter of a circle is called its **circumference**. It is found with

$$\text{Circumference} = 2\pi r = \pi d,$$

where $r$ is the radius and $d$ is the diameter (twice the radius, so $d = 2r$).

**Example 1 — a square.** Calculate the perimeter of a square of side $15\mathrm{cm}$.

Every side is $15\mathrm{cm}$, so use $4L$:

$$P = 4 \times 15\mathrm{cm} = 60\mathrm{cm}.$$

**Example 2 — a rectangle.** Find the perimeter of a rectangle whose length is $10\mathrm{cm}$ and breadth is $7\mathrm{cm}$ (fig-06).

Add each side round the shape:

$$P = L + b + L + b = 10\mathrm{cm} + 7\mathrm{cm} + 10\mathrm{cm} + 7\mathrm{cm}.$$

Group the equal lengths:

$$P = 2(10) + 2(7) = 2(10 + 7) = 2(17) = 34\mathrm{cm}.$$

**Example 3 — working backwards.** The perimeter of a rectangle is $60\mathrm{cm}$ and its length is $17\mathrm{cm}$. Calculate its breadth $b$.

Write the perimeter formula and put in what you know:

$$60\mathrm{cm} = 2(17\mathrm{cm} + b) = 34\mathrm{cm} + 2b.$$

Collect like terms:

$$60\mathrm{cm} - 34\mathrm{cm} = 2b$$

$$2b = 26\mathrm{cm}.$$

Divide both sides by $2$:

$$b = \frac{26\mathrm{cm}}{2} = 13\mathrm{cm}.$$

So the breadth is $\mathbf{13\mathrm{cm}}$.

blocks.caption: A rectangle with both long sides marked $L$, the top one also 10cm, and both short sides marked $b$, the right-hand one also 7cm.

blocks.text:
**Example 4 — a trapezium.** Find the perimeter of the trapezium whose sides are $a = 11\mathrm{cm}$, $b = 9\mathrm{cm}$, $c = 5\mathrm{cm}$ and $d = 4\mathrm{cm}$ (fig-08).

Add all four sides:

$$P = a + b + c + d = 11\mathrm{cm} + 9\mathrm{cm} + 5\mathrm{cm} + 4\mathrm{cm} = 29\mathrm{cm}.$$

**Example 5 — a parallelogram.** Find the perimeter of the parallelogram whose base is $9\mathrm{cm}$ and slanted side is $5\mathrm{cm}$ (fig-09).

A parallelogram has two bases and two slanted sides, so:

$$P = 2(a + b) = 2(9\mathrm{cm} + 5\mathrm{cm}) = 2(14\mathrm{cm}) = 28\mathrm{cm}.$$

**Example 6 — a regular hexagon.** Find the perimeter of a regular hexagon whose sides are each $5.2\mathrm{cm}$ (fig-10).

A hexagon has $6$ equal sides, so multiply one side by $6$:

$$P = 6 \times 5.2\mathrm{cm} = 31.2\mathrm{cm}.$$

blocks.caption: A regular hexagon, named above the drawing, with each of its six sides marked 5.2cm.

A parallelogram with a single arrow on each of its four sides: the two horizontal ones both lettered $a$, the lower also measured 9cm, and the two slanted ones both lettered $b$, the right-hand one also measured 5cm.
A trapezium with each side lettered and measured: the top $c$, 5cm; the left $b$, 9cm; the right $d$, 4cm; the base $a$, 11cm.

blocks.text:
**Example 7 — circumference of a circle.** Calculate the perimeter (circumference) of a circle of radius $7\mathrm{cm}$. Use $\pi = 3\frac{1}{7}$ (fig-11).

Using $2\pi r$:

$$C = 2 \times 3\tfrac{1}{7} \times 7\mathrm{cm} = 2 \times \frac{22}{7} \times 7\mathrm{cm}.$$

The $7$ cancels the $7$ in the denominator:

$$C = 2 \times 22\mathrm{cm} = 44\mathrm{cm}.$$

Using $\pi d$ gives the same answer: since $d = 2r = 14\mathrm{cm}$,

$$C = \frac{22}{7} \times 14\mathrm{cm} = 22 \times 2 = 44\mathrm{cm}.$$

**Example 8 — a rope round a cylinder.** A rope is wound $50$ times round a cylinder of radius $25\mathrm{cm}$. How long is the rope? Use $\pi = 3.14$ (fig-12).

One turn of the rope equals the circumference of the cylinder:

$$C = 2\pi r = 2 \times 3.14 \times 25\mathrm{cm} = 157\mathrm{cm}.$$

Fifty turns give fifty times this:

$$\text{Total} = 157\mathrm{cm} \times 50 = 7850\mathrm{cm}.$$

blocks.caption: An upright cylinder with a rope wound round it, drawn as a series of turns spiralling down the body from the top face to the base.
A circle with a radius drawn from the centre to the right of the circumference, marked 7cm.

blocks.text:
**Example 9 — from circumference to radius.** The circumference of a circle is $440\mathrm{cm}$. Find its radius. Use $\pi = \frac{22}{7}$ (fig-13).

Put the known circumference into the formula $C = 2\pi r$:

$$440\mathrm{cm} = 2 \times \frac{22}{7} \times r.$$

Since $2 \times \frac{22}{7} = \frac{44}{7}$:

$$440\mathrm{cm} = \frac{44r}{7}.$$

Cross-multiply:

$$440 \times 7 = 44r$$

$$3080 = 44r.$$

Divide both sides by $44$:

$$r = \frac{3080}{44} = 70\mathrm{cm}.$$

**Example 10 — a quarter circle.** The shape below is a quarter of a circle: two straight sides of $4.9\mathrm{cm}$ meet at a right angle, and an arc closes them. Calculate its perimeter (fig-14).

First find the length of the curved part. A quarter circle is $\tfrac14$ of a full circumference:

$$\text{Arc} = \frac14 \times 2\pi r = \frac14 \times 2 \times \frac{22}{7} \times 4.9\mathrm{cm}.$$

Simplify step by step:

$$= \frac14 \times \frac{44}{7} \times \frac{49}{10} = \frac{11}{7} \times \frac{49}{10} = \frac{11 \times 7}{10} = \frac{77}{10} = 7.7\mathrm{cm}.$$

The perimeter is the arc plus the two straight sides:

$$P = 4.9\mathrm{cm} + 4.9\mathrm{cm} + 7.7\mathrm{cm} = 17.5\mathrm{cm}.$$

blocks.caption: A quarter circle: an upright side and a base meeting at a right angle, each marked 4.9cm, with an arc closing them from the top of the upright to the end of the base.
A circle with a radius drawn from the centre to the right of the circumference, marked $r$.
A square, named *Square* at its left, with all four sides marked twice — $L$ and 15cm.
A rectangle with both long sides marked $L = 17$cm and both short sides marked $b$.

sections.title: Volume of a cube, a cuboid and a prism

blocks.text:
Volume is the amount of space a shape takes up. For a cuboid — a box with a rectangular base — you find the volume by multiplying the length, the breadth and the height:

$$\text{Volume of a cuboid} = \text{length} \times \text{breadth} \times \text{height} = lbh$$

You can also think of it as the area of the base times the height. Since the base is a rectangle of area $l \times b$, multiplying by the height $h$ gives $lbh$.

A cube is a cuboid whose length, breadth and height are all the same. If each side is $l$, then:

$$\text{Volume of a cube} = l \times l \times l = l^3$$

For a prism — a solid with a constant cross-section — the volume is the area of the base (the end face) times the height:

$$\text{Volume of a prism} = \text{area of base} \times \text{height}$$

You use whichever end face is constant, find its area, then multiply by how far the prism runs back.

**Example 1. Find the volume of a cuboid of length 3 cm, breadth 2 cm and height 8 cm.**

$$\text{Volume} = L \times b \times h$$

Length $= 3\text{ cm}$, breadth $= 2\text{ cm}$, height $= 8\text{ cm}$.

$$\text{Volume} = 3\text{ cm} \times 2\text{ cm} \times 8\text{ cm} = 48\text{ cm}^3$$

So the cuboid holds $48\text{ cm}^3$.

---

**Example 2. The volume of a cuboid is $24\text{ cm}^3$. If its base is 6 cm by 2 cm, find its height.**

$$\text{Volume} = L \times b \times h$$

Length $= 6\text{ cm}$, breadth $= 2\text{ cm}$, height $= h$ (unknown).

$$24\text{ cm}^3 = 6\text{ cm} \times 2\text{ cm} \times h$$

$$24\text{ cm}^3 = 12\text{ cm}^2 \times h$$

Divide both sides by $12\text{ cm}^2$:

$$\frac{24\text{ cm}^3}{12\text{ cm}^2} = \frac{12\text{ cm}^2 \times h}{12\text{ cm}^2}$$

$$2\text{ cm} = h$$

So the height is $2\text{ cm}$.

---

**Example 3. Find the volume of a cube of side 3 cm.**

$$\text{Volume of a cube} = l^3$$

$$V = (3\text{ cm})^3 = 3\text{ cm} \times 3\text{ cm} \times 3\text{ cm} = 27\text{ cm}^3$$

---

**Example 4. Find the volume of the triangular prism**, where the triangular end has a base of 5 m and a height of 3 m, and the prism runs back 10 m.

First find the area of the triangular base:

$$\text{Area of triangle} = \tfrac{1}{2} \times \text{base} \times \text{height} = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 5 \times 3 = 7.5\text{ m}^2$$

Then multiply by the length of the prism (10 m):

$$\text{Volume of prism} = \text{area of base} \times \text{height} = 7.5\text{ m}^2 \times 10\text{ m} = 75\text{ m}^3$$

blocks.caption: A triangular prism lying on its rectangular face. The triangular end has a base of 5 m and a height of 3 m, and the prism runs back 10 m.

sections.title: Volume of a cube, a cuboid and a prism

blocks.text:
Volume is the amount of space a solid takes up. Three simple formulas cover the shapes in this step.

**Cuboid:** A cuboid is a box whose faces are rectangles. Its volume is
Volume = length × breadth × height = lbh
This is the same as area of the base rectangle × height.

**Cube:** A cube is a cuboid whose length, breadth and height are all equal. If one side is l, then
Volume = l × l × l = l³

**Prism:** A prism has the same end face all the way through. Its volume is
Volume = area of the end face × height (the distance the prism runs)

The only tricky part is knowing whether the end-face area has already been found for you. When a question gives the end face as an area — for example “end face 4 cm²” — that number is ready to use. Multiply it by the prism height only; do not halve it or re-find its area. When a question instead gives the base and height of a triangular end, calculate ½ × base × height first, and then multiply by the prism’s height.

**Example 1. Find the volume of a cuboid of length 3 cm, breadth 2 cm and height 8 cm.**

Volume = length × breadth × height
= 3 cm × 2 cm × 8 cm
= 48 cm³

So the cuboid holds 48 cm³.

---

**Example 2. The volume of a cuboid is 24 cm³ and its base is 6 cm by 2 cm. Find its height.**

Let height = h.

24 cm³ = 6 cm × 2 cm × h
24 cm³ = 12 cm² × h

Divide both sides by 12 cm²:

h = 24 cm³ ÷ 12 cm² = 2 cm

So the height is 2 cm.

---

**Example 3. Find the volume of a cube of side 3 cm.**

Volume of a cube = l³
V = 3 cm × 3 cm × 3 cm = 27 cm³

---

**Example 4. A triangular prism has a triangular end with base 5 m and height 3 m, and the prism runs back 10 m. Find its volume.**

First find the area of the triangular end:

Area = ½ × base × height = ½ × 5 m × 3 m = 7.5 m²

Then multiply by the run of the prism:

Volume = area of end face × height = 7.5 m² × 10 m = 75 m³

---

**Example 5. The end face of a prism has area 4 cm², and the prism’s height is 35 cm. Find its volume.**

The end-face area is already given, so go straight to:

Volume = area of end face × height = 4 cm² × 35 cm = 140 cm³

A common slip here is to write ½ × 35 × 4 or to halve the 4 cm². Resist that: 4 cm² is already an area, not a base length, so it must not be halved again.

---

**Example 6. A prism has volume 140 m³ and its end face has area 14 m². Find the prism’s height.**

Volume = area of end face × height, so

height = volume ÷ area of end face = 140 m³ ÷ 14 m² = 10 m

The units also guide you: m³ ÷ m² = m, so the answer is a length, 10 m, not an area. A common mistake is to halve 14 to 7 and divide 140 by 7; the question gives the full end-face area, so use 14 m² directly.

sections.title: Volume of a cube, a cuboid and a prism

blocks.text:
Volume is the amount of space a shape takes up. For a cuboid — a box with a rectangular base — you find the volume by multiplying the length, the breadth and the height:

$$\text{Volume of a cuboid} = \text{length} \times \text{breadth} \times \text{height} = lbh$$

You can also think of it as the area of the base times the height. Since the base is a rectangle of area $l \times b$, multiplying by the height $h$ gives $lbh$.

A cube is a cuboid whose length, breadth and height are all the same. If each side is $l$, then:

$$\text{Volume of a cube} = l \times l \times l = l^3$$

For a prism — a solid with a constant cross-section — the volume is the area of the base (the end face) times the height:

$$\text{Volume of a prism} = \text{area of base} \times \text{height}$$

You use whichever end face is constant, find its area, then multiply by how far the prism runs back.

**Example 1. Find the volume of a cuboid of length 3 cm, breadth 2 cm and height 8 cm.**

$$\text{Volume} = L \times b \times h$$

Length $= 3\text{ cm}$, breadth $= 2\text{ cm}$, height $= 8\text{ cm}$.

$$\text{Volume} = 3\text{ cm} \times 2\text{ cm} \times 8\text{ cm} = 48\text{ cm}^3$$

So the cuboid holds $48\text{ cm}^3$.

---

**Example 2. The volume of a cuboid is $24\text{ cm}^3$. If its base is 6 cm by 2 cm, find its height.**

$$\text{Volume} = L \times b \times h$$

Length $= 6\text{ cm}$, breadth $= 2\text{ cm}$, height $= h$ (unknown).

$$24\text{ cm}^3 = 6\text{ cm} \times 2\text{ cm} \times h$$

$$24\text{ cm}^3 = 12\text{ cm}^2 \times h$$

Divide both sides by $12\text{ cm}^2$:

$$\frac{24\text{ cm}^3}{12\text{ cm}^2} = \frac{12\text{ cm}^2 \times h}{12\text{ cm}^2}$$

$$2\text{ cm} = h$$

So the height is $2\text{ cm}$.

---

**Example 3. Find the volume of a cube of side 3 cm.**

$$\text{Volume of a cube} = l^3$$

$$V = (3\text{ cm})^3 = 3\text{ cm} \times 3\text{ cm} \times 3\text{ cm} = 27\text{ cm}^3$$

---

**Example 4. Find the volume of the triangular prism**, where the triangular end has a base of 5 m and a height of 3 m, and the prism runs back 10 m.

First find the area of the triangular base:

$$\text{Area of triangle} = \tfrac{1}{2} \times \text{base} \times \text{height} = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 5 \times 3 = 7.5\text{ m}^2$$

Then multiply by the length of the prism (10 m):

$$\text{Volume of prism} = \text{area of base} \times \text{height} = 7.5\text{ m}^2 \times 10\text{ m} = 75\text{ m}^3$$

sections.title: Volume of a cube, a cuboid and a prism

blocks.text:
Volume is the amount of space a shape takes up, measured in cubic units. For a cuboid — a box with a rectangular base — you find the volume by multiplying its length, breadth and height:

$$\text{Volume of a cuboid} = \text{length} \times \text{breadth} \times \text{height} = lbh$$

You can also think of it as the area of the base times the height, because the rectangular base has area $l \times b$.

A cube is a cuboid with all three edges equal. If each side is $l$, then:

$$\text{Volume of a cube} = l \times l \times l = l^3$$

For a prism, the two end faces are identical, so the volume is the area of one end face multiplied by the height (the distance between the end faces):

$$\text{Volume of a prism} = \text{area of end face} \times \text{height}$$

**Watch out for a common slip here.** If the end-face area of a prism is already given, do not put the same numbers into $\frac12 \times \text{base} \times \text{height}$ again. The formula $\frac12 bh$ is used only to *find* the area of a triangular end from its triangle dimensions. Once that area is known, skip straight to multiplying it by the prism’s height.

Also keep the units straight. Length is measured in cm, area in $\text{cm}^2$, and volume in $\text{cm}^3$. Since $\text{cm}^2 \times \text{cm} = \text{cm}^3$, a volume should not be left as $\text{cm}^2$.

**Example 1. Volume of a cuboid**

A cuboid is 3 cm long, 2 cm wide and 8 cm high.

$$V = L \times b \times h = 3 \times 2 \times 8 = 48\text{ cm}^3$$

---

**Example 2. Height of a cuboid from its volume**

The volume of a cuboid is $24\text{ cm}^3$ and its base is 6 cm by 2 cm. Find its height.

The area of the base is $6 \times 2 = 12\text{ cm}^2$, so

$$24\text{ cm}^3 = 12\text{ cm}^2 \times h$$

$$h = \frac{24\text{ cm}^3}{12\text{ cm}^2} = 2\text{ cm}$$

---

**Example 3. Volume of a cube**

Find the volume of a cube of side 3 cm.

$$V = l^3 = 3\text{ cm} \times 3\text{ cm} \times 3\text{ cm} = 27\text{ cm}^3$$

---

**Example 4. Volume of a triangular prism when the end-face area is not given**

A triangular prism has a triangular end with base 5 m and height 3 m, and the prism is 10 m long.

First find the area of the triangular end:

$$\text{Area} = \frac12 \times 5 \times 3 = 7.5\text{ m}^2$$

Then multiply by the length of the prism:

$$\text{Volume} = 7.5\text{ m}^2 \times 10\text{ m} = 75\text{ m}^3$$

---

**Example 5. Volume of a prism when the end-face area is already given**

A prism has a triangular end face of area $4\text{ cm}^2$ and a height of 35 cm.

The area has already been worked out, so do not recalculate it with $\frac12 \times 35 \times 4$. Multiply the given area by the height:

$$\text{Volume} = 4\text{ cm}^2 \times 35\text{ cm} = 140\text{ cm}^3$$

Notice the unit is $\text{cm}^3$, not $\text{cm}^2$: area multiplied by length gives a volume.

---

**Example 6. Finding the height of a prism from its volume**

A prism has an end face of area $14\text{ m}^2$ and a volume of $140\text{ m}^3$. Find its height.

$$\text{Volume} = \text{area of end face} \times \text{height}$$

$$140\text{ m}^3 = 14\text{ m}^2 \times h$$

$$h = \frac{140\text{ m}^3}{14\text{ m}^2} = 10\text{ m}$$

\[\text{Volume of a cube}=l \times l \times l=l^3.\]

\[\text{Volume of a prism}=\text{area of the end face} \times \text{length}.\]

**Three habits that prevent the common slips.**

1. **Write down each number before substituting.** Check each number against the question. A common slip is writing 7 for a height that the question gives as 2; copying the number correctly changes \(9 \times 4 \times 2 = 72\) into a wrong answer. Always read the data line one more time.

2. **When one side is missing, divide instead of multiplying.** If \(V = l \times b \times h\) and only \(h\) is missing, the volume \(V\) is not another number to multiply in. The two known sides have already been multiplied to make \(l \times b\). To solve for the missing side, use

\[h = V \div (l \times b).\]

3. **Keep units together.** Lengths measured in centimetres give cubic centimetres, \(\text{cm}^3\). Lengths measured in metres give cubic metres, \(\text{m}^3\). If no length was converted, do not suddenly change the unit in the answer.

**Worked Example 1 — Volume of a cuboid (all three sides given).**

A cuboid is 3 cm long, 2 cm wide and 8 cm high. First write the data:

\(l=3\text{ cm},\quad b=2\text{ cm},\quad h=8\text{ cm}.\)

Then apply the formula:

\[V = l \times b \times h = 3 \times 2 \times 8 = 48.\]

The lengths are in centimetres, so the volume is \(48\text{ cm}^3\).

---

**Worked Example 2 — Finding the height of a cuboid from its volume.**

A cuboid has volume \(24\text{ cm}^3\). Its base is 6 cm by 2 cm. Find its height.

Let the height be \(h\). Since \(V = l \times b \times h\),

\[24 = 6 \times 2 \times h = 12h.\]

Here is the important step: the volume 24 is not to be multiplied by 6 and 2. It is placed on one side of the equation because it is already the product. To remove the factor 12, divide both sides by 12:

\[\frac{24}{12}=h,\qquad h=2.\]

Using units, \(24\text{ cm}^3 \div 12\text{ cm}^2 = 2\text{ cm}\). The height is \(2\text{ cm}\).

---

**Worked Example 3 — Volume of a cube.**

A cube has side 3 cm. Its volume is

\[V = l^3 = (3\text{ cm})^3 = 3 \times 3 \times 3 = 27\text{ cm}^3.\]

---

**Worked Example 4 — Volume of a triangular prism.**

The prism in fig-03 has a triangular end with base 5 m and height 3 m, and the prism runs back 10 m.

First find the area of the triangular end:

\[\text{Area}=\frac{1}{2} \times 5 \times 3 = 7.5\text{ m}^2.\]

Then multiply by the prism length:

\[\text{Volume}=7.5 \times 10 = 75\text{ m}^3.\]

---

**Worked Example 5 — Finding a prism length from its volume.**

A prism has an end-face area of \(14\text{ m}^2\) and a volume of \(140\text{ m}^3\). Find how long the prism is.

Using \(\text{Volume}=\text{area of end face} \times \text{length}\), write

\[140 = 14 \times \text{length}.\]

Divide both sides by 14:

\[\text{length}=\frac{140}{14}=10.\]

The length is \(10\text{ m}\), not \(10\text{ cm}\), because the measurements given were in metres.

sections.title: Volume of a cube, a cuboid and a prism

blocks.text:
Volume is the amount of space a shape takes up. For a cuboid — a box with a rectangular base — you find the volume by multiplying the length, the breadth and the height:

$$\text{Volume of a cuboid} = \text{length} \times \text{breadth} \times \text{height} = lbh$$

You can also think of it as the area of the base times the height. Since the base is a rectangle of area $l \times b$, multiplying by the height $h$ gives $lbh$.

A cube is a cuboid whose length, breadth and height are all the same. If each side is $l$, then:

$$\text{Volume of a cube} = l \times l \times l = l^3$$

For a prism — a solid with a constant cross-section — the volume is the area of the base (the end face) times the height:

$$\text{Volume of a prism} = \text{area of base} \times \text{height}$$

You use whichever end face is constant, find its area, then multiply by how far the prism runs back.

**Example 1. Find the volume of a cuboid of length 3 cm, breadth 2 cm and height 8 cm.**

$$\text{Volume} = L \times b \times h$$

Length $= 3\text{ cm}$, breadth $= 2\text{ cm}$, height $= 8\text{ cm}$.

$$\text{Volume} = 3\text{ cm} \times 2\text{ cm} \times 8\text{ cm} = 48\text{ cm}^3$$

So the cuboid holds $48\text{ cm}^3$.

---

**Example 2. The volume of a cuboid is $24\text{ cm}^3$. If its base is 6 cm by 2 cm, find its height.**

$$\text{Volume} = L \times b \times h$$

Length $= 6\text{ cm}$, breadth $= 2\text{ cm}$, height $= h$ (unknown).

$$24\text{ cm}^3 = 6\text{ cm} \times 2\text{ cm} \times h$$

$$24\text{ cm}^3 = 12\text{ cm}^2 \times h$$

Divide both sides by $12\text{ cm}^2$:

$$\frac{24\text{ cm}^3}{12\text{ cm}^2} = \frac{12\text{ cm}^2 \times h}{12\text{ cm}^2}$$

$$2\text{ cm} = h$$

So the height is $2\text{ cm}$.

---

**Example 3. Find the volume of a cube of side 3 cm.**

$$\text{Volume of a cube} = l^3$$

$$V = (3\text{ cm})^3 = 3\text{ cm} \times 3\text{ cm} \times 3\text{ cm} = 27\text{ cm}^3$$

---

**Example 4. Find the volume of the triangular prism**, where the triangular end has a base of 5 m and a height of 3 m, and the prism runs back 10 m.

First find the area of the triangular base:

$$\text{Area of triangle} = \tfrac{1}{2} \times \text{base} \times \text{height} = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 5 \times 3 = 7.5\text{ m}^2$$

Then multiply by the length of the prism (10 m):

$$\text{Volume of prism} = \text{area of base} \times \text{height} = 7.5\text{ m}^2 \times 10\text{ m} = 75\text{ m}^3$$

sections.title: Volume of a cube, a cuboid and a prism

blocks.text:
Volume is the amount of space a shape takes up. For a cuboid — a box with a rectangular base — you find the volume by multiplying the length, the breadth and the height:

$$\text{Volume of a cuboid} = \text{length} \times \text{breadth} \times \text{height} = lbh$$

You can also think of it as the area of the base times the height. Since the base is a rectangle of area $l \times b$, multiplying by the height $h$ gives $lbh$.

A cube is a cuboid whose length, breadth and height are all the same. If each side is $l$, then:

$$\text{Volume of a cube} = l \times l \times l = l^3$$

For a prism — a solid with a constant cross-section — the volume is the area of the base (the end face) times the height:

$$\text{Volume of a prism} = \text{area of base} \times \text{height}$$

Two habits make these calculations reliable:
- **Multiply in steps.** For $l \times b \times h$, multiply two numbers first, then multiply that result by the third. For example, $9 \times 4 \times 2 = (9 \times 4) \times 2 = 36 \times 2 = 72$.
- **Use the base area if it is already given.** If the area of an end face is stated in square units, do not work it out again or halve it — multiply that area straight by the height.

**Example 1. Find the volume of a cuboid of length 3 cm, breadth 2 cm and height 8 cm.**

Use the formula $V = l \times b \times h$.

Length $= 3\text{ cm}$, breadth $= 2\text{ cm}$, height $= 8\text{ cm}$.

Multiply in steps:

$$3\text{ cm} \times 2\text{ cm} = 6\text{ cm}^2$$

$$6\text{ cm}^2 \times 8\text{ cm} = 48\text{ cm}^3$$

So the cuboid holds $48\text{ cm}^3$.

---

**Example 2. The volume of a cuboid is $24\text{ cm}^3$. If its base is 6 cm by 2 cm, find its height.**

$V = l \times b \times h$, with the height $h$ unknown.

$$24\text{ cm}^3 = 6\text{ cm} \times 2\text{ cm} \times h$$

$$24\text{ cm}^3 = 12\text{ cm}^2 \times h$$

Divide both sides by $12\text{ cm}^2$:

$$h = \frac{24\text{ cm}^3}{12\text{ cm}^2} = 2\text{ cm}$$

---

**Example 3. Find the volume of a cube of side 3 cm.**

For a cube, all three sides are equal, so:

$$V = l^3 = (3\text{ cm})^3 = 3\text{ cm} \times 3\text{ cm} \times 3\text{ cm}$$

Multiply in steps: $3 \times 3 = 9$, then $9 \times 3 = 27$.

$$V = 27\text{ cm}^3$$

---

**Example 4. Find the volume of the triangular prism whose triangular end has base 5 m and height 3 m, and whose length is 10 m.**

The triangular end is the base, so first find its area:

$$\text{Area of triangle} = \tfrac{1}{2} \times \text{base} \times \text{height} = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 5\text{ m} \times 3\text{ m} = 7.5\text{ m}^2$$

Then multiply by the length of the prism:

$$\text{Volume of prism} = \text{area of base} \times \text{length} = 7.5\text{ m}^2 \times 10\text{ m} = 75\text{ m}^3$$

**Checkpoint.** In Example 4, the area of the end face was not given, so we found it first using the triangle-area formula. If the area of an end face *is* already given, go straight to $\text{area of base} \times \text{length}$. For example, an end face of $4\text{ cm}^2$ and a length of $35\text{ cm}$ gives volume $4\text{ cm}^2 \times 35\text{ cm} = 140\text{ cm}^3$ — no halving is needed.

sections.title: Volume of a cube, a cuboid and a prism

blocks.text:
Volume is the amount of space a solid fills. For these three solids the same core idea repeats: **multiply an area by a height or length**.

- **Cuboid** (rectangular box): $V = \text{length} \times \text{breadth} \times \text{height} = lbh$. The base is a rectangle, so its area $l \times b$ times the height $h$ gives the same result.
- **Cube**: every edge is the same length $l$, so $V = l \times l \times l = l^{3}$.
- **Prism**: the end face is constant along the solid, so $V = \text{area of the base} \times \text{height}$, where the height is how far the prism runs back.

Since these formulas are already familiar to you, the main skill to practise is solving backwards: when the volume is given but one dimension is missing, divide the volume by the area you already know.

**Quick revision 1.** A cuboid has length 3 cm, breadth 2 cm and height 8 cm.

$$V = 3 \times 2 \times 8 = 48\text{ cm}^{3}$$

**Quick revision 2.** A cuboid has volume 24 cm³ and its base is 6 cm by 2 cm.

$$24 = 12h \Rightarrow h = 2\text{ cm}$$

**Quick revision 3.** A cube of side 3 cm has volume

$$V = 3^{3} = 27\text{ cm}^{3}$$

**Quick revision 4.** In fig-03, the triangular end has area $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 5 \times 3 = 7.5\text{ m}^{2}$, and the prism runs back 10 m, so

$$V = 7.5 \times 10 = 75\text{ m}^{3}$$

practice.prompt: A cuboid has a square base of side 5 cm and a volume of 250 cm³. What is its height?
practice.worked_solution: Area of the square base $= 5 \times 5 = 25\text{ cm}^{2}$. Since $V = \text{base area} \times h$, we have $250 = 25h$, so $h = 250 \div 25 = 10\text{ cm}$.

practice.prompt: The volume of a cube is 216 cm³. How long is one edge of the cube?
practice.worked_solution: For a cube, $V = l^{3}$. We need $l^{3} = 216$. Since $6 \times 6 \times 6 = 216$, the edge length is $l = 6\text{ cm}$.

practice.prompt: The triangular end of a prism has a base of 6 m and a perpendicular height of 4 m. The volume of the prism is 120 m³. How long is the prism?
practice.worked_solution: Area of the triangular base $= \tfrac{1}{2} \times 6 \times 4 = 12\text{ m}^{2}$. Then $120 = 12 \times \text{length}$, so length $= 120 \div 12 = 10\text{ m}$.

practice.prompt: A cube has edge 3 cm. A second cube has every edge twice as long. How many times as great is the volume of the second cube?
practice.worked_solution: First cube: $3^{3} = 27\text{ cm}^{3}$. Second cube: $6^{3} = 216\text{ cm}^{3}$. Ratio $= 216 \div 27 = 8$. Equivalently, doubling every edge multiplies the volume by $2^{3} = 8$.
